Introduction
介绍
I T CAN BE A HARD WORLD to be soft in—to remove the Teflon we wear amid all the impatience and cynicism around us just to be there for someone who needs our love and support. Qualities like gentleness, patience, warmth, and empathy can be so undervalued in this day and age that when we need to sit down with someone devastated by a loss or turbulent change in their lives, we often feel unsure about what to say or do.
在这个充满急躁和愤世嫉俗的世界里，保持温柔有时并不容易——我们需要卸下伪装的“特氟龙”，才能在需要爱与支持的人身边给予关怀。温柔、耐心、热情和同理心等品质在当今社会常常被低估，以至于当我们需要坐下来陪伴那些因失去亲人或生活剧变而备受打击的人时，我们常常不知所措，不知道该说些什么，该做些什么。
Given how uncomfortable the act of comforting can feel, many people completely avoid getting close to a distressed or grieving person. They either barely acknowledge or say nothing at all about what the person is going through. Others offer cheerful remarks or uplifting platitudes, such as “Something good will come out of this” or “God will show you the way.” Still others drop off food, flowers, or gifts, only to disappear after a week or two. Yet the person in pain can feel as isolated by the smiling well-wishers as by the avoidant ones. Sometimes grieving people find it easier to just hide, thinking that, at least this way, they won’t make others feel bad.
鉴于安慰他人可能会让人感到不自在，许多人会完全避免接近痛苦或悲伤的人。他们要么几乎不理会对方的遭遇，要么干脆对对方的处境只字不提。有些人会说些轻松愉快的话或安慰的话语，比如“一切都会好起来的”或“上帝会指引你”。还有一些人会送来食物、鲜花或礼物，但一两周后就消失得无影无踪。然而，那些面带微笑的好心人和那些避而远之的人一样，都会让痛苦的人感到孤立无援。有时，悲伤的人会觉得躲起来更容易些，他们认为，至少这样就不会让别人感到难过。
But highly comforting people still prevail, albeit quietly in the background and without much fanfare. And they have much to teach those of us who wish to restore the lost art of comforting into our lives.
但善于安慰他人的人依然存在，尽管他们默默无闻，不张扬。对于我们这些希望重拾安慰之道的人来说，他们有很多值得学习的地方。


I N THE FIRST BLEAK MONTHS after my divorce, I returned to my home state of Virginia after five years of following my husband’s career moves to Minnesota and New Jersey. Heartbroken and homesick, traveling with my faithful, adaptable cat, Ivan, I imagined my homecoming would be wonderful and warm, surrounded by welcoming old friends, family, and colleagues.
离婚后最初几个月，我过得异常艰难。五年来，我一直跟随丈夫的职业调动，辗转于明尼苏达州和新泽西州，最终回到了家乡弗吉尼亚州。我心碎不已，思乡之情也难以抑制。旅途中，我带着忠诚而适应力强的猫咪伊万，憧憬着回家后会是温馨美好的景象，身边会有热情的老朋友、家人和同事。
To my surprise and dismay, people were disappointingly unforthcoming. I was not automatically invited to parties, dinners, reunions, and gatherings. I could hardly get folks to commit to a cup of coffee or to stop over to my modest apartment for a pasta salad. So busy with their own families, jobs, problems, and responsibilities, it seemed no one could squeeze me in for some “quality” time. But I was offered plenty of advice, platitudes, opinions, and cheer about how to move forward with my new life. “You’re better off without him.” “You need to find a singles support group.” “Living well is the best revenge.” My Christian friends told me to pray more, and my New Age friends chided me to meditate more. I should practice yoga, read self-help books, open up a savings account, travel, take flute lessons, stop seeking approval from others, tap into my playful inner child. When offered these tips to get over my grief, as if just being handed a brochure about my condition by a hurried doctor, I felt pushed away. Did anyone, besides a therapist or pastor, have the time, let alone the patience and interest, to sit down with me, to talk heart-to-heart? But God forbid anyone spot my neediness, or worse, my loneliness! So, for the purpose of maintaining my reputation as a likable, invitation-worthy person, I hid my hunger for comfort from people. I resorted to holding Ivan in my lap at night, with a box of tissues, popcorn, and Animal Planet on TV.
令我惊讶又沮丧的是，人们的热情程度令人失望。我并没有被主动邀请参加派对、晚宴、同学聚会和各种聚会。我甚至很难说服别人抽出时间喝杯咖啡，或者顺道来我那简朴的公寓吃顿意面沙拉。他们忙于自己的家庭、工作、问题和责任，似乎没有人能挤出时间来和我共度“美好”时光。但我却收到了大量的建议、陈词滥调、意见和鼓励，告诉我该如何开启新生活。“你离开他之后会过得更好。”“你应该加入单身互助小组。”“好好生活就是最好的报复。”我的基督徒朋友劝我多祷告，我的新时代朋友则责备我多冥想。我应该练习瑜伽、阅读自助书籍、开个储蓄账户、去旅行、学习长笛、停止寻求他人的认可，唤醒我内心那个爱玩的小孩。当别人给我提供这些走出悲伤的建议时，我感觉就像匆匆忙忙的医生递给我一份关于我病情的宣传册，却被我拒之门外。除了心理咨询师或牧师，还有谁有时间，更别提有耐心和兴趣，坐下来和我促膝长谈呢？但天哪，千万别让任何人发现我的需要，更别提我的孤独了！所以，为了维持我讨人喜欢、值得邀请的形象，我向人们隐藏了自己对安慰的渴望。我只能在夜里抱着伊万，身边放着一盒纸巾、爆米花，电视上播放着动物星球频道。
One day, Morna, an old friend from Scotland, phoned and asked if she could come visit me soon. She could take a week off from her psychotherapy practice and “really wanted” to see me. We hadn’t met for years, and I had missed her terribly. I was ecstatic, but had to keep my neediness in check. I invited her to come in October, offering my foldout sofa bed and free home-cooked food.
一天，我的老朋友莫娜，一位来自苏格兰的老朋友，打电话问我她能不能尽快来看我。她可以从心理治疗工作中抽出一个星期的时间，而且“非常想”见我。我们已经好几年没见了，我非常想念她。我欣喜若狂，但不得不克制住自己的渴望。我邀请她十月份过来，并提供了我的折叠沙发床和免费的家常菜。
When she arrived at my spruced-up apartment, we immediately opened a bottle of sherry and lit candles to celebrate. She gave me gifts, a beautiful green agate stone and a book of poems, and I entertained her with the latest movies, a fun itinerary of sights to see, and a show-and-tell of the pillows I had made for three chairs. We were off to a good start.
她来到我精心布置的公寓时，我们立刻打开一瓶雪利酒，点燃蜡烛庆祝。她送了我礼物：一块漂亮的绿色玛瑙石和一本诗集；我则为她准备了最新的电影、一份有趣的旅游攻略，还向她展示了我亲手为三把椅子做的靠垫。我们相聚的第一天就非常愉快。
My neediness was kept buttoned-down fairly successfully for the next three days. Morna, with her impeccable Scottish manners and brisk humor, seemed quite happy with my fake-it-to-make-it strategy of performing as a gracious hostess. Certainly, after her effort to travel across the ocean to spend her precious time with me, she deserved the best of me and the best views of Virginia, with a drive through the Blue Ridge Mountains and a stroll in the gardens of Monticello. She gently asked how I was coping with being alone, but I assured her I was learning how to keep positive and busy. She offered me opportunities to open up and talk, but I didn’t dare expose my neediness.
接下来的三天，我成功地压抑住了自己的依赖。莫娜举止优雅，带着苏格兰人特有的风度和幽默感，似乎很满意我这种假装热情好客的策略。毕竟，她不远万里来到我身边，享受宝贵的时光，理应得到我最好的款待，以及弗吉尼亚最美的景色——驱车穿越蓝岭山脉，漫步蒙蒂塞洛花园。她轻声询问我独处时感觉如何，我向她保证，我正在学习如何保持积极乐观，让自己充实起来。她给了我一些倾诉的机会，但我不敢暴露自己的依赖。
Finally, a year’s worth of pent-up grief and despair erupted in my kitchen on Morna’s fourth day with me. Fixing her an omelet and sausages for breakfast, I burned myself and dropped the frying pan full of grease all over the floor. I snapped, threw the spatula against the wall, slammed my fist on the cupboard, kicked sausages across the floor, and yelled a slew of profanities. I crawled down on the floor to wipe up the battered eggs and mess, and collapsed into tears.
终于，一年来积压的悲伤和绝望在莫娜来到我家的第四天，在我的厨房里彻底爆发了。我给她做煎蛋卷和香肠当早餐，结果烫伤了自己，煎锅也掉在了地上，油洒了一地。我彻底崩溃了，把锅铲摔到墙上，一拳砸在橱柜上，把香肠踢得满地都是，还破口大骂。我爬到地上，擦掉溅出的蛋液和残渣，然后瘫倒在地，嚎啕大哭起来。
“I’m such a loser!” I wailed. “I can’t even fry eggs for you!”
“我真是个废物！”我哀嚎道，“我连煎个鸡蛋都做不好！”
Huddled on my knees, sobbing, I hadn’t noticed that Morna had quietly approached me. She sat down on the kitchen floor next to me and softly put her hand on my shoulder.
我蜷缩在地上，哭泣不止，完全没有注意到莫娜悄悄地走到我身边。她在我旁边的厨房地板上坐下，轻轻地把手放在我的肩膀上。
I glanced at her quickly without making eye contact and said, “Now you see what a basket case I really am.”
我迅速地瞥了她一眼，没有和她对视，然后说：“现在你明白我到底是个多么糟糕的人了吧。”
“I see someone who is in pain . . . a lot of pain.”
“我看到有人很痛苦……非常痛苦。”
I wept longer, letting her words sink in. She was right. I felt relief just hearing her say the truth out loud.
我哭了更久，让她的话语在我心中沉淀。她说得对。听到她把真相说出来，我感到如释重负。
“Yes, that’s right. I’ve been really, really hurt. I feel so alone. I am so afraid no one wants to be with me anymore.”
“是的，没错。我真的非常非常伤心。我感到好孤独。我好害怕再也没有人愿意和我在一起了。”
Morna made herself more comfortable on the floor, sitting cross-legged. “I don’t mind listening, if you want to talk about this now.”
莫娜在地板上盘腿坐下，让自己更舒服些。“如果你现在想谈谈这件事，我不介意听。”
I remembered she was a professional counselor and blushed. “You sure you aren’t just playing counselor with me? You’re supposed to be getting a break from listening to people in pain all the time.”
我突然想起她是一位专业心理咨询师，脸红了。“你确定你不是在跟我玩心理咨询师的游戏吗？你不是应该休息一下，不用总是听别人诉苦吗？”
She smiled softly, and paused. “I’m your friend . Why do you think I’m sitting here on the floor with you?”
她温柔地笑了笑，停顿了一下。“我是你的朋友。你以为我为什么会和你一起坐在地板上呢？”
Feeling welcomed to speak from my heart, uncensored, I took the plunge to trust her. The floodgates opened. We sat on the kitchen floor for another hour, until our legs ached, then moved to the sofa and talked nonstop until 3 a.m. In the next day’s storytelling marathon we cried, ranted, laughed, ate chocolates, threw toys for Ivan, and cursed at the lawyers, doctors, creditors, lovers, and in-laws who had screwed us over. By evening, my rip-roaring emotions felt purged well enough to suggest to Morna we go out for sushi.
感觉可以毫无顾忌地敞开心扉，我鼓起勇气信任她。思绪瞬间奔涌而出。我们在厨房地板上又坐了一个小时，直到腿都酸了，然后才移步沙发，一直聊到凌晨三点。第二天，我们继续马拉松式地讲述故事，哭过、发泄过、笑过，吃过巧克力，还把玩具扔给伊万玩，咒骂那些坑害我们的律师、医生、债主、情人以及姻亲。到了晚上，我感觉自己终于平复了情绪，于是提议莫娜带我去吃寿司。
Still, I soaked up some tears with my napkin over our dinner on our last night together, yet felt completely accepted and at ease.
尽管如此，在我们共进晚餐的最后一晚，我还是用餐巾擦去了眼泪，但我感到自己完全被接纳和放松。
In my last few minutes with her at the airport, as she was about to step past the gate for her plane, I repeatedly blurted out, “Morna, I can’t thank you enough.”
在机场和她相处的最后几分钟，当她即将踏出登机口时，我反复脱口而出：“莫娜，我真是太感谢你了。”
She paused and put down her suitcase.
她停顿了一下，放下了行李箱。
I shrugged anxiously, “How can I ever repay you?”
我焦虑地耸了耸肩，“我该如何报答你呢？”
She gave me a long, mighty hug, then looked boldly into my eyes. “You’ve already paid me back. You’ve given me your trust, after all the hurt you’ve been through. You’ve given me more than I ever dreamed of. Thank you. ”
她给了我一个长长的、充满力量的拥抱，然后勇敢地看着我的眼睛。“你已经回报了我。你经历了那么多伤痛，却依然信任我。你给予我的远超我梦寐以求。谢谢你。”
Too moved to speak, I barely nodded and hugged her quickly one last time.
我感动得说不出话来，只是轻轻点了点头，最后一次匆匆拥抱了她。
I watched her disappear into the crowds to board her plane, still filled with the warmth and tenderness she had bestowed upon me. As an ocean of people passed by me, I made my way through the maze of lobbies and escalators to my car.
我目送她消失在熙熙攘攘的人群中，登上飞机，心中依然充满着她给予我的温暖和柔情。人潮涌动，我穿过迷宫般的候机大厅和自动扶梯，走向我的车。
Then, in the parking lot of Dulles Airport at rush hour, with roaring planes coming and going overhead, I paused to marvel at a blazing October sunset. Standing under a wild sky bursting with gold and crimson light, I realized I could bear my raw, unruly grief with acceptance and even love. Though I might never heal completely, as long as I could find comfort with at least one true friend, the beauty of the sky, and one old sweet cat, I was going to be okay.
然后，在杜勒斯机场的停车场，正值高峰期，飞机轰鸣着起降，我停下脚步，惊叹于十月绚烂的日落。站在金红交织的壮丽天空下，我意识到我可以接纳甚至爱自己那原始而难以控制的悲伤。虽然我可能永远无法完全痊愈，但只要我能从至少一个真正的朋友、美丽的天空和一只可爱的老猫身上找到慰藉，我就能好起来。
# ↩

A Rare Skill

一项罕见的技能

Morna’s visit provided me with the comfort I had been craving, but it also left me wondering why comforting people were so hard to find. And even if we do find those who are willing and ready, why is it so hard for people to just sit with someone who is suffering without trying to make their pain go away so they can just “get over it”?
莫娜的来访给了我渴望已久的安慰，但也让我不禁思考，为什么能安慰人的人如此难寻？即便我们找到了愿意且乐意帮忙的人，为什么人们就不能静静地陪伴一个正在受苦的人，而不试图消除他们的痛苦，让他们“好起来”呢？
Further, I knew that providers around me, including psychotherapists, pastoral counselors, nurses, physicians, yoga instructors, and other healers were not paid to simply comfort people like me in the rawest, most acute stages of grieving. Though knowledgeable and well trained, and often warm and caring, these professionals were paid to heal people, change people, treat people, and do this as efficiently as possible—to give us their “bang” for our buck. Of course, especially in America, where health care costs consumers so much of their hard-earned money, professionals were trained to fix us as quickly as possible. Not much time for sitting with us while we have a good cry or stare hopelessly at the walls trying to wrap our overwhelmed minds around scary things like our “future,” or our “recovery,” let alone our sky-high pile of bills. Like many people going through difficult times, I wasn’t quite ready for healing yet—I needed comforting first and foremost. And the lack of available comforters made my grief twice as painful.
此外，我知道我身边的医护人员，包括心理治疗师、牧师、护士、医生、瑜伽教练和其他疗愈人员，他们的职责并非仅仅是安慰像我这样处于最痛苦、最剧烈悲伤阶段的人。尽管他们知识渊博、训练有素，而且通常热情关怀，但这些专业人士的职责是治愈病人、改变病人、治疗病人，并且尽可能高效地完成这一切——让我们觉得物有所值。当然，尤其是在医疗保健费用高昂的美国，专业人士接受的训练是尽快治好我们的病。他们没有多少时间陪伴我们痛哭一场，或者让我们绝望地盯着墙壁，试图理清那些令人恐惧的思绪，比如我们的“未来”或“康复”，更不用说我们堆积如山的账单了。像许多经历困境的人一样，我还没有做好疗愈的准备——我首先需要的是安慰。而缺乏安慰者，让我的悲伤加倍痛苦。
Morna offered me something that few professionals or laypeople are willing or even able to offer: She allowed me to fall apart in her presence. She didn’t judge me, diagnose me, hire me or fire me, fix me, bill me, instruct me, save me, or heal me. She wasn’t trying to be absolutely unconditionally loving or saintly. She wasn’t even trying to make me smile. She just sat with me amid the mess in my kitchen, the mess in my life, and the mess in my heart and allowed me to be in my pain. Unfazed by all this mess, she sat there and held it all together with her mere presence.
莫娜给了我一些专业人士或普通人很少愿意甚至能够给予的东西：她允许我在她面前崩溃。她没有评判我，没有诊断我，没有雇佣我或解雇我，没有纠正我，没有向我收费，没有指导我，没有拯救我，也没有治愈我。她并非试图表现得绝对无条件的爱或圣洁。她甚至没有试图让我微笑。她只是坐在我凌乱的厨房、凌乱的生活和凌乱的内心中，允许我沉浸在痛苦之中。面对这一切混乱，她毫不动摇，仅仅凭借她的存在，就将一切维系在一起。
Presence. Unshakable, steady, tender, and empathic presence. Soft strength. That was comfort. That was Morna’s gift to me.
存在感。坚定不移、沉稳、温柔而又充满同理心的存在感。一种柔和的力量。那就是安慰。那就是莫娜送给我的礼物。
Think about what a cast or a brace does for a broken arm or leg. They hold the broken part of our body in place until that part can get strong and grow back again. They support and hold us together until we can stand up, or walk, or run again. A comforter’s em brace does the same thing, holding us together when we feel broken. A comforter doesn’t need anything from us, not even for us to heal or get better or get well. Something about Morna’s peaceful and gentle acceptance of my vulnerability gave me the chance to em brace the fractured, shadow parts of myself. She saw the good, the bad, and the hidden parts of me. Then, with nothing to hide, nothing to cover up or make up, I said nothing and she said nothing. This nothing moment of sitting on the kitchen floor in the mess changed my life.
想想石膏或支具对骨折的胳膊或腿的作用。它们固定住我们身体的受伤部位，直到它恢复强壮并重新生长。它们支撑着我们，让我们重新站起来、行走或奔跑。安慰者的拥抱也起到同样的作用，在我们感到破碎时将我们紧紧地包裹起来。安慰者不需要我们付出任何东西，甚至不需要我们痊愈、好转或康复。莫娜平和温柔地接纳我的脆弱，让我有机会拥抱自己破碎的、阴暗的一面。她看到了我的优点、缺点和隐藏的部分。然后，没有什么需要隐藏，没有什么需要掩盖或伪装，我什么也没说，她也什么也没说。这短暂的、坐在凌乱的厨房地板上的“无声时刻”改变了我的人生。
# ↩

Writing the Book I Couldn’t Find

写一本我找不到的书

Later, after I’d grown a little stronger, I moved from Virginia to Maine. At first I envisioned Maine as a temporary respite, a place to live for a couple of years while I reinvented my life. Coastal Maine, Vacationland, was safe, rural, and quiet enough for me to heal, away from the din and drama of the bigger cities I had once thrived in as I pushed myself hard for upward mobility, along with my highly ambitious husband. Finally, I could slow down, soften, and find my inner voice, sitting on sun-soaked mossy rocks beside rivers and bays watching blue herons, egrets, and ospreys.
后来，等我身体稍微好转一些后，我从弗吉尼亚搬到了缅因州。起初，我只是把缅因州当作一个暂时的避风港，一个可以让我重新规划人生、住上几年的地方。缅因州沿海地区，这片度假胜地，安全、乡村气息浓厚、宁静祥和，让我得以疗愈身心，远离我曾经为了向上攀升而拼命奋斗的大城市的喧嚣与纷扰。我和我那雄心勃勃的丈夫也曾身处其中。终于，我可以放慢脚步，放松身心，找回内心的声音，坐在阳光普照、长满青苔的河湾边岩石上，观赏苍鹭、白鹭和鹗。
But Maine grew on me, and I’ve stayed here. I made new friends and discovered a genuine, unique community in the town of Yarmouth, where I settled for good. I found peace, my own serene providence on the rocky coast near a colony of blue herons, one of the largest sanctuaries for herons in New England. On some summer mornings, I can see as many as eighteen herons standing still at low tide, silhouetted against the sunrise.
但我渐渐爱上了缅因州，并留了下来。我在雅茅斯镇结识了新朋友，发现了一个真诚而独特的社区，并最终定居于此。我在岩石海岸附近找到了宁静，找到了属于我自己的安宁，那里栖息着一群蓝鹭，是新英格兰地区最大的苍鹭保护区之一。在一些夏日的清晨，我可以看到多达十八只苍鹭在退潮时静静地伫立，在日出的映衬下勾勒出优美的轮廓。
I eventually took a job as a bereavement coordinator for a hospice in 2004. I had previously worked as a rehabilitation counselor at a hospital in Richmond, Virginia, serving cancer patients and their families, as well as rehab programs with Veterans Affairs clients and other groups of people in turbulent stages of their lives. Since 1992, I had specialized in facilitating support groups for issues such as grief and bereavement, coping with chronic illness, job loss, and other kinds of loss, such as loss of a home, or bankruptcy. I enthusiastically launched a popular training course for facilitators of grief support groups in Bridgton, Maine, and later, as a consultant, provided training for support group facilitators throughout Maine.
2004年，我最终在一家临终关怀中心找到了一份丧亲辅导员的工作。此前，我曾在弗吉尼亚州里士满的一家医院担任康复咨询师，为癌症患者及其家属、退伍军人事务部客户以及其他处于人生动荡阶段的人群提供康复服务。自1992年以来，我一直专注于为人们提供互助小组服务，帮助他们应对悲伤和丧亲之痛、慢性疾病、失业以及其他类型的损失，例如失去家园或破产。我曾在缅因州布里奇顿热情地创办了一门广受欢迎的悲伤互助小组辅导员培训课程，后来，作为一名顾问，我为缅因州各地的互助小组辅导员提供培训。
My rehabilitation counseling background had offered rich opportunities to learn the art of comforting with a wide range of groups, but in particular I learned from the group participants themselves who told me what specifically comforted them. I was heartened to realize that what I had felt from Morna’s comfort was very similar to what others had felt when truly comforted. There were common threads of comforting, certain words, actions, and gestures that people cherished from comforters who kindly and patiently stepped into their lives. In dozens and dozens of support groups, people told me the same things about comforters. But why was this practical wisdom about the art of comforting not common knowledge? Even individuals whose professions directly or indirectly seemed to require comforting skills appeared to lack them. Maybe we saw some of them in our health care, pastoral care, and psychiatric services, or in human services and social work fields. Too many experts did not have the basic comforting skills generously exhibited by the ordinary, untrained individuals in the support groups I had facilitated. Why was the world so lacking in people who could just sit gently with us at painful times?
我的康复咨询背景让我有机会在各种各样的群体中学习如何安慰他人，尤其是从小组成员身上，他们告诉我具体是什么让他们感到安慰。我欣慰地发现，我从莫娜那里感受到的安慰，与其他人真正感受到的安慰非常相似。安慰的方式有很多共通之处，人们珍视那些善良而耐心地走进他们生活的安慰者所给予的某些言语、行为和姿态。在几十个互助小组中，人们都向我讲述了同样的感受。但是，为什么这种关于安慰艺术的实用智慧没有成为常识呢？即使是那些职业似乎直接或间接需要安慰技巧的人，似乎也缺乏这种技巧。也许我们在医疗保健、牧灵关怀、精神科服务，或者在社会服务和社会工作领域见过一些这样的人。太多专家并不具备我在互助小组中带领的那些普通人所展现的基本安慰技巧。为什么这个世界如此缺乏能够在我们痛苦的时候温柔地陪伴在我们身边的人？
Many of these humble support group participants possessed a practical wisdom of the heart that some highly educated healers too often lack or gloss over. These experts could provide amazing remedies, therapies, medicines, and sound advice, but were not necessarily comforting in their manner. Sadly, there are even highly lauded spiritual healers who appear unable or unwilling to offer the sort of warm greeting and genuine smile that put others at ease.
许多参与互助小组的谦逊人士都拥有着一种务实的心灵智慧，而这种智慧往往是一些受过高等教育的治疗师所缺乏或忽略的。这些专家或许能够提供神奇的疗法、药物和中肯的建议，但他们的态度未必令人感到舒适。令人遗憾的是，甚至有些备受赞誉的灵性治疗师似乎也无法或不愿给予他人那种温暖的问候和真诚的微笑，从而让人感到放松自在。
As a bereavement consultant and educator, I found plenty of sound, effective resources, courses, and books for understanding grief and loss, for grounding the principles of hospice care, and for facilitating support groups. It surprised me, however, that very little how-to literature for the average, nonprofessional layperson was out there about the art of comforting others in distress. Sure, there were books that showed readers how to comfort themselves , such as the Chicken Soup for the Soul books or the Cup of Comfort series, but I could not put my hands on a practical book about how to comfort others . It seemed to me that what was sorely needed was a book that explicitly and accessibly spelled out what to say and do to comfort people in distress.
作为一名丧亲辅导员和教育工作者，我发现有很多可靠的、有效的资源、课程和书籍，可以帮助人们理解悲伤和失落，奠定临终关怀的原则基础，并促进互助小组的开展。然而，令我惊讶的是，面向普通非专业人士的、关于如何安慰处于痛苦中的人的实用指南却寥寥无几。当然，也有一些书籍教读者如何安慰自己，例如《心灵鸡汤》系列或《一杯安慰》系列，但我却找不到一本关于如何安慰他人的实用书籍。在我看来，人们迫切需要的是一本能够清晰易懂地阐述如何安慰处于痛苦中的人的书籍。
Then, one day, sitting by the Casco Bay, on my favorite mossy spot, gazing in wonder at my beloved blue herons, I had a revelation: I was the one to write the book I couldn’t find. I would share with the world what all the wonderful, grieving folks in those support groups as well as professionals in the front lines who possessed the rare gift of comfort had been teaching me for decades—the language of comforting. After all we had been through and witnessed, I knew that we had a book’s worth of everyday comforting wisdom to offer. And more than anything, we understood how important it was to make this easy, enjoyable, and practical enough for anyone to read, especially busy, often tired, caregivers.
有一天，我坐在卡斯科湾边我最喜欢的苔藓地上，凝望着我挚爱的蓝鹭，心中充满惊奇，突然顿悟：我就是那个能写出我一直找不到的那本书的人。我要把那些在互助小组里经历丧亲之痛的人们，以及那些身处一线、拥有抚慰人心这种罕见天赋的专业人士，几十年来一直在教给我的东西——抚慰的语言——分享给全世界。经历了这一切，见证了这一切，我知道我们积累了足够写成一本书的日常抚慰智慧。更重要的是，我们明白，让这本书足够简单易懂、轻松愉快、实用易读，让每个人都能读懂，尤其是那些忙碌疲惫的照护者。
Welcome, and please join me and the comforting professionals and laypeople who have so graciously offered their wisdom in these pages.
欢迎各位读者，请与我以及在这几页书中慷慨分享智慧的专业人士和普通读者一起，共同阅读这篇令人感到慰藉的文章。

What Makes People Comforting?

The Language of Comforting

安慰的语言

A CCORDING TO the Oxford Dictionary, the word comfort originates from the Old French comfort, meaning “to be strong with.” It’s heartening to notice how this definition emphasizes being strong with, rather than being strong for. Being strong with someone means creating a sanctuary for someone in pain, a respite from the busy, indifferent world around us, just sitting down, listening, and allowing the person to acknowledge his or her pain.
根据牛津词典，“comfort”（安慰）一词源于古法语“comfort”，意为“与……同在”。令人欣慰的是，这个定义强调的是“与……同在”，而非“替……代劳”。与他人同在意味着为痛苦之人创造一个避风港，让他们暂时远离周围喧嚣冷漠的世界，只需静静地坐下来，倾听，允许他们正视自己的痛苦。
I believe that the reason many of us feel uncomfortable in the role of comforters is because the act of comforting tends to go against our common societal approaches to helping each other. We Americans especially value solution-focused, goal-oriented, and fast, efficient methods for offering assistance to others. We like our efforts to work , to “fix it” in a time-measured manner. We think that helping someone in pain means helping them “get over” the problem—and fast. But with comforting, communication can be slow, uneven, unpredictable, and confusing. As such, we comforters need to “be strong with” the person experiencing distress, accepting with them their uncertainty, a process that requires great patience and calm steadiness.
我认为，我们很多人之所以对安慰者的角色感到不自在，是因为安慰这种行为往往与我们社会普遍的互助方式相悖。我们美国人尤其重视以解决问题为导向、目标明确、快速高效的方式来帮助他人。我们希望自己的努力能够奏效，能够在规定的时间内“解决问题”。我们认为，帮助痛苦的人意味着帮助他们“克服”问题——而且要快。但是，在安慰的过程中，沟通可能会变得缓慢、不顺畅、难以预测，甚至令人困惑。因此，我们这些安慰者需要“坚定地支持”正在经历痛苦的人，接纳他们的不确定感，而这需要极大的耐心和沉着冷静。
We are far less comfortable being in a receptive, open, listening role—which is just what people in distress need most. In learning the language of comforting, we might imagine that we are learning the language of a whole different culture, of a foreign land where the customs differ significantly from what we have been socialized to do.
我们不太习惯扮演一个接纳、开放、倾听的角色——而这恰恰是身处困境的人们最需要的。在学习安慰的语言时，我们可能会觉得自己在学习一种截然不同的文化语言，一个与我们从小接受的社会化教育大相径庭的异国他乡的语言。
On the following pages are some major contrasts between the messages our mainstream culture tends to believe are helpful and what we in the world of comforting have found to be actually helpful.
接下来的几页将对比我们主流文化中人们认为有帮助的信息与我们这些在抚慰人心的世界里发现的真正有帮助的信息之间的一些主要差异。

In the Presence of a Comforting Person

在一位安慰者的陪伴下

Take a moment and remember your response to being with a comforting person. What was it about their presence that heartened you, made you feel lighter? It might have just been a reassuring smile, or a hug. It might have been some kind words, or a generous act that went beyond the “call of duty.” It might even have been someone simply stopping to help when we needed directions. One of the best ways to understand how to be truly comforting is to review our own encounters with comforting people and notice how they comforted us.
花点时间回想一下，你和一位让你感到安慰的人在一起时的感受。他们的存在究竟有什么让你感到温暖，让你轻松许多？也许只是一个令人安心的微笑，或者一个温暖的拥抱。也许是几句温暖的话语，或者一个超越职责范围的慷慨举动。甚至可能只是在我们需要指路时，有人停下来帮助我们。想要真正理解如何去安慰别人，最好的方法之一就是回顾我们自己与那些给予我们安慰的人的相遇，并留意他们是如何安慰我们的。
For many years, in support groups I’ve facilitated or participated in, I have heard the same words used to describe what it feels like to be effectively comforted. Following are the most common responses.
多年来，在我主持或参与的互助小组中，我经常听到人们用同样的词语来描述被有效安慰的感觉。以下是最常见的几种表达方式。
# ↩

UNIVERSAL RESPONSES TO BEING WITH COMFORTING PEOPLE

与令人感到安慰的人在一起时的普遍反应

Relief
“I felt more normal.”
“I felt lighter, less burdened.”
解脱id_00001}}
“我感觉更正常了。”id_00003}}“我感觉轻松了，负担减轻了。”
One woman in a support group for breast cancer survivors, struggling with the double whammy of keeping up her chemo treatments and facing the foreclosure of her home, told us how she was comforted by a complete stranger.
一位乳腺癌幸存者互助小组的成员告诉我们，她正承受着化疗和房屋被取消抵押赎回权的双重打击，一位完全陌生的人安慰了她。
“She was an accounting clerk at the hospital, and I was crying hysterically over a bill I couldn’t pay, sitting at her cubicle. She listened like she really cared for a few minutes, and handed me a tissue. I said I couldn’t even concentrate on reading the forms I had to sign. Then she smiled and told me that was why she kept a box of tissues at this table, which made me laugh. She added that I was handling my situation as well as anyone she’d known. It was as if she was saying, ‘Welcome to the club.’ Believe it or not, I settled down quickly after that and managed to fill out the form. The feeling I got from this wonderful person was a sense of being normal, accepted—and this gave me some relief. I felt lighter, less burdened.”
“她是医院的会计，当时我坐在她的隔间里，因为付不起账单而歇斯底里地哭泣。她认真地听了我几分钟，然后递给我一张纸巾。我说我根本没法集中精力看要签的表格。她笑着告诉我，这就是为什么她在这张桌子上放了一盒纸巾，这让我笑了。她还说，我处理得比她认识的任何人都好。就好像她在说，‘欢迎加入我们’。信不信由你，在那之后我很快就平静下来，顺利地填完了表格。这位好心人让我感到自己很正常，被接纳——这让我如释重负。我感觉轻松多了，压力也减轻了。”

“Heard,” Validated

“我的担忧和感受很重要。”

“Things couldn’t have been more depressing. Everyone I knew had tried to talk me out of how bad I was feeling, though I knew I was more exhausted than I’d ever been. My worries and feelings mattered. Thankfully, he did some follow-up lab work, because it turned out I had diabetes.”

In a support group for people who suffer from anxiety and panic disorder, Jim shared this story about facing his fear of public speaking, and how his sense of connection with his colleagues helped him get through the stage fright.
在一个为焦虑症和恐慌症患者提供的互助小组中，吉姆分享了他克服对公开演讲的恐惧的故事，以及他与同事之间的联系如何帮助他克服了怯场。
“I was freaking out, because I had to give a speech at our annual meeting. I’m petrified of public speaking, and thought I was going to faint! I felt I belonged there in that room with everyone, as they smiled warmly at me. I felt safe with them, and realized this speech wasn’t the end of the world. Then I gave a pretty good talk after all!”
“我当时紧张得要命，因为我要在年会上发言。我超级害怕公开演讲，感觉自己都要晕过去了！在我发言之前，我的同事，也是发言者之一，转向我，向大家介绍了我。我完全没想到他会这么做。他向在场的听众说了许多关于我的好话，赞扬了我的敬业精神和团队精神。这让我一下子放松了下来，就像破冰一样。大家对我微笑，我感觉自己融入了这个房间，和每个人都在一起。和他们在一起，我感到很安心，也意识到这次演讲并不是世界末日。结果，我的演讲还不错！”

After her sister’s death, a woman in a grief support group warmly recounted a touching story about a thoughtful gift made for her by her nephew.

I was so touched by his thoughtfulness. I felt softer, so special to him. It seemed he knew what was in my soul, just by the particular songs he chose.”
“卡伦去世后的头几个月，我侄子鲍勃为我做了一件既贴心又美好的事。他给我做了一张CD，里面都是我最喜欢的音乐剧里的歌曲。他的这份心意让我非常感动。我感觉自己在他心中变得如此特别，内心也变得柔软起来。他挑选的歌曲似乎都了解我的内心世界。”

It’s amazing what showing respect for someone’s time and effort will do. Dan had been in a support group for job seekers, and spoke about how employers at his interviews had affected his self-esteem.

They were polite and patient and asked really intelligent questions, as if they expected their candidates to be knowledgeable. This made me feel worthy of their time, and encouraged me to be more confident about my qualifications. Also, whether or not I got the job, just the way they treated me gave me back my dignity. It turns out, however, I did get that job, and I still feel valued there.”
“过去一个月我参加了十二次面试，但进展甚微。说实话，我对这些工作都没什么好感，因为没有一个雇主真正重视我，更别提像样的面试了。他们催促我，显得心不在焉，跟我说话就像自动语音推销一样。这让我感觉很没尊严，自信心也受到了打击。最后，我终于遇到了一个非常专业的面试小组，虽然我有点紧张，但他们给了我充足的时间回答问题。他们很有礼貌，也很有耐心，问的问题也很有深度，仿佛他们期望应聘者具备相应的知识储备。这让我觉得自己值得他们花时间，也让我对自己更有信心。而且，不管我最终是否得到了这份工作，他们对待我的方式都让我重拾了尊严。结果，我最终得到了那份工作，而且我仍然觉得在那里很受重视。”

This woman in a caregiver support group admitted how lost she felt when she first heard of her mother’s diagnosis. But with one twenty-minute phone call on a hotline with a well-trained volunteer, things began to get clear.
这位参加照护者互助小组的女士坦言，当她第一次听到母亲的诊断结果时，感到多么茫然无措。但通过热线电话与一位训练有素的志愿者进行了一次20分钟的通话后，一切开始变得清晰起来。

Later in the phone call, the worker was able to reflect back to me what my concerns were, showing me she had really followed me, instead of telling me what to do. This helped to clarify my feelings, as well as to make some priorities about how to take care of myself. I could see the next step to take—to go to a caregiver support group.”
“当我第一次得知母亲患有阿尔茨海默病时，我完全不知所措。我拨打了阿尔茨海默病协会的热线电话，接线员认真倾听了我的问题。她让我意识到，我之前没有采取更多措施，这让我感到很内疚。仅仅是向她倾诉我复杂的心情，就让我安心了不少，也让我意识到自己并没有那么迷茫。在通话的后半段，接线员能够准确地复述我的担忧，这让我感受到她真正理解了我的感受，而不是直接告诉我该怎么做。这帮助我理清了思绪，也让我明确了照顾自己的优先事项。我明白了下一步该怎么做——参加照护者互助小组。”

“我感觉自己准备好采取行动了。”
When Ron’s wife lost her job, the same month his daughter had gone to the ER after a car accident, huge financial problems and debt pushed him into foreclosure of his home. He felt terrible as a failed provider for his family, and struggled to keep his own job.
罗恩的妻子失业后，他的女儿又因车祸被送进急诊室，这导致他面临巨大的经济困难和债务，最终房子被银行收回。他觉得自己没能成为家里的顶梁柱，感到非常愧疚，而且他自己的工作也岌岌可危。
“Losing my home made me feel like a real loser. I was living a nightmare, making it hard to focus on my job. Then, out of the blue, one of my coworkers approached me, and kindly said he was sorry to hear what happened. He invited me to join him for lunch at a diner near our office. He confided to me his brother had also just lost his home, and was feeling pretty bad. He thought maybe I could meet his brother and talk, to support each other, and maybe network together. This gave me a shot in the arm, and snapped me out of my funk. I had been wallowing in feelings of shame, but I felt reassured by my coworker that other people were in the same boat, and that there was no reason to be so hard on myself. Soon I met his brother, John, and we started helping each other look for places to rent. By both of us working on our searches together, I knew that somehow I would get through this time. And week by week, when we checked in with each other on Twitter, I thought that if John could keep going, then I could, too.”
失去房子让我觉得自己真是个彻头彻尾的失败者。我感觉自己像在噩梦中，根本无法集中精力工作。就在这时，一位同事突然走过来，友好地安慰我说，听到我的遭遇他很难过。他邀请我去办公室附近的一家餐馆吃午饭。他告诉我，他的兄弟也刚刚失去了房子，心情非常糟糕。他觉得或许我可以和他兄弟见见，聊聊，互相支持，或许还能拓展人脉。这番话给了我莫大的鼓励，让我从低落的情绪中走了出来。我一直沉浸在羞愧之中，但同事的话让我感到安慰，让我知道还有其他人也面临着同样的困境，我没必要对自己那么苛责。不久后，我见到了他的兄弟约翰，我们开始互相帮忙找房子。我们一起努力寻找，我知道总有一天我会渡过难关。每周，我们都会在推特上互相问候，我想，如果约翰都能坚持下去，那我一定也能挺过去。如果去了，我也能去了。”

O UR RESPONSES such as feeling heard, connected, cared for, or hopeful revealed that our comforters were often good listeners, fully present, able to make us feel we were more important than anything else in that moment. Comforting people were usually acting from their empathy. They felt our emotions with us. They were willing to avail their human-to-human, warmhearted qualities to us.
我们感受到的被倾听、被理解、被关怀或充满希望等反馈表明，安慰我们的人往往是优秀的倾听者，他们全神贯注地陪伴在我们身边，让我们觉得在那一刻，我们比任何事都重要。安慰我们的人通常是出于同理心。他们感同身受，体会着我们的情绪。他们愿意将人与人之间温暖的品质传递给我们。
# ↩

We Are All Comforting in Our Own Ways

我们都用自己的方式给予安慰

Though we know how it feels to be in the presence of a comforting person, we often doubt or undervalue our own innate ability to comfort others. We tend to compare ourselves to images and stereotypes of comforters in our culture. Unfortunately, many of us have gotten the message that only certain people can be truly comforting. We believe some people just have a knack for it, were born with it. We think one has to be exceptionally compassionate, charismatic, or generous, or have years of training in counseling, social work, or pastoral care to be qualified to comfort others. We think we should only comfort people who are going through things familiar to us, and not dare to help when we have little or no experience with their situation. Or we tell ourselves we don’t have enough available time on our hands for comforting, that we should leave it to our grandparents or other elders who are freer to give of their time.
虽然我们都知道被安慰的感觉，但我们常常怀疑或低估自己安慰他人的能力。我们倾向于将自己与文化中那些安慰者的形象和刻板印象进行比较。不幸的是，我们中的许多人都接收到这样的信息：只有特定的人才能真正给予安慰。我们认为有些人天生就具备这种能力。我们认为一个人必须特别富有同情心、魅力四射或慷慨大方，或者接受过多年的咨询、社会工作或牧灵关怀方面的培训，才有资格安慰他人。我们认为，我们只能安慰那些经历与我们相似的人，而不敢在自己对他们的处境知之甚少或一无所知时伸出援手。或者，我们告诉自己，我们没有足够的时间去安慰别人，应该把这项工作留给更有空闲时间的祖父母或其他长辈。
These myths about being qualified for comforting have perpetuated stereotypes about comforters, upstaging our natural abilities and common sense. Sadly, we’ve come to believe we either need to be experts at comforting, or we need to be extraordinarily gifted at it. These idealized, self-imposed expectations can diminish our confidence in our own natural ways of caring for others, and can inhibit us when we are sitting with someone in distress.
这些关于安慰他人是否合格的迷思，强化了人们对安慰者的刻板印象，掩盖了我们与生俱来的能力和常识。可悲的是，我们开始相信，要么我们需要成为安慰专家，要么我们需要在这方面天赋异禀。这些理想化的、自我强加的期望会削弱我们对自身自然关怀他人方式的信心，也会在我们陪伴处于痛苦中的人时，让我们感到束手束脚。
Following are common myths about comforters that interfere with trusting our innate abilities to comfort others.
以下是一些关于安慰者的常见误解，这些误解会妨碍我们相信自己与生俱来的安慰他人的能力。
# ↩

COMMON MYTHS ABOUT COMFORTERS

关于被子的常见误解

MYTH: Comforters are always warm and fuzzy, touchy-feely, and big huggers.
误区：被子总是温暖柔软、触感舒适、让人感觉温暖。
Comforting people can be shy, stoic, or reserved, and might prefer to help people in some not-so-touchy ways. The one who runs the errands is as comforting as the one who gives the hugs.
善于安慰人的人可能比较害羞、沉稳或内敛，他们或许更倾向于用一些不那么直接的方式帮助别人。跑腿办事的人和拥抱安慰他人的人一样，都能给人带来慰藉。

MYTH: Comforters are only the ones with whom we have heart-to-heart talks.
误区：安慰者只是那些能与我们进行推心置腹谈话的人。
We can comfort others in hundreds of ways: buying their groceries, sending a thoughtful card, playing golf, going out together to a movie, knitting a scarf, walking their dogs. Comforting doesn’t always involve conversation.
我们可以用数百种方式安慰他人：帮他们买菜、送一张贴心的卡片、一起打高尔夫、一起去看电影、织一条围巾、帮他们遛狗。安慰并不总是需要交谈。

MYTH: Comforters always know what to say.
误区：安慰者总是知道该说什么。
We don’t have to know the right thing to say. Sometimes there is really nothing that can be said. But comforters still offer to show up, even if we don’t know what to say, because there are many, many ways to connect and communicate, depending on what that person desires—listening to their favorite songs, bringing catnip for their cat, baking a meat loaf, dumping their trash, playing a game of cards, doing their nails, watching American Idol together. We offer our time and our presence, and see what happens. Even Tweeting our comfort in little ways helps, by saying, “I’m thinking about you now, and I hope you are getting through today.”
我们不必非得知道该说什么。有时候，真的什么都说不出来。但即便我们不知道该说什么，安慰者仍然会主动出现，因为有很多种方式可以建立联系和沟通，这取决于对方的意愿——听他们喜欢的歌，给他们的猫带猫薄荷，烤个肉饼，帮他们倒垃圾，陪他们玩牌，帮他们做美甲，一起看《美国偶像》。我们付出时间和陪伴，看看会发生什么。即使是发条推特表达一点小小的安慰，比如“我现在在想你，希望你今天一切顺利”，也能有所帮助。

MYTH: Comforters are always there when people need them. (“Call me if you need me.”)
误区：安慰者总会在人们需要的时候出现。（“如果你需要我，就给我打电话。”）
We need to be honest about our availability to help, and communicate this clearly. It’s always better to be proactive in letting them know what we can actually do for them. We can offer a simple, concrete thing (“I can call you Monday night”). People in distress suffer more when they are “left in the dark” about when contact will be made. No one wants to appear needy by having to call out for help.
我们需要坦诚地说明我们能够提供帮助的时间，并清晰地传达这一点。主动告知他们我们能为他们做些什么总是更好的。我们可以提供简单具体的建议（例如“我周一晚上可以给你打电话”）。如果让身处困境的人对何时联系你一无所知，他们会更加痛苦。没有人愿意因为需要求助而显得自己很需要帮助。

MYTH: Comforters have lots of time to provide enough comfort. We can be comforting in a matter of minutes, even in seconds. Little acts of caring can make a big difference for someone in distress.
误区：安慰者需要很多时间才能给予足够的安慰。其实，我们可以在几分钟，甚至几秒钟内给予安慰。微小的关怀举动，对身处困境的人来说意义重大。

MYTH: Comforters are supposed to cheer people up when they are down, and tell them to be positive.
误区：安慰者应该在人们情绪低落时让他们振作起来，并告诉他们要保持积极乐观的态度。
Being comforting doesn’t mean showering the person in pain with “look at the bright side” platitudes. It is important to acknowledge that the person is in pain as opposed to attempting to get them to “snap out of it.”
安慰并不意味着用“往好处想”之类的陈词滥调来敷衍痛苦的人。重要的是承认对方正在承受痛苦，而不是试图让他们“振作起来”。

MYTH: Comforters need to have much in common with the person in distress to be effective.
误区：安慰者需要与处于困境中的人有很多共同点才能有效安慰他们。
We can feel someone else’s pain even if we cannot identify with their story or background. We are all connected in common sorrows and human life passages. No one has the last word on human suffering.
即使我们无法感同身受他人的经历或背景，也能体会到他们的痛苦。我们都因共同的悲伤和人生阶段而彼此相连。没有人能对人类的苦难拥有最终的发言权。
Complicating these myths about comforters are the market-driven habits of our culture that diminish how much value we place on our innate comforting skills, especially empathic listening. We have learned to speak in dehumanized, commoditized languages, serving our functions to meet bottom lines and deadlines, and to make headlines. In these sink-or-swim environments, comforting people often suppress their wonderful, softhearted tendencies, or avoid high-profile appearances where they would have to go against the ways of their true empathic natures.
使我们对安慰者的固有认知更加复杂的是，我们文化中以市场为导向的习惯削弱了我们对自身与生俱来的安慰能力（尤其是同理心倾听）的重视。我们学会了用冷漠、商品化的语言交流，为了完成业绩目标、达成截止日期以及博取眼球而服务于自身职能。在这种适者生存的环境中，善于安慰的人往往会压抑自己美好而温柔的本性，或者避免在需要违背自身真正同理心的场合高调露面。
I do believe our communication practices, sped up considerably since the advent of the Internet in the mid-’90s, discourage us from slowing down enough to be comforting. This is a hard world to be soft in, to be patient in, to allow vulnerable people to express themselves, to give them the time to find their words. Grieving and devastated people have difficulty concentrating, and struggle for clarity as they battle overwhelming, often mixed and contradictory emotions. They often repeat themselves, or can’t get to the point, or are too afraid or depressed to say much. And even though people in distress have great access on the Web to connections with others, they still need our face-to-face, heart-to-heart, hand-to-hand presence. It’s ironic how the easier it is to communicate instantly, by cell, by e-mail, by fax, by Twitter, the harder it gets to be fully present with the ones who need us, right where we are.
我相信，自上世纪90年代中期互联网出现以来，我们沟通方式的节奏显著加快，这让我们难以放慢脚步，给予他人安慰。在这个世界上，保持温柔、耐心、允许脆弱的人表达自己、给他们时间找到合适的词语，都变得异常艰难。悲伤和痛苦的人难以集中注意力，在与汹涌澎湃、往往复杂矛盾的情绪作斗争时，他们难以理清思绪。他们常常重复自己的话，或者无法切入主题，或者因为恐惧或沮丧而不敢多说。即使身处困境的人们可以通过网络与他人建立联系，他们仍然需要我们面对面、心连心、手牵手的陪伴。讽刺的是，通过手机、电子邮件、传真、推特等即时通讯方式越是便捷，我们就越难全身心地陪伴那些需要我们的人，无论他们身在何处。
Given the “nice guys finish last” habits of our culture, it’s amazing we have held on to our civility as much as we have, let alone our comforting skills. It’s heartening to remember that in spite of how ugly it gets out there, our natural relational ability to provide comfort for others still remains, even if we can’t see it ourselves. The fact is that our best comforting qualities often seem so ordinary that we tend to take them for granted. We overlook some of our solid, reliable attributes that may indeed be dearly comforting to others.
鉴于我们文化中“好人没好报”的观念，我们还能保持如此之高的礼貌和善解人意的能力，简直令人惊叹。令人欣慰的是，即便外界环境如此丑陋，我们与生俱来的安慰他人的能力依然存在，即使我们自己可能意识不到。事实上，我们最能抚慰人心的品质往往显得如此平凡，以至于我们常常习以为常。我们忽略了自身一些可靠的特质，而这些特质或许真的能给他人带来莫大的安慰。
Here is a list of comforting traits I have gathered from responses of more than five hundred participants in recent years, from teaching classes in the art of comforting, training group facilitators, and facilitating support groups. I promise that you will find that you possess a number of the following twenty qualities, and I invite you to use them as your foundation for building upon your comforting skills.
以下是我近年来从五百多位参与者的反馈中总结出的令人感到安慰的特质，这些反馈来自我教授安慰技巧课程、培训团体引导员以及带领互助小组的经历。我保证你会发现自己具备以下二十种特质中的许多，我邀请你以此为基础，进一步提升你的安慰技巧。
# ↩

The Top Twenty Attributes of Comforting People

令人感到安慰的人的二十个主要特质

BEING PRESENT AND LISTENING

专注当下，认真倾听

Of all the qualities of comforting, the most essential are our presence and good listening, laying the foundation for all other comforting skills.
在所有安慰的品质中，最重要的是我们的陪伴和良好的倾听，这为所有其他安慰技巧奠定了基础。
Our best human strengths and virtues will not be effective without the basic, underlying ability to be present to each other. We can have great intentions, be spiritually motivated, be politically correct, be organized and smart, or be downright nice, but if we don’t bring ourselves fully into the present moment with others, we lose our attunement to one another’s needs, feelings, and cues.
即使我们拥有最优秀的人性优势和美德，如果没有彼此专注的基本能力，这些优势和美德也无法发挥作用。我们可以怀揣美好的愿望，拥有精神追求，注重政治正确，做事井井有条、聪明睿智，或者待人友善，但如果我们不能全身心地投入到与他人相处的当下，我们就无法感知彼此的需求、感受和信号。
“Being there” for someone does not necessarily mean being always there, but it does require us to be all there, with our undivided attention. Being present involves engaging our nonverbal communication, our facial expressions, eye contact, gestures, and voice intonations, as the language of comforting is at least 80 percent nonverbal. (Though some people say they listen better when they are doodling or texting, it is not comforting for the person in distress speaking to us, who needs to see our responses.)
“陪伴”并不一定意味着时刻在场，而是要求我们全神贯注，全神贯注地倾听。这种陪伴包括运用非语言沟通，例如面部表情、眼神交流、手势和语调，因为安慰的语言至少有80%是非语言的。（虽然有些人说他们在涂鸦或发短信时更容易倾听，但这对于正在经历痛苦的人来说并不能带来安慰，他们需要看到我们的回应。）

PRESENT — “ there , ” listens well, gives their full attention, in the moment, focused
专注当下——“在那里”，认真倾听，全神贯注，全神贯注。
In the language of comforting, listening is as important as using words. In the Oxford Dictionary , to listen means to “pay attention to.” If all we did was listen, paying full attention, we would be well on our way to being comforting.
在安慰的语言中，倾听与言语同样重要。《牛津词典》对“倾听”的定义是“注意”。如果我们只是倾听，全神贯注，我们就能很好地给予他人安慰。
When we pay full attention to someone, we are showing this person that he or she matters to us, that their dilemma matters to us. When it comes to comforting, the simplest, most honest human-to-human kinds of communication serve us best. Sometimes all we can say is we are sorry things are so hard, and be with someone in naked silence.
当我们全神贯注地倾听他人时，我们就是在向对方表明，我们重视他/她，关心他的困境。说到安慰，最简单、最真诚的人际沟通方式往往最有效。有时，我们所能做的只是简单地表达“很遗憾你的处境如此艰难”，然后静静地陪伴他/她。
Here is a story about the power of our presence from Patricia Ellen, a grief counselor and chaplain, working with grieving families at the Center for Grieving Children in Portland, Maine. (She will be profiled later as one of our guides to the practice of comforting.)
以下是来自帕特里夏·艾伦的故事，她是一位悲伤辅导员和牧师，在缅因州波特兰市的儿童悲伤中心为悲伤的家庭提供帮助。她讲述了我们陪伴的力量。（稍后我们将介绍她，她是安慰实践方面的指导者之一。）
Patricia’s Story of Being Comforted
帕特里夏被安慰的故事
1988 was a time of excruciating grief and darkness after my son, Doug, fourteen years old, had committed suicide. Eight months after his death, I was comforted by a particular experience that happened very gently and naturally one summer evening in Portsmouth, New Hampshire.
1988年，我14岁的儿子道格自杀身亡，那一年我陷入了极度的悲痛和黑暗之中。在他去世八个月后，一个夏日傍晚，在新罕布什尔州朴茨茅斯，我经历了一件特别的事情，这件事非常平静自然，也让我得到了慰藉。
Two friends came to visit me and invited me to take a long walk with them. We walked mostly in silence by lush gardens and trees in the balmy summer air. My friends only said about four sentences for the whole evening. But in that silence I felt their love and care in waves of comfort streaming from their hearts. In their soft presence, I softened along with them and opened up to behold the beauty of nature around me.
两位朋友来拜访我，邀请我一起散步。我们沿着绿树成荫、花园环绕的小径，在和煦的夏日微风中漫步，一路沉默。整个晚上，朋友们只说了寥寥几句话。但在这份静谧中，我感受到了他们如潮水般涌来的关爱与温暖。在他们温柔的陪伴下，我也渐渐放松下来，敞开心扉去欣赏周围的自然之美。
It was a transformative experience for me to feel the comfort of my dear friends and the earth, mostly without words, teaching me the sacredness of being present.
对我来说，这是一次意义非凡的经历，我感受到了亲爱的朋友和大地的慰藉，虽然大多无需言语，却教会了我活在当下的神圣。
Silence can truly be golden if we take the leap of faith that listening is all we need to do. Moments of silence are sacred, bonding us in soulful ways, sometimes the best medicine of all.
如果我们愿意相信聆听就足够了，那么沉默的确可以成为一种金子。沉默的时刻是神圣的，它能以触动灵魂的方式将我们联系在一起，有时甚至是最好的良药。
# ↩

The Importance of Empathy

同理心的重要性

NEXT TO BEING PRESENT AND LISTENING WELL, THE SECOND MOST IMPORTANT COMFORTING TRAIT IS EMPATHY.

除了专注倾听之外，第二重要的安慰特质是同理心。

EMPATHIC— senses the feelings of another person
有同理心——能感受到他人的感受
Empathy is feeling what another human being feels, whether or not we identify with their beliefs, status, or background. We can feel the sorrow of someone else, even if their life experience is nothing like ours, because we all know sorrow by having lived through loss in our own lives. Our commonality of human challenges and suffering is far greater than our separate ideologies, religions, cultures, or genders.
同理心是指感受他人的感受，无论我们是否认同他们的信仰、地位或背景。即使他人的生活经历与我们截然不同，我们也能感受到他们的悲伤，因为我们都曾经历过失去亲人的痛苦。人类面临的挑战和苦难的共通之处，远远大于我们不同的意识形态、宗教、文化或性别。
Most of us possess a great amount of empathy, but, unfortunately, our culture has developed uncomforting habits that suppress this vital capacity. One destructive habit in particular is the tendency to compare one person’s suffering to another’s. And this can be disastrous for our language of comforting.
我们大多数人都拥有很强的同理心，但不幸的是，我们的文化已经养成了一些令人不安的习惯，这些习惯压制了这种至关重要的能力。其中一个特别有害的习惯就是将一个人的痛苦与另一个人的痛苦进行比较。而这会对我们安慰他人的语言造成灾难性的后果。
In our society, we often find ourselves getting sucked into downward spirals of “their-misery-is-worse-than-yours” comparisons and contrasts, mistakenly thinking we are lessening someone’s distress by “putting it in perspective”: “You think your foreclosure was bad—but look, the Hurricane Katrina folks had it much worse than you.” (Or the homeless folks in tent cities have it worse, or the poor kids in the ghettos of New York, or in the refugee settlements in Darfur, or in the slums of Brazil or India. . . .) But it’s just not comforting for anyone in distress to be compared to anyone else, anywhere else.
在我们的社会里，我们常常陷入“他们的苦难比你的更甚”的比较和对比的恶性循环，错误地认为通过“换个角度看问题”就能减轻他人的痛苦：“你觉得你的房屋被取消抵押赎回权很糟糕——但你看，卡特里娜飓风的灾民比你惨多了。”（或者帐篷城里的无家可归者处境更糟，纽约贫民窟的穷孩子，达尔富尔难民营的难民，巴西或印度贫民窟的难民……）但对于任何身处困境的人来说，被拿来与其他地方的任何人比较，都并不能带来安慰。
Though in our legal and financial systems, we compare and quantify pain and suffering constantly, this practice does not apply to our role as comforters with one another. If we are to be effective comforters, it is better to respect that pain is downright painful for anyone and everyone, whatever the reason or cause.
虽然在我们的法律和金融体系中，我们不断地比较和量化痛苦，但这种做法并不适用于我们彼此安慰的角色。如果我们想要有效地安慰他人，最好尊重这样一个事实：无论出于何种原因，痛苦对任何人来说都是切肤之痛。
A woman in a divorce support group, Jan, tells us her story about two married women friends who did not open their hearts with empathy, but instead compared her situation to theirs, trying to downplay her distress.
离婚互助小组的一位名叫简的女士向我们讲述了她的故事：她的两位已婚女友非但没有对她表示同情，反而将她的情况与她们的情况进行比较，试图淡化她的痛苦。
Meeting together at a Thai restaurant, Jan told her friends how hard it was adjusting to life as a single woman. Her friends began comparing their marital woes to her woes, chiding her, “It’s lonelier being in a bad marriage than being single. You’re free now. You have a whole new life ahead of you.” Her friends might have meant well, trying to convince Jan she shouldn’t be feeling so bad, but this actually minimized her pain. Jan got the not-so-comforting message that her distressed feelings were unwarranted, according to her friends, and therefore she was not worthy of their empathy. She felt worse, even lonelier, after hearing their comments.
在一家泰国餐厅聚会时，简向朋友们倾诉了自己单身生活的艰难。朋友们却开始拿她们的婚姻问题和她的困境作比较，并责备她说：“糟糕的婚姻比单身更孤独。你现在自由了，你的人生才刚刚开始。” 朋友们或许是出于好意，想安慰简，让她别那么难过，但这反而让她更加痛苦。简从朋友们那里得到的却是这样的信息：她的悲伤毫无道理，因此不值得她们的同情。听到这些话，她反而感觉更糟，更加孤独了。
Jan lingered at the restaurant after the two women left, and the Thai restaurant owner, a woman about her age, chatted with her for a while, as business was slow that night. She told Jan her story of coming to America, and how she had left behind much of her family. She was struggling and working hard to raise her two children without her husband, who had recently been forced to return to Thailand.
那两个女人离开后，简在餐馆里逗留了一会儿。餐馆老板娘是一位和她年纪相仿的泰国女性，当晚生意清淡，便和她聊了起来。老板娘向简讲述了自己来到美国的经历，以及她如何抛下大部分家人。她独自一人艰难地抚养两个孩子，丈夫最近被迫返回泰国。
Touched, Jan briefly shared she was on her own, too. “It’s hard, isn’t it? My marriage ended and I’m trying to find my way.”
简深受感动，简短地分享了自己也是独自一人。“这很艰难，不是吗？我的婚姻结束了，我正在努力寻找自己的方向。”
The Thai woman asked, “Do you have kids?”
泰国女子问道：“你有孩子吗？”
When Jan answered she did not have children, the woman softly touched her arm and said, “So, you are all alone, no husband, no kids . . . that sounds sad. I am so sorry to hear this.”
当简回答说她没有孩子时，那位女士轻轻地碰了碰她的胳膊，说：“所以，你孤身一人，没有丈夫，没有孩子……听起来真令人难过。听到这个消息我很难过。”
Fighting back her tears, Jan smiled and thanked her. This woman had no idea how much her simple words meant to her. They genuinely felt one another’s sorrow.
简强忍着泪水，微笑着向她道谢。这位女士并不知道她这几句简单的话语对她有多么重要。她们真切地感受到了彼此的悲伤。
When we don’t compare suffering between ourselves, we can indeed comfort one another with our empathy, whether it be with toddlers with scraped knees, with lovesick adolescents, with heartbroken widows, or with hungry refugees.
当我们不将彼此的苦难进行比较时，我们确实可以用同理心来安慰彼此，无论是膝盖擦破的幼儿、失恋的青少年、心碎的寡妇，还是饥饿的难民。
No matter what society tells us about how different we are, we all have the same feelings at heart. Certainly our beloved animal companions know what we feel, as do our children and our greatest artists, storytellers, and healers, but many of us have suppressed this beautiful gift of empathy.
无论社会如何告诉我们彼此有多么不同，我们内心深处都拥有相同的情感。当然，我们挚爱的动物伙伴能理解我们的感受，我们的孩子、最伟大的艺术家、故事讲述者和治疗师也一样，但我们中的许多人却压抑了这种美好的同理心。

GENUINE— sincere, has integrity
真诚——坦率、正直
The Thai woman in the previous story about empathy was willing to open up and show her genuine feelings and her true self. It was comforting just to see the honest caring in her eyes. When we really mean what we say, sometimes we don’t have to say as much.
前一个关于同理心的故事中，那位泰国女性愿意敞开心扉，展现她真挚的情感和真实的自我。仅仅是看到她眼中流露出的真诚关怀，就让人感到无比温暖。当我们言行一致时，有时无需赘言。

RESPECTFUL— honors people as human beings first and foremost above all roles or status
尊重——首先将人视为人而加以尊重，高于一切角色或地位。
If we think back and remember times people have comforted us, we can review how they gave us their respect, or at least their respectful courtesy. They did not push us, rush us, dismiss us, stereotype us, manipulate us. They listened, and welcomed our opinion, even if they did not agree with it. They saw the dignity in us, and honored us.
如果我们回想过去，想起那些曾给予我们安慰的人，我们会发现他们是如何尊重我们，或者至少是给予我们应有的礼貌和尊重的。他们没有催促我们、冲我们、忽视我们、给我们贴标签、操纵我们。他们倾听，并欢迎我们的意见，即使他们并不认同。他们看到了我们身上的尊严，并给予我们尊重。
Comforters deeply value all the years we have spent dealing with the universal challenges of being human, whether we were getting to age forty, or thirteen, or eighty. They believe everyone works hard to get to where they are, so we are all important.
安慰者们深深珍视我们多年来应对人类普遍挑战的经历，无论我们当时是四十岁、十三岁还是八十岁。他们相信每个人都努力奋斗才走到今天，所以我们每个人都很重要。
The comforting people we know are often quite gifted at making people feel vital to any meeting, gathering, or group. Good group facilitators, for example, encourage everyone’s opinions, but also respect those who do not feel ready or willing to speak.
我们认识的那些善于安慰人的人，往往很擅长让每个人都觉得自己在任何会议、聚会或团体中都至关重要。例如，优秀的团体组织者会鼓励每个人发表意见，同时也尊重那些感觉还没准备好或不愿意发言的人。

PATIENT— allows people to move, speak, and think at their own pace; doesn’t rush people
耐心——允许人们按照自己的节奏行动、说话和思考；不催促人们。
It’s a great relief for people in distress to find a patient person. Often people in times of loss and crisis have difficulty trying to explain their needs or their desires, and others tune them out before they can finish what they are saying. Unfortunately in our culture, some people rush them to “get to the point,” or push them, saying, “Stop repeating yourself—you’ve already said that twice!” People in pain or in crisis cannot concentrate well, and need our help by allowing them to gather their thoughts, or maybe to think out loud until they are clear with their message.
对于身处困境的人来说，遇到一位耐心倾听的人无疑是莫大的安慰。人们在经历失去亲人和危机时，往往难以清晰地表达自己的需求或愿望，而其他人则常常在他们说完之前就置之不理。不幸的是，在我们的文化中，有些人会催促他们“直奔主题”，或者咄咄逼人地说：“别重复了——你已经说过两遍了！”痛苦或危机中的人难以集中注意力，他们需要我们的帮助，比如允许他们整理思绪，或者让他们大声思考，直到思路清晰为止。

CARING— kind, compassionate, thoughtful, considerate
关爱——善良、富有同情心、体贴、周到
In the language of comforting, the little acts of caring mean everything. One recently bereaved, elderly man told me how comforting it was to have his shy, fifteen-year-old neighbor come by every day to help him walk his dogs. “We hardly ever said a word, but that boy loved my dogs and showed up right at four o’clock every afternoon, for about thirty minutes, rain or shine. He played Frisbee with my dogs and perked them up—and that perked me up, too.”
在抚慰人心的语言中，那些微小的关怀举动意义非凡。一位最近失去亲人的老人告诉我，他那腼腆的十五岁邻居每天都来帮他遛狗，这让他感到多么温暖。“我们几乎不说话，但那男孩很喜欢我的狗，每天下午四点准时出现，风雨无阻，每次大约半小时。他和我的狗玩飞盘，让它们精神焕发——这也让我感到很温暖。”

RELIABLE— dependable, trustworthy, will do what they say they will do, keeps commitments
可靠——值得信赖，言出必行，信守承诺
Reliability is extremely important for people in distress. In their complicated, uncertain, and overwhelming situations, they need to count on us. It’s better to offer a single commitment we can honor realistically, a sure bet, rather than make a promise that might overextend us. It’s safer to stand by one simple, specific act such as making a phone call on Monday night, instead of promising to call every week, or assuring them, “I’m there for you—just call anytime.” We honestly need to assess and clarify our availability and capacity to be in the comforting role for someone, no matter how much we care. We can only “be there” when we offer the specifics and follow through.
对于身处困境的人来说，可靠性至关重要。在他们复杂、不确定且令人不知所措的处境中，他们需要依靠我们。与其做出可能超出我们能力范围的承诺，不如提供一个我们能够切实履行的、有把握的承诺。与其承诺每周都打电话，或者向他们保证“我随时都在，随时都可以打电话”，不如坚持一个简单具体的行动，比如在周一晚上打个电话。无论我们多么关心他们，我们都需要认真评估并明确自己是否有能力扮演安慰者的角色。只有当我们做出具体承诺并付诸行动时，我们才能真正做到“陪伴在他们身边”。
I’ve heard grieving and distraught people lament how others didn’t follow through with their promises, which hurt them more than anyone’s lack of affection or warmth. Their friendly, sunny friends who promised to “be there” for them “fell off the face of the earth” after they dropped off their casseroles during the first days of the tragedy. Surprisingly, sometimes the more modest, “sensible” people in the background turned out to be the real comforters, checking in regularly for many weeks afterward. These true-blue folks brought by vegetables from their garden, or met us for coffee after church, or picked up our mail while we were stuck in the hospital.
我曾听过悲痛欲绝的人们抱怨，别人没有兑现承诺，这比任何人的冷漠或缺乏温暖都更让他们伤心。那些曾经热情友善、承诺“会一直陪伴”他们的朋友们，在悲剧发生后的最初几天送来几份热腾腾的饭菜后，就如同人间蒸发一般消失了。令人惊讶的是，有时那些默默无闻、看似“理智”的人，反而成了真正的安慰者，在接下来的几周里定期关心我们。这些真诚善良的人会送来自家花园的蔬菜，或者在教堂礼拜后和我们一起喝咖啡，或者在我们住院期间帮我们取邮件。

CLEAR— lets people in distress know what we can realistically do for them, and clarifies our role as comforters, while keeping firm with our boundaries
清晰明确——让身处困境的人知道我们能切实为他们做些什么，并明确我们作为安慰者的角色，同时坚定地维护我们的界限。
Comforters cannot be everything to everybody. We need to make it clear the ways we can and cannot comfort others. This is an important aspect of being reliable and realistically available to people in distress. Our boundaries keep us from getting hooked into doing more than we are comfortable doing, and prevent us from feelings of resentment from doing too much.
安慰者不可能满足所有人的所有需求。我们需要明确自己能够安慰他人和不能安慰他人的方式。这是在他人痛苦时，能够可靠且切实地提供帮助的重要方面。设定界限可以避免我们过度付出超出自身能力范围的事情，也能防止我们因付出过多而产生怨恨。
One newly bereaved man in a grief support group tells us how a little clarity goes a long way in comforting:
“It’s funny how the person who was most comforting to me was only able to see me once a month. Though plenty of people said they would stop in and see me more often, half the time they didn’t, and I wished they had not been so vague—leaving me hanging. But my friend was very clear and direct about what he could actually do. He even admitted he didn’t know how to talk about my grief issues, but he did say he could at least be my movie buddy. One Saturday every month, we went to see a movie and then shared a pizza. Perfect.”
一位刚失去亲人的男士在悲伤互助小组里讲述了清晰的沟通如何带来莫大的安慰：“说来也奇怪，最能安慰我的人却只能一个月见我一次。虽然很多人都说会经常来看我，但实际上他们有一半时间都没来，我真希望他们当初不要那么含糊其辞，让我一直悬着心。但我的朋友却非常坦诚地告诉我他能做些什么。他甚至承认自己不知道该如何谈论我的悲伤，但他表示至少可以陪我一起看电影。每个月的一个周六，我们一起去看电影，然后一起吃披萨。完美！”
WARM— welcoming, gracious, greets others with a sincere smile, approachable
热情——待人友善、和蔼可亲，面带真诚的微笑迎接他人，平易近人
Being able to greet and introduce one another is key to establishing a comforting encounter. The art of graciousness is a more public aspect of comforting that we sometimes see in our media.
能够互相问候和介绍是建立融洽关系的关键。这种彬彬有礼的艺术，是我们在媒体上偶尔看到的，更偏向于公开场合的慰藉方式。
If we think of our favorite talk show hosts and news anchors, those who have been going strong for many years, we can observe their remarkable greeting and hosting skills. They use their warmth and graciousness in quite varied ways to get their guests to feel comfortable at the start of their interviews. If we have a favorite talk show host, news anchor, or journalist, we might study what it is that makes them comforting in how they handle their guests. I’ve heard people in support groups comment on their favorites:
如果我们想想自己最喜欢的脱口秀主持人或新闻主播，那些多年来一直活跃在荧屏上的主持人，我们就能注意到他们卓越的待客之道和主持技巧。他们以各种方式展现热情和亲切，让嘉宾在采访开始时感到自在舒适。如果我们有自己喜欢的脱口秀主持人、新闻主播或记者，不妨研究一下他们是如何以令人感到舒适的方式对待嘉宾的。我曾在一些互助小组里听到人们谈论他们最喜欢的主持人：
“Ellen DeGeneres seems relaxed and easygoing. Her dancing thing always cracks me up—a great icebreaker.”
“艾伦·德杰尼勒斯看起来很放松，也很随和。她跳舞的样子总是让我捧腹大笑——真是个很好的破冰方式。”
“Ann Curry’s warm voice is calming, and her eye contact with her guests is welcoming.”
“安·柯里温暖的声音令人平静，她与客人的眼神交流也让人感到亲切。”
“Bill Moyers listens so quietly, patiently, and has a soft voice.”
“比尔·莫耶斯倾听时非常安静、耐心，而且声音很轻柔。”

ACCEPTING— open-minded, nonjudgmental, receptive, willing to learn from others
接纳——思想开放、不带偏见、乐于接受、愿意向他人学习
We all know people who sincerely seem to be interested in other people, curious about them, yet tolerant when opinions clash. They like learning from others, asking questions and exploring different perspectives, whether or not they fit with their own worldview.
我们都认识一些真心对他人感兴趣、充满好奇心，且在意见相左时也能保持宽容的人。他们喜欢向他人学习，乐于提问，探索不同的视角，无论这些视角是否符合他们自身的价值观。
Here is what a cancer support group member said about an open-minded, friendly hairstylist she sees every other month:
“Betty doesn’t miss a thing. She remembers everything I told her two months ago, and asks how Jamie’s doing every time I see her. It is downright comforting to have someone who wants to hear what’s going on, following my family’s ups and downs. She doesn’t judge me. She just seems fascinated in what I tell her. I confide things with her about Jamie I’d never tell to my closer friends.”
一位癌症互助小组的成员这样评价她每隔一个月都会光顾的、思想开放又友善的发型师：“贝蒂什么都记得清清楚楚。她还记得我两个月前跟她说过的所有事，每次见到她都会问起杰米的情况。有人愿意倾听我的心声，了解我家的喜怒哀乐，这真的让我感到很温暖。她不会评判我，只是对我的讲述很感兴趣。我会跟她倾诉一些关于杰米的事，有些事我甚至不会跟更亲密的朋友说。”
CALM— centered, steady, quiet, still, serene
平静——专注、沉稳、安静、平静、安详
Some comforters emanate calmness and groundedness. They don’t get rattled too easily, so there is no need to censor what we say, pile on the Teflon, or walk on eggshells.
有些被照顾者散发着平静和沉稳的气息。他们不容易被激怒，所以我们无需斟酌言辞，无需过度保护，也无需小心翼翼。
A colleague of mine, a hospice nurse, possesses a lovely steadiness and calmness, enhancing the tranquil, quiet environment of the hospice house and gardens. Families seek her out when they feel frantic, and she makes a difference in their lives within a few minutes in her presence. Her nonverbal communication is calming, with her tone of voice, gestures, and facial expressions.
我的一位同事，一位临终关怀护士，拥有令人喜爱的沉稳和冷静，为临终关怀中心和花园营造了宁静祥和的氛围。家属们在感到焦躁不安时会来找她，而她只需几分钟的陪伴就能让他们的生活发生改变。她通过语调、手势和面部表情等非语言沟通方式，给人以平静之感。

HOPEFUL— believes that people will find their own way to healing, instills hope without being “preachy” or giving advice
充满希望——相信人们会找到自己的疗愈之路，传递希望而不显得“说教”或提供建议。
Though it may seem obvious, it’s comforting to declare that comforters of our world tend to have a hopeful outlook on humanity. They believe in the resourcefulness of our human hearts and spirits. Often highly comforting people have suffered their own grueling slew of ordeals, even inhumane ordeals, and have come through it all to love their lives as well as the true grit in all of us.
虽然这看似显而易见，但令人欣慰的是，我们这个世界上的安慰者往往对人性抱有乐观的态度。他们相信我们人类心灵和精神的无限潜能。很多极具安慰力的人都曾经历过种种磨难，甚至是非人道的苦难，但他们最终都战胜了困境，热爱生活，也看到了我们每个人身上都蕴藏的坚韧不拔的精神。
Jeff Lewis, a nurse practitioner working at a veterans hospital (one of our comforters profiled later), tells us he encourages hope in his patients, even at the end of their lives. He helps them find what keeps them hopeful—what keeps them going. One of Jeff’s patients told him, though facing only a few weeks of life in his terminal condition, “I’m holding on so I can hug my grandson when he comes back from Iraq next month.”
杰夫·刘易斯是一位在退伍军人医院工作的执业护士（我们稍后会介绍他，他是我们关怀病人的榜样之一）。他告诉我们，他会鼓励病人保持希望，即使在他们生命的尽头。他帮助他们找到让他们心怀希望、让他们坚持下去的动力。杰夫的一位病人告诉他，尽管身患绝症，生命只剩下几周，“但我坚持下去，是为了下个月我的孙子从伊拉克回来时能拥抱他。”

HUMBLE— honors his or her own human limitations and vulnerabilities
谦逊——尊重自身的人性局限和脆弱之处
Often we seek out comforters who stand modestly in the background. They quietly offer their comfort without expectations or need for acknowledgment. They’ve observed the humbling truth that no one human being has the last word on any subject, and accepts their limitations in seeing all of “the big picture.”
我们常常会寻找那些默默无闻、默默给予安慰的人。他们不求回报，默默地给予我们慰藉。他们领悟到，没有人能在任何问题上拥有最终的发言权，也坦然接受自己在洞察全局方面的局限性。
Having humility helps us understand the shadow sides and vulnerabilities of ourselves and others. A good comforter has faced the good, the bad, and the ugly in themselves, and has been able to honestly integrate these aspects into their love of humanity. These are the people we know who have “been there,” who can handle hearing about our most vulnerable, shameful, or embarrassing moments.
谦逊能帮助我们理解自身和他人的阴暗面和脆弱之处。一个好的安慰者曾直面过自己身上美好、丑陋甚至不堪的一面，并能坦诚地将这些面向融入他们对人类的爱中。我们认识的这些人“感同身受”，能够理解我们最脆弱、最羞愧或最尴尬的时刻。

SUPPORTIVE, VALIDATING— offers words, gestures, and actions that build on a person’s strengths and preferences, “strengths-based”
支持性的、认可性的——提供以个人优势和偏好为基础的言语、姿态和行动，“基于优势”
Some people are brilliant at reflecting back to us our best qualities. They “get” us, maybe better than we “get” ourselves. Good comforters often have this ability to hone in on our strengths, shine a light on them, and bring them forth. They show us how to build on these qualities in ourselves without preaching to us about “living up to our potential” or giving us pep talks. Instead, they just believe in us, period.
有些人很擅长发现我们身上最优秀的品质。他们“懂”我们，甚至比我们自己更了解我们。好的安慰者往往拥有这种能力，能够精准地把握我们的优势，让它们闪耀光芒，并激发它们发挥出来。他们会引导我们如何利用这些自身优势，而不是对我们说教“发挥潜能”或进行空洞的激励。他们只是单纯地相信我们。
One of the best career counselors I ever met was a genius at validating the strengths of her clients. She helped clients write amazing résumés that perfectly described their best qualities. When these clients went on job interviews, they glowed from their faith in the gifts of their character and accomplishments. They had been validated, with the “good to go” stamp of this counselor, and impressed employers with their confidence.
我遇到过的最优秀的职业顾问之一，她非常擅长发掘客户的优势。她帮助客户撰写出色的简历，完美地展现了他们的最佳品质。当这些客户去参加面试时，他们因对自己性格和成就的自信而容光焕发。他们得到了这位顾问的肯定，获得了“一切就绪”的认可，并以自信给雇主留下了深刻的印象。

APPRECIATIVE— grateful, recognizes the value of others, and “counts” their blessings
感恩的——心怀感激，认可他人的价值，并“数算”自己拥有的福气
There’s nothing like a heartfelt thank-you from someone. Showing our appreciation for others provides relief from the hard tasks and chores of our daily life. Taking a moment to express gratitude is a marvelous comforting tool for any occasion or group. It creates a bit of breathing space to pause and give thanks, as well as makes a safe place for counting our blessings that have appeared along the way.
没有什么比一句发自内心的感谢更令人感动。表达对他人的感激之情，能让我们暂时摆脱日常生活的繁琐事务。在任何场合或任何群体中，抽出一点时间表达感恩都是一种绝妙的慰藉方式。它能让我们稍作喘息，停下来表达谢意，也能让我们安心地细数一路走来所拥有的种种恩赐。

GENEROUS— giving, without expectations, often spontaneously
慷慨——给予而不求回报，通常是自发的
Some people surprise us with spontaneous acts of generosity. Here’s one example from a man in a chemical dependency rehab program, who believes this encounter opened his eyes to his recovery.
有些人会以出人意料的慷慨之举让我们感到惊喜。这里有一个例子，一位正在接受药物依赖康复治疗的男士，他认为这次偶遇让他对自己的康复有了新的认识。
“I met an old friend for coffee. At first, I thought we’d just be together for about an hour, but afterward, he offered to walk with me to a bookstore I loved. He said he was enjoying my company, and wanted to spend time browsing through books we both liked. We had a good time, and we bought a couple of great inspirational memoirs. Sometimes the unexpected things people do with us are the most fun and rewarding.”
“我和一位老朋友约了咖啡。起初，我以为我们只会待一个小时左右，但之后，他提出陪我去我常去的一家书店。他说他很享受和我在一起的时光，想花点时间一起看看我们都喜欢的书。我们玩得很开心，还买了几本很棒的励志回忆录。有时候，人们为我们做的那些意想不到的事情，反而是最有趣、最有意义的。”
GENTLE, TENDER— soft, can sensitively allow for the other person to respond
温柔、体贴——轻柔，能够体贴地给予对方回应的空间。
The gentlest gestures, such as handing someone a tissue, or softly touching their arm can make a world of difference in trying times. Here is what a nervous flyer told us:
“I hate being on airplanes, especially in turbulence. It was pretty bumpy, and I was not doing well. A sweet older woman sitting next to me gently touched my arm, and asked if I was okay. I must have looked really pale and awful. I reached to hold her hand, and looking at her sparkling eyes and soft smile, I could see she was really sensitive and understanding about this.”
在艰难时刻，最温柔的举动，比如递给别人一张纸巾，或者轻轻触碰对方的手臂，都能带来巨大的安慰。一位紧张的乘客告诉我们：“我讨厌坐飞机，尤其是在遇到气流颠簸的时候。飞机当时非常颠簸，我感觉很不舒服。坐在我旁边的一位和蔼的老太太轻轻地碰了碰我的手臂，问我是否还好。我当时一定脸色苍白，状态很差。我伸手去握她的手，看着她闪亮的眼睛和温柔的笑容，我知道她真的很体贴，很能理解我的感受。”
ADAPTABLE— can respond to changes, flexible, resourceful, can “go with the flow”
适应性强——能够应对变化，灵活，足智多谋，能够“顺其自然”。
Comforting people are often good at thinking on their feet and going with the flow of the moment. Without being over-accommodating, they can adjust schedules, topics, or settings to help other people feel more comfortable. Even just tweaking a few words or details for a meeting or a speech can put people at ease. They stay attuned to the mood, needs, and nonverbal messages of those around them, and sense when to make adjustments to enhance communication.
善于安慰人的人通常思维敏捷，能随机应变。他们不会过度迁就他人，而是会调整日程安排、话题或环境，让对方感到更自在。即使只是在会议或演讲中稍作措辞或细节上的调整，也能让人感到放松。他们时刻关注周围人的情绪、需求和非语言信息，并能敏锐地察觉何时做出调整以促进沟通。

WISE/EXPERIENCED— mature, has life experience, has been through demanding challenges and losses
睿智/经验丰富——成熟稳重，拥有丰富的人生阅历，经历过严峻的挑战和损失。
Sometimes a wiser individual sits in the background, quietly listening to an awkward or painful conversation about a difficult issue, and then, at a well-timed interval, offers a personal story to shed light on a particular concern. Our elders often have emotional maturity and a seasoned perspective on our life’s challenges. Comforting people have usually gone through their own losses and have gained some insight on their own rocky journeys. Without giving advice or interfering in what we choose to do, they share their own stories of what they’ve learned.
有时，一位睿智的人会静静地坐在一旁，倾听着关于棘手问题的尴尬或痛苦的对话，然后在恰当的时机，分享自己的故事，为某个特定的担忧提供启发。长辈们往往拥有成熟的情感和阅历，能够以更深刻的视角看待我们生活中的挑战。那些给予我们安慰的人，通常都经历过自己的失去，并在坎坷的人生旅程中积累了深刻的感悟。他们不会给出建议，也不会干涉我们的选择，而是分享他们自己的人生故事和感悟。

STRONG— persevering, resilient, enduring, confident
坚强——坚持不懈、韧性十足、持之以恒、自信
Especially when we are ill or feeling tired and weak, it is comforting to have someone around who is energetic, strong, and confident. These hardy folks can give us a boost, helping us to do the physically demanding or emotionally draining things, such as dumping the trash, cleaning the cat litter box, or calling the insurance company to straighten out claims forms and bills. They are up to the task when we feel incapable of handling it.
尤其是在我们生病或感到疲惫虚弱的时候，身边有精力充沛、强壮自信的人会让我们感到无比安慰。这些坚强的人能给我们力量，帮我们完成那些体力消耗大或精神压力大的家务，比如倒垃圾、清理猫砂盆，或者打电话给保险公司处理理赔表格和账单。当我们感觉力不从心时，他们总能挺身而出。
F ORTUNATELY, WE ALL HAVE SOME of these comforting traits. Our unique clusters of attributes define the ways we are most authentic in comforting others, though some traits may strengthen or diminish over the years, reflecting our values and goals. Most people find they have certain highly reliable attributes, and put these into practice as relational skills throughout their lifetime.
幸运的是，我们每个人都具备一些令人感到温暖的特质。我们独特的特质组合决定了我们安慰他人的最真诚的方式，尽管有些特质可能会随着时间的推移而增强或减弱，这反映了我们的价值观和目标。大多数人发现自己拥有某些非常可靠的特质，并在人生的各个阶段将其运用到人际交往中。
Looking over this list again, we might assess our own comforting traits, choosing our top five strengths that stand out. Or, if we want to use a bit more scrutiny (in a comforting way, of course), we could score ourselves, ranging from 1 (lowest) to 10 (highest) on our various comforting abilities.
再次审视这份清单，我们可以评估自身的一些令人感到安慰的特质，并选出其中最突出的五项优势。或者，如果我们想更深入地审视一下（当然，是以一种令人感到安慰的方式），我们可以对自己各项安慰能力进行评分，从1分（最低）到10分（最高）。
Being present and listening

充满希望id_00011}}谦逊
支持和认可id_00013}}感激
慷慨大方id_00015}}温柔体贴id_00016}}适应力强id_00017}}睿智id_00018}}坚强
For example, picking five of these attributes that best reflect me, I am strong in the qualities of empathy, warmth, supportiveness, reliability, and genuineness. My most prominent and enduring trait is empathy.
例如，如果要从这些特质中挑选五项最能代表我，我会说我具有很强的同理心、热情、乐于助人、可靠和真诚。我最突出、最持久的特质是同理心。
My lowest five, my least developed qualities, include being present, calm, patient, and accepting. I am still not a very good listener (I give myself a score of 4), even though I’ve had gazillions of hours of training in counseling practices! My empathy gets me too carried away with another person’s emotions, and it all goes to my mouth. I need to be careful that I don’t blurt things out, working at taking breaths, focusing my attention, and doing little tension relievers to stay centered. Playing to my strengths, I tend to be a better comforter with groups, as a speaker and trainer, rather than in one-on-one work, though I am eternally improving. Certainly, with my “lovingly honest” colleagues and loved ones, I practice my not-so-developed comforting skills, especially good listening.
我最差的五项特质，也就是我最不擅长的品质，包括专注、冷静、耐心和接纳。我仍然不是一个好的倾听者（我给自己打4分），尽管我接受过无数小时的咨询培训！我的同理心让我太容易被他人的情绪所左右，最终脱口而出。我需要注意不要脱口而出，努力深呼吸，集中注意力，做一些放松的小事来保持内心的平静。发挥我的优势，我更擅长在团体中、作为演讲者和培训师时给予安慰，而不是一对一的咨询，尽管我一直在不断进步。当然，在和那些“真诚友善”的同事和亲人相处时，我会练习我并不十分擅长的安慰技巧，尤其是倾听。
Our best comforting traits are there for us to claim and nurture, foundations for building our skills and practices as comforters, for others as well as ourselves. Introverts among us can be comforting with their quiet presence and calm, patient listening. Talkative types can share their caring and warmth by advocating for their loved ones. Accepting, humble, and nonjudgmental people can sit down with us when we feel too ashamed or embarrassed to go to a support group. Reliable, kindhearted, but not-so-touchy-feely types can comfort us with little acts of caring such as making a meal, running an errand, or doing a special favor. Certainly, any thoughtful act of kindness can be comforting to anyone. We don’t need any extraordinary comforting qualifications to comfort people when we genuinely care and take action.
我们身上最能抚慰人心的特质，需要我们去发掘和培养，它们是我们提升抚慰技巧和实践的基础，无论对他人还是对自己都是如此。内向的人可以用他们安静的陪伴和耐心倾听来抚慰人心。健谈的人可以通过为所爱之人发声来传递关爱和温暖。当我们因为羞愧或尴尬而不敢参加互助小组时，那些接纳、谦逊、不带偏见的人可以坐下来陪伴我们。那些可靠、善良但不太喜欢肢体接触的人，可以用一些小小的关怀之举来安慰我们，比如做顿饭、跑腿办事或帮个小忙。当然，任何体贴的善意之举都能给人带来安慰。我们不需要任何特殊的“抚慰者”资质，只要我们真心关心他人并付诸行动，就能抚慰人心。
# ↩

CHAPTER 2
第二章
Comforting in Action
行动中的安慰
# ↩

A Calling

召唤

F IVE YEARS AGO, I faced something worse than compassion fatigue—a sense of dismay at the lack of compassion throughout our society. What was happening to our safety nets for people in need? Like many Americans, I was aghast at the cuts in social services around the country amid rising health care, education, housing, and child care costs. The once-flourishing mental health and vocational rehabilitation agencies where I had worked back in the 1990s were now cutting vital programs for poor and isolated people coping with serious mental illness. And more cuts were on the way. I watched some of my rehabilitation colleagues growing more despondent and cynical. It was getting tougher and tougher out there for those of us who were frail, fragile, or poor, without social support systems in their lives.
五年前，我面临的困境比同情疲劳更甚——一种对我们整个社会缺乏同情心的沮丧感。我们为弱势群体提供的社会保障体系究竟出了什么问题？和许多美国人一样，我震惊于在医疗、教育、住房和儿童保育成本不断上涨的情况下，全国各地的社会服务却在不断削减。我曾在上世纪90年代工作过的那些曾经蓬勃发展的精神健康和职业康复机构，如今却在削减那些为贫困且孤立无援、身患严重精神疾病的人们提供的关键项目。而且，更多的削减还在后面。我眼睁睁地看着一些康复领域的同事变得越来越沮丧和愤世嫉俗。对于我们这些体弱多病、脆弱无助、贫困潦倒，且缺乏社会支持系统的人来说，生活变得越来越艰难。
Like many of my former clients who had been “dumped” by their social services providers, I felt undervalued and dehumanized by my own health care providers. I didn’t feel I mattered or had a voice when I was reaching out to the people I needed to help me. Trying to find someone to really hear me and give me the time of day had nearly become a full-time job. Going from doctor to doctor, I had been seeking help for some strange, troubling sensations in my heart and upper abdomen, but no one had listened carefully and patiently enough, and my symptoms had been dismissed as anxiety. I had expected to be taken seriously when I tried to describe a frightening incident of nearly collapsing in a bookstore. Instead, I was told to take relaxation classes and do more walking.
就像我很多被社会服务机构“抛弃”的前客户一样，我感觉自己被自己的医疗保健人员轻视，被他们非人化对待。当我向需要帮助的人求助时，我感觉自己无关紧要，也没有发言权。寻找一个真正倾听我、愿意花时间听我倾诉的人几乎成了我的全职工作。我辗转于各个医生之间，寻求帮助，希望能缓解心脏和上腹部一些奇怪而令人不安的感觉，但没有人认真耐心地倾听，我的症状都被轻描淡写地归咎于焦虑。我本以为，当我试图描述在书店里差点晕倒的惊险经历时，他们会认真对待。然而，他们却建议我去上放松课，多散步。
To make a long, frustrating story short, I finally located two astute and respectful female physicians who ordered a thorough workup, including an echocardiogram, stress test, many EKGs, and other lab tests. They found problems in the functioning of my left ventricle, and needed to control my blood pressure and heart rhythms more aggressively with several stronger medications. If I hadn’t listened to my intuition and my own heart, and if no one had listened to me, I may have ended up with heart failure within a few years.
长话短说，我最终找到了两位医术精湛、待人尊重的女医生，她们为我安排了全面的检查，包括心脏超声、运动负荷试验、多次心电图以及其他实验室检查。她们发现我的左心室功能存在问题，需要用几种更强效的药物来更积极地控制我的血压和心律。如果我当初没有听从自己的直觉和内心的声音，如果当初没有人听取我的建议，我可能几年之内就会患上心力衰竭。
My physician, a D.O., and later my cardiologist, were two women who skillfully practiced the language of comforting. Fully present, listening with respect and empathy, they gently provided me with a vital opportunity to speak up honestly, thoroughly, and comfortably. Not only was I heard, supported, and calmed in their presence, I was literally given the right treatment, medically, ethically, and compassionately. Finally, I felt human again. Normal again. Dignified again. My heart disease was not “all in my head” after all.
我的内科医生（一位整骨医生）和后来的心脏病专家都是女性，她们都非常擅长用安慰的语言与我交流。她们全神贯注地倾听，带着尊重和同理心，温柔地给予我一个至关重要的机会，让我能够坦诚、完整、自在地表达自己的想法。在她们的陪伴下，我不仅感到被倾听、被支持、被安抚，而且还得到了真正恰当的治疗，从医学、伦理和人文关怀的角度出发。最终，我感觉自己又重新做回了人，又恢复了正常，又重拾了尊严。我的心脏病并非“只是我的臆想”。
Profoundly inspired by the life-saving implications of my providers’ comforting practices, I had a revelation: Comforting skills were more than soft, feel-good accessories for enhancing our connections—they were essential for clear, open, and honest communication. If people didn’t feel genuinely welcomed and encouraged to tell what really had happened to them, then what did our providers and loved ones have to go on? The art of comforting meant creating a safe place for telling the truth, which, as in my case, could even save a life. We needed the “soft” skills of comforting to establish reliable lines of communication, especially in places where “hard” medical science was supposed to heal us.
深受医护人员的安慰之举所启发，我恍然大悟：安慰技巧不仅仅是增进彼此关系的轻柔手段，更是清晰、开放、坦诚沟通的基石。如果人们感受不到真诚的欢迎和鼓励，不敢倾诉自己的真实经历，那么医护人员和亲人又该如何判断呢？安慰的艺术在于创造一个可以畅所欲言的安全空间，而正如我的经历，这甚至可以挽救生命。我们需要这些“软性”的安慰技巧来建立可靠的沟通渠道，尤其是在那些本应依靠“硬性”医学手段来治愈我们的地方。
After reflecting on the importance of the comforting skills my two doctors had practiced so well, I felt called to learn more about this practical wisdom from other professionals. I wanted to find compassionate comforters skilled at creating safe places for communicating difficult and painful things, for telling the truth of our experiences, without being rushed, judged, pegged, or ignored. These comforters were out there, busy on their jobs, but gifted at giving us their genuine acceptance, respect, and care when we were feeling vulnerable. They could assure us that, in a world hard to be soft in, we could be little sanctuaries of comfort for each other.
在反思两位医生精湛的安慰技巧后，我感到自己有责任向其他专业人士学习更多这方面的实用智慧。我渴望找到富有同情心的安慰者，他们擅长营造安全的环境，让我们能够倾诉那些艰难痛苦的经历，讲述真实的感受，而不会被催促、评判、贴标签或忽视。这些安慰者就在那里，他们虽然工作繁忙，却拥有在脆弱无助时给予我们真诚接纳、尊重和关怀的天赋。他们让我们确信，在这个难以敞开心扉的世界里，我们可以彼此成为对方的慰藉之所。
# ↩

Calling All Comforters!

呼叫所有爱心人士！

I didn’t need to search the planet for highly comforting people to interview. I already knew many remarkable professionals who had heartened and motivated me over the years, when my compassion had needed a boost. I started rounding up exceptionally comforting colleagues in different occupations from several states I had lived in and visited. I was also given recommendations of other comforters by my colleagues.
我无需费尽心思在全球范围内寻找能给人带来慰藉的人进行采访。多年来，每当我的同情心需要鼓励时，我都会遇到许多杰出的专业人士，他们给予我鼓励和动力。于是，我开始联系我曾经居住和到访过的几个州、从事不同职业的、特别能给人带来慰藉的同事。我的同事们也向我推荐了一些其他能给人带来慰藉的人。
Gradually and naturally, through casual discussions, and later, through more formal interviews, I gathered the insights and suggestions of thirteen comforters. They each had their own unique perspectives, viewed from their particular occupation, but, reassuringly, I discovered they were all speaking the same language of comforting, putting universal comforting skills into practice every day in their jobs. They might be rushing through their days as a nurse practitioner, a grief counselor, or a police liaison, but they each had effective and quick ways of putting comforting into action. As I learned their how-to’s of comforting, I was relieved to discover many of their practices only involved a minute of their time, though making a huge difference in the people they served. To my surprise and joy, I found their recommended activities to be highly applicable for most of us, at home and at work.
通过与他人的非正式交流，以及后来的正式访谈，我逐渐收集到了十三位安慰者的见解和建议。他们每个人都从各自的职业角度出发，拥有独特的视角，但令人欣慰的是，我发现他们都在用同一种语言表达安慰，并在日常工作中实践着通用的安慰技巧。他们或许是忙碌的执业护士、悲伤辅导员或警务联络员，但他们都有着高效快捷的安慰方法。在学习他们的安慰技巧时，我欣慰地发现，他们的许多做法只需花费一分钟的时间，却能给他们服务的对象带来巨大的改变。令我惊喜的是，我发现他们推荐的方法对我们大多数人来说都非常适用，无论是在家还是在工作中。
Every one of my highly comforting guides told me their most recommended practice was to establish a human-to-human connection before “getting down to business.” Putting the human relationship first, no matter how much we had to accomplish, was at the heart of comforting. Above and beyond our agendas, our titles, our purpose, our roles, honoring the relationship for its own sake was essential for comforting in all personal and professional activities.
我所有给予我极大安慰的导师都告诉我，他们最推荐的做法是在“开始谈正事”之前建立人与人之间的联结。无论我们有多少任务要完成，把人际关系放在首位，才是安慰的核心所在。超越我们的议程、头衔、目标和角色，尊重人际关系本身，对于所有个人和职业活动中的安慰都至关重要。
Comforters were skilled at greeting us warmly and inviting us into their space, making us feel we belonged there with them, no matter what the purpose of the occasion was supposed to be. We lost the magic of a comforting moment when we rushed to extract and abstract from someone what we needed to meet our goals and serve our purpose. We dampened our sense of belonging with each other if we bypassed the little acts of caring that didn’t quite fit our schedules.
那些善于安慰他人的人，懂得热情地迎接我们，邀请我们融入他们的空间，让我们感到自己是他们中的一员，无论当时的场合目的是什么。当我们急于从他人身上索取和提取我们所需，以达到自身目标和目的时，我们就失去了安慰时刻的魔力。如果我们忽略了那些不合时宜的、细微的关怀之举，我们彼此之间的归属感就会减弱。
Expediency was the greatest threat to comforting, according to my colleagues. If people were only there to serve a purpose, to move along in our assembly-line mentality of being productive, then, of course, our souls got the not-so-comforting message that we only mattered for our functions.
