And that made us feel like machines, commodities, objects, and not warm-blooded, caring human beings.
我的同事们认为，权宜之计是对慰藉的最大威胁。如果人们存在的意义仅仅是为了服务于某种目的，为了在流水线式的生产思维中按部就班地工作，那么，我们的灵魂自然会接收到一个令人不安的信息：我们存在的价值仅仅在于我们的功能。这让我们觉得自己像机器、商品、物品，而不是有血有肉、充满爱心的人。
It was possible to comfort people even in hectic jobs with demanding schedules, and establishing good connections saved time in the long run. A little bit of rapport-building at the beginning made all the difference. Taking a few minutes to connect with a person individually could ensure good communication at later times when that person’s concerns became more complicated and stressful.
即使在工作繁忙、日程紧张的情况下，安慰他人也是可能的，而且从长远来看，建立良好的人际关系可以节省时间。一开始花一点时间建立融洽的关系至关重要。花几分钟时间与对方进行一对一的交流，可以确保在日后对方遇到更复杂、更棘手的问题时，能够进行有效的沟通。

Following is a list of the core comforting skills displayed universally by the master comforters I interviewed:
1. Preparation skills for comforters to inform themselves about the situation being faced by the person in distress before meeting with them.
2. Greeting skills for establishing a warm and welcoming connection, and putting the person at ease.
3. Acquainting, orienting, and hosting skills to calm, support, and reassure the person in distress, especially when in unfamiliar surroundings and when meeting new people.
4. Skills in creating comforting environments and atmospheres for working, healing, and recreation.
5. Conversation skills to foster comfortable, relaxed opportunities to communicate with empathic comments and open-ended questions.
6. Facilitation skills for guiding and engaging people in comforting activities such as playing board games, baking bread, or beading necklaces.
以下是我采访过的所有安慰大师普遍展现的核心安慰技巧：1. 准备技巧：在与受助者见面之前，了解他们所处的困境。2. 问候技巧：建立温暖友好的联系，让受助者感到放松自在。3. 熟悉、引导和接待技巧：安抚、支持和安慰受助者，尤其是在陌生环境和结识新朋友时。4. 营造舒适的工作、疗愈和休闲环境的技巧。5. 沟通技巧：通过富有同理心的评论和开放式提问，营造轻松舒适的沟通氛围。6. 引导技巧：引导和带领人们参与舒适的活动，例如玩棋盘游戏、烘焙面包或串珠项链。
In this chapter, five talented, friendly, and articulate professional caregivers, all with at least fifteen years’ experience in their fields, will be serving as personal guides to these skills and practices of comforting. They will each show us how they establish human-to-human connections in their busy jobs, as well as their concrete, simple ways of comforting others, verbally and nonverbally.
在本章中，五位才华横溢、友善健谈的专业护理人员，均拥有至少十五年的从业经验，将作为我们的亲身导师，指导我们掌握这些安慰技巧和方法。他们将分别向我们展示如何在繁忙的工作中建立人与人之间的联结，以及他们如何运用具体、简便的方法，通过语言和非语言的方式安慰他人。
But just as important as their practical how-to’s of comforting, I couldn’t help noticing the outstanding personal qualities of these individuals. Each comfort guide possesses distinct attributes, and generously applies them when sharing their knowledge and skills, putting comfort into action in their own way. If we recall the Twenty Top Comforting Qualities introduced earlier, we can see how each guide shines from their own comforting qualities, playing to their strengths. Though all comfort guides have their bundle of abilities, and all possess a good amount of empathy and presence, particular atributes stand out in each of them.
但与他们提供的实用安慰技巧同样重要的是，我注意到这些人的卓越个人品质。每位安慰导师都拥有独特的特质，并在分享知识和技能时慷慨地运用这些特质，以各自的方式将安慰付诸实践。如果我们回顾一下前面提到的二十项最佳安慰特质，就能看出每位导师是如何凭借自身的安慰特质，发挥自身优势而熠熠生辉的。虽然所有安慰导师都具备一系列能力，并且都拥有相当的同理心和亲和力，但每个人身上都有一些特别突出的特质。
# ↩

PUTTING THE HUMAN CONNECTION ABOVE EVERYTHING ELSE

将人际关系置于一切之上

Jeff Lewis, N.P.
杰夫·刘易斯，执业护士
Nurse Practitioner, Cardiology Unit (2002-2008)
心脏病科执业护士（2002-2008）
Togus Veterans Affairs Medical Center, Augusta, Maine
缅因州奥古斯塔市托格斯退伍军人事务医疗中心
Anytime a patient shares something personal about their history, I tell them, “It’s a privilege to know this about you.”
每当有病人分享他们的个人经历时，我都会告诉他们：“能够了解您的这些经历是我的荣幸。”
Core Comforting Qualities: Appreciation and Respect
核心安慰特质：欣赏和尊重
Feeling shy and a little nervous about calling Jeff at work, I was hoping I could just leave a friendly, concise voice mail asking him for an interview. Instead, he answered the phone. I told him who I was and what my call was about in my nine-second, well-rehearsed blurb, and modestly asked, “Do you have a minute?”
我有点害羞，也有些紧张，因为要打电话给杰夫，我原本希望可以留个友好简洁的语音留言，请求他给我一个采访机会。没想到，他接了电话。我用事先准备好的九秒钟简短介绍自己，说明了来意，然后谦虚地问道：“您有空吗？”
To my surprise and relief, he cheerfully replied, “I’ve got exactly three minutes.”
令我既惊讶又欣慰的是，他愉快地回答说：“我还有三分钟时间。”
At the end of our three minutes, we had scheduled a series of short interviews during his lunch breaks on Mondays at Togus Veterans Affairs Medical Center. It was now four minutes into our call, and I was aware our time was up. “That was a productive three minutes, and I’ll let you go . . . thank you so much.”
三分钟通话结束时，我们已安排好每周一他在托格斯退伍军人事务医疗中心午休时间进行一系列简短采访。通话已经进行了四分钟，我知道时间到了。“这三分钟很有成效，就此挂断……非常感谢。”
In closing Jeff said, “Thank you for calling, a nice surprise today. It’s an honor to be asked to be interviewed about something as important as comforting—and I’ve got some great stories to share with you.”
最后，杰夫说道：“谢谢你的来电，今天真是个惊喜。能受邀接受关于抚慰人心这样重要话题的采访，我感到非常荣幸——而且我有很多精彩的故事想和你分享。”
My instincts that Jeff would be an ideal candidate as a guide to comforting were validated by this brief exchange. He could work wonders in four minutes of a conversation, by putting a person at ease while getting down to business. Yes, there did exist in this world some kind, respectful, and appreciative individuals who could be comforting and productive at the same time, even at crowded, humongous veterans hospitals.
我之前的直觉——杰夫是安抚他人的理想人选——在这次简短的交流中得到了证实。他能在短短四分钟的谈话中发挥奇效，既能让人放松下来，又能直入主题。是的，这世上确实存在一些善良、尊重他人、懂得感恩的人，他们既能给人以安慰，又能高效地完成工作，即使是在人满为患、规模庞大的退伍军人医院里也是如此。
On his Monday lunch breaks on the cardiology unit, Jeff and I have had wonderful heart-to-heart talks about comforting. We were interrupted about every six minutes by patients popping into his office, and each time Jeff would calmly and masterfully switch gears back to focusing on our conversation, tuning out everything around him, listening closely, as if I mattered more than anything in the entire hospital, at least for a few minutes.
周一中午，杰夫在心脏科病房午休时，我们经常促膝长谈，探讨如何安慰病人。大约每隔六分钟，就会有病人突然走进他的办公室，打断我们的谈话。但每次杰夫都能沉着冷静、巧妙地将注意力重新集中到我们的对话上，屏蔽掉周围的一切，全神贯注地倾听，仿佛我比整个医院里任何人都重要——至少在那几分钟里是这样。
Our meetings have convinced me it’s possible to be fully present, comfortable, and happily engaged in the most hectic of settings. A few minutes of Jeff’s attention is fulfilling and downright fun. Giving me his smiles, nods, sympathetic shrugs, laughs, and “I know what you mean” expressions, he heartily follows what I’m saying about my passion for the art of comforting. With his lively curiosity and rapt interest in my questions, we go through scenarios to describe how he comforts his patients.
我们的会面让我确信，即使在最繁忙的环境中，也能全神贯注、自在放松、积极投入。杰夫的几分钟专注倾听，让我感到充实而愉悦。他面带微笑，点头，同情地耸耸肩，开怀大笑，还用“我懂你”的表情回应我，认真聆听我讲述我对安慰艺术的热情。他充满好奇，全神贯注地回答我的问题，我们一起探讨各种情景，了解他是如何安慰病人的。
“My patients blow me away.” He shakes his head in amazement. “They’re stronger than you think—they comfort me half the time.”
“我的病人让我惊叹不已。”他惊讶地摇了摇头。“他们比你想象的要坚强得多——他们常常安慰我。”
Watching the faces of Jeff’s patients light up when they enter his office, how he welcomes and attends to them in a brisk and affectionate way, I can see why he is so popular with veterans, and why award plaques cover his wall. And as I learned more about Jeff’s remarkable background, I discovered that he’s had a lifetime of dedication to comforting people in distress and trauma.
看着杰夫的病人走进诊室时脸上绽放的笑容，看着他热情而亲切地迎接和照顾他们，我明白了为什么他如此受退伍军人欢迎，也明白了为什么他的墙上挂满了奖牌。随着我对杰夫非凡经历的了解加深，我发现他一生都致力于安慰那些身处困境和创伤中的人们。
“My father died at only thirty-nine years of age when I was twelve. He had been diagnosed with colon cancer, had a colostomy, and later the cancer spread to his liver. I observed how well he adapted to living with a terminal illness, and learned much about comforting from him.
“我父亲在我十二岁那年去世，年仅三十九岁。他被诊断出患有结肠癌，做了结肠造口术，后来癌细胞扩散到了肝脏。我亲眼目睹了他如何很好地适应与绝症抗争的生活，并从他身上学到了很多关于如何安慰他人的技巧。”
“Though he was the one with the illness—the one in pain—he gave us comfort by showing us how much we meant to him. He strongly believed in keeping positive, not for himself so much as for others around him. He told me repeatedly, ‘If you are having a good day, you can make someone’s bad day better, but when you are having a bad day, you can make someone’s good day worse.’ He taught me that we had a great effect on each other’s days, for better or worse, just with our demeanor, mood, and outlook. With his short life, he showed me that we mattered by making others feel they mattered.
“虽然他身患疾病，饱受病痛折磨，但他用行动告诉我们，我们对他来说有多么重要，这给了我们莫大的安慰。他坚信要保持积极乐观，这不仅是为了自己，更是为了身边的人。他反复告诉我：‘如果你心情好，就能让别人的坏心情好起来；但如果你心情不好，也会让别人的好心情变得更糟。’他教会我，无论好坏，我们的举止、情绪和人生观都会对彼此的生活产生巨大的影响。在他短暂的一生中，他让我明白，我们之所以重要，是因为我们让别人感受到了他们的重要性。”
“Before my dad got cancer, I had been a typical self-centered and manipulative kid, who couldn’t have cared less if I had teased some classmate at school or picked a fight with my brother. But once my father was ill, I watched my worried mother and siblings trying to take care of him. They were so afraid they weren’t doing enough for him. He reassured them by holding their hands and telling them how well they were helping him. I saw how he comforted the comforters and the comforters comforted him. Soon, encouraged and coached by my father, I was putting into practice some comforting behaviors of my own, and felt the difference in the tension level of our household. To my surprise, I discovered I liked being a comforter, a nurturer, a caregiver. No wonder I ended up working in nursing and emergency medical services!”
“在我父亲患癌之前，我是一个典型的以自我为中心、爱耍手段的孩子，根本不在乎自己是否在学校里捉弄过同学，或者和弟弟打过架。但父亲生病后，我看到忧心忡忡的母亲和兄弟姐妹们竭尽全力地照顾他。他们害怕自己做得不够好。父亲握着他们的手，告诉他们他做得很好，以此来安慰他们。我看到他如何安慰那些照顾他的人，而那些照顾他的人又如何安慰他。很快，在父亲的鼓励和指导下，我也开始尝试一些安慰别人的方法，并感受到家里的气氛明显缓和了。令我惊讶的是，我发现自己喜欢安慰别人、照顾别人、关爱别人。难怪我最终会从事护理和急救工作！”
In his teens, he volunteered for his local EMS (Emergency Medical Services) department, and learned to calm and attend to frightened patients in ambulances. He later served as a part-time paramedic firefighter for twelve years, while working as an ER nurse for fifteen years. He has been a nurse-practitioner at Togus Veterans Affairs Medical Center for seven years. All of his positions have involved following strict, rapid-response protocols for patients in acute crisis. Almost daily for thirty years, he has practiced the skills of comforting in the most dire, life-and-death situations.
十几岁时，他就在当地的急救部门做志愿者，学会了如何在救护车上安抚和照顾受惊的病人。后来，他做了十二年的兼职急救员兼消防员，同时在急诊室做了十五年的护士。七年来，他一直在托格斯退伍军人事务医疗中心担任执业护士。他的所有工作都要求严格遵循快速反应流程，为处于急性危机中的病人提供服务。三十年来，他几乎每天都在练习如何在最危急、生死攸关的时刻给予病人安慰。
Wherever he goes, he taps the nurturing wisdom of his father. “Every day, when I walk into this hospital to work, I carry with me my father’s words and love of life. I practice ‘having a good day’ for the sake of others around me, and this certainly helps my day, too.” If anyone in the world knows how to create a comfort zone in the midst of chaos, Jeff does.
无论走到哪里，他都汲取着父亲的智慧和教诲。“每天走进医院上班，我都会想起父亲的话语和他对生活的热爱。我努力让自己‘过好每一天’，为了身边的人，这当然也让我自己过得更好。” 如果说世上有人懂得如何在混乱中营造舒适感，那非杰夫莫属。
# ↩

JEFF’S MOST IMPORTANT QUALITIES OF A COMFORTING PERSON

杰夫作为令人感到安慰的人所具备的最重要的品质

Jeff designated the following as the most vital abilities of comforters:
• Warm and welcoming, takes time to greet the person
“Being a comforting presence means paying personal attention to the patient and getting to know them as a real person. It’s essential that we take the time to establish rapport and trust first, before we do anything else. I’ve learned that if I rush through my first few minutes with a patient, preoccupied with treating them before I really listen to them, then it’s harder for both of us to move forward with each other as partners in healing. So, taking the time at the beginning to get to know a patient really saves time in the long run.”
• Appreciates what a person has to say, and shows it
“I deeply believe in the power of appreciating people. Showing my gratitude and respect, especially with veterans, has helped to develop healthy, trusting bonds. My father taught me the benefits of letting people know how important they are, by recognizing the ways they are contributing to the relationship, not just to the ‘program.’ Expressing gratitude openly to people creates an opportunity to point out their strengths, values, and personal traits, a natural kind of positive reinforcement.”
• Can tune out distractions and tune in to the person
• Finds out what is comforting for that person in particular
杰夫认为，安慰者最重要的能力包括：• 热情友好，花时间问候对方。“成为一个令人感到安慰的人意味着要关注患者，了解他们作为一个人的真实情况。在做任何其他事情之前，我们必须先花时间建立融洽的关系和信任。我发现，如果我匆匆忙忙地度过与患者的最初几分钟，一心只想治疗他们而没有真正倾听他们的心声，那么我们双方就很难像合作伙伴一样携手共进，共同康复。因此，在开始时花时间了解患者，从长远来看真的能节省很多时间。” • 欣赏他人的话语，并表达出来。“我深信欣赏他人的力量。表达我的感激和尊重，尤其是在对待退伍军人时，有助于建立健康、信任的关系。我的父亲教导我，要让人们知道他们有多重要，要认可他们对这段关系的贡献，而不仅仅是对‘项目’的贡献。公开表达感激之情，能让我们有机会指出他们的优点、价值观和个人特质，这是一种自然的积极强化。” • 能够排除干扰，专注于对方。• 了解什么能让对方感到特别舒适。
# ↩

JEFF’S COMFORTING PRACTICES IN HIS WORK

杰夫在工作中采取的安慰性做法

1. Learn about the person’s background and situation before you meet with them—if that information is available.
1. 在与对方见面之前，了解对方的背景和情况——如果可以获取这些信息的话。
Jeff believes it’s important to prepare ourselves with any accessible information before approaching the person we want to help.
杰夫认为，在接近我们想要帮助的人之前，事先掌握所有可获取的信息非常重要。
“Before meeting with the person, I find out about the person’s situation with any accurate information that is available. This helps me think ahead about some of the issues the person may be dealing with. I study their social support networks, and especially pay attention to people who have little social support. I check to see if they have sustained any major losses recently. For example, when I see that their spouse has died in the past year, or that they have recently relocated to a nursing facility, I am prepared to address any grief or stress that might interfere with their medical treatment.”
“在与对方见面之前，我会尽可能了解对方的情况，获取所有可用的准确信息。这有助于我提前思考对方可能面临的一些问题。我会研究他们的社会支持网络，尤其关注那些缺乏社会支持的人。我会了解他们近期是否遭受过重大损失。例如，如果我发现他们的配偶在过去一年中去世，或者他们最近搬进了养老院，我就会做好准备，帮助他们应对可能影响其医疗治疗的任何悲伤或压力。”
Jeff says another reason to find out about the person’s situation is that we need to avoid asking them too many questions. “The person may be in emotional or physical pain, and not be ready to articulate and explain what has been going on very clearly or specifically.”
杰夫说，了解当事人情况的另一个原因是，我们需要避免问他们太多问题。“当事人可能正承受着情感或身体上的痛苦，无法清晰或具体地表达和解释发生了什么。”
Extreme stress and grief can affect our cognitive abilities, our memory, our concentration, and our reasoning skills. It’s not very comforting for distressed people to answer a barrage of questions from someone on a probing, fact-finding mission. We need to be gentle with our “what happened?” questioning while we interact with the person. We might not get all the information, or the correct information, all at once. But gradually, by accepting and appreciating what they are able to tell us with our patience, good listening, and gratitude, the person might eventually be better able to communicate more information.
极度的压力和悲痛会影响我们的认知能力、记忆力、注意力以及推理能力。对于正处于痛苦中的人来说，回答那些刨根问底、刨根问底的问题，无疑是一种折磨。在与他们交流时，我们需要温柔地询问“发生了什么事？”。我们可能无法一次性获得所有信息，或者所有信息都准确无误。但是，通过耐心倾听、心怀感激地接受并欣赏他们所能讲述的内容，他们最终或许能够更好地表达更多信息。

2. Welcome people with warm, respectful greetings, and introduce yourself and your role.
2. 用热情、尊重的问候欢迎他人，并介绍自己和自己的职务。
I watched Jeff in action at the hospital, as he welcomed his patients and enjoyed the back and forth banter of their casual conversation. It was obvious the patients relaxed within only thirty seconds of chatting. Jeff says:
“I introduce myself, telling them that I am a nurse practitioner by choice (why I chose this career over being a cardiologist), and invite them to use me as a ‘go-to’ person for their questions. Then, I ask them what’s been going on in their world, and listen closely to what they tell me has happened recently. Once again, taking the time at the beginning to get to know a person really pays off later in more efficient communication when facing challenges along their course of treatment.”
我在医院亲眼目睹了杰夫的工作，他热情地迎接病人，并乐于与他们轻松愉快地交谈。很明显，病人在短短三十秒的聊天后就放松了下来。杰夫说：“我会先自我介绍，告诉他们我是一名执业护士（这也是我选择这份职业而不是成为心脏病专家的原因），并邀请他们把我当作可以随时咨询的人。然后，我会询问他们最近的生活状况，并认真倾听他们讲述的经历。再次强调，在治疗初期花时间了解病人，对于之后在治疗过程中遇到挑战时更高效的沟通至关重要。”
Jeff’s words as a nurse-practitioner apply to all of us as comforters. Greetings are essential for establishing a comforting encounter. When we walk into an unfamiliar building to meet a new provider, or we travel to meet a friend at their home, or we meet a new colleague, having our host meet us and greet us with welcoming gestures relaxes and reassures us. We get the message: “It’s good to see you!” But, when we don’t get that message, we worry about what might be wrong, and maybe even fret that the host does not honestly want to meet us. It’s not only rude not to greet people, it’s downright destructive to establishing trust and basic eye-to-eye contact.
作为一名执业护士，杰夫的话对我们所有人来说都适用，因为我们都是安慰者。问候对于建立令人安心的会面至关重要。当我们走进一栋陌生的建筑去见一位新的医护人员，或者去朋友家拜访，又或者去见一位新同事时，如果主人热情地迎接我们，并以亲切的姿态问候我们，我们会感到放松和安心。我们能感受到对方的诚意：“很高兴见到你！”但如果我们没有感受到这种诚意，我们就会担心是不是出了什么问题，甚至会担心主人其实并不真心想见我们。不打招呼不仅失礼，而且会严重破坏信任的建立和基本的眼神交流。

3. Follow the lead of the people you’re serving, and share in their concerns. They give you cues as to what concerns are bothering them.
3. 听从你所服务对象的引导，分担他们的担忧。他们会向你透露他们关心的问题。
When we comfort someone, we need to begin with the understanding that even if their concern doesn’t seem to us to be the “real” issue or the “problem,” we need to respect the reality of their pain, and tune in through their eyes to how their situation is impacting them. In Jeff’s work, he needs to identify the concerns of his patients because these can be barriers to their treatment. It might be their financial concerns, transportation problems, insurance issues, housing issues, marital issues, or dietary issues that might interfere with the patient focusing on their treatment. Jeff needs to know these and address them, but first he uses his active listening skills to elicit from patients those barriers. “I’ve seen some patients completely unable to relax without their rosaries, who needed to hold them in their hands the whole time they were being examined. So, I take their personal requests seriously, if this means they are able to feel more comforted and relaxed in a medical setting. Or, say, if someone is really angry, and that presents a barrier, I need to support them in vocalizing what is making them upset. It helps to establish trust by allowing that person to vent their concerns or complaints while I listen and take the time we need.”
当我们安慰他人时，首先要明白，即使他们的担忧在我们看来并非“真正”的问题或“症结所在”，我们也需要尊重他们痛苦的真实感受，并设身处地地从他们的角度去体会他们的处境如何影响着他们。在杰夫的工作中，他需要了解患者的担忧，因为这些担忧可能会成为他们治疗的障碍。这些担忧可能包括经济问题、交通问题、保险问题、住房问题、婚姻问题或饮食问题，这些都可能干扰患者专注于治疗。杰夫需要了解并解决这些问题，但他首先会运用积极倾听的技巧，引导患者说出这些障碍。 “我见过一些病人，没有念珠就完全无法放松，他们在接受检查时必须一直握在手里。所以，如果这意味着他们能在医疗环境中感到更舒适、更放松，我会认真对待他们的个人需求。或者，比如说，如果有人真的很生气，这造成了沟通障碍，我需要支持他们表达自己的不满。允许他们倾诉自己的担忧或抱怨，我会认真倾听，并花必要的时间与他们沟通，这有助于建立信任。”
We comforters need to show our appreciation and respect for any obstacles or problems the person in distress is communicating to us. Comforters are not the ones to judge these barriers as “excuses,” “rationalizations,” or “BS” when we don’t agree that their “issues” are keeping them from taking action or making important decisions. As comforters, we accept that any concerns a person in distress shares with us are whatever that person is ready to handle or address. Maybe later that person will be ready to face challenges in a more head-on way, but in the acute stages of crisis or grief, a person may not be ready for that.
我们这些安慰者需要对身处困境的人向我们倾诉的任何障碍或问题表示理解和尊重。当我们不认同他们的“问题”确实阻碍了他们采取行动或做出重要决定时，安慰者不应该将这些障碍斥为“借口”、“合理化”或“胡说八道”。作为安慰者，我们理解身处困境的人向我们倾诉的任何担忧，都取决于他们自身能够承受或解决的程度。或许日后他们会准备好以更积极的方式面对挑战，但在危机或悲痛的初期阶段，他们可能还没有做好准备。

4. Find what keeps the person hopeful.
4. 找到让这个人保持希望的原因。
Instilling hope is a powerful comforting tool. Jeff emphasizes, “We can listen closely and discover whatever it is that person is looking forward to—and it just might surprise us.” Comforters don’t have to offer cheery, hopeful platitudes, or “you’ll be fine” assurances, but they can help the person in distress connect with something they hope to do in the near future. It could be a visit with a pet therapy dog, or a Sunday dinner with their sister, or a long-awaited movie release. I’ve known people who held on to their sanity just by looking forward to the latest episode of Dancing with the Stars . Jeff says even people at the end of their lives with terminal illnesses find things to keep them going strong.
传递希望是一种强有力的安慰方式。杰夫强调：“我们可以仔细倾听，发现对方真正期待的是什么——这或许会让我们感到意外。”安慰者不必说些欢快的、充满希望的陈词滥调，或者诸如“你会好起来的”之类的保证，但他们可以帮助身处困境的人与近期内想要做的事情联系起来。这可以是和宠物治疗犬的互动，或是和姐妹共进周日晚餐，又或是期待已久的电影上映。我认识一些人，他们仅仅依靠期待最新一期的《与星共舞》节目来保持理智。杰夫说，即使是身患绝症、生命垂危的人，也能找到让他们保持坚强的动力。
“Keeping hope alive is important, even when the person is facing terminal illness. Instilling hope doesn’t mean giving people false hope or trying to cheer them up. It means listening to their hopes, joining them in envisioning their dreams, wishes, and goals, whether they have six months to live or sixty years. As a cardiac nurse-practitioner, for the sake of their hearts, I try to keep their spark of hope alive—such as helping someone live for a few more weeks to make it to the birth of their grandchild.”
“即使身患绝症，保持希望也至关重要。给予希望并非虚假的希望或试图让他们振作起来，而是倾听他们的希望，与他们一起展望梦想、愿望和目标，无论他们只剩下六个月的生命还是六十年。作为一名心脏科执业护士，为了他们的心脏健康，我努力守护他们心中的希望之火——例如，帮助患者多活几周，让他们能够迎来孙辈的出生。”
5. Show your appreciation when people tell you personal things about themselves.
5. 当别人告诉你一些关于他们自己的私事时，要表达你的感激之情。
As comforters, when people in distress offer to tell us confidential and deeply private things, we can gently express our appreciation for this. It takes courage for people to open up and trust each other with painful issues. We might say, as comforters, “I am honored that you shared this with me. It sounds like this was hard to tell anyone.” Here’s what Jeff says to his patients that confide in him:
“Any time a patient shares something important about themselves, I tell them, ‘It is a privilege to know this about you.’ I let them know how deeply grateful I am to be the one they have confided in, even though, as a health care professional I am ‘supposed’ to know their health histories or habits. Histories are personal, and sometimes hard to share. Working with veterans here at Togus, I am always honored, sometimes amazed, when they open up with their honesty and humility. This deepens our relationship, and they will keep coming back to me when they need to ask hard questions about their prognosis or their functional limitations.”
作为安慰者，当身处困境的人愿意向我们倾诉私密且极其私人的事情时，我们可以温和地表达我们的感激之情。人们需要勇气才能敞开心扉，彼此信任，倾诉痛苦的经历。作为安慰者，我们可以说：“我很荣幸您能与我分享这些。听起来，这些事很难开口。”杰夫是这样对那些向他倾诉的病人说的：“每当病人分享一些重要的个人信息时，我都会告诉他们：‘能够了解您的这些经历是我的荣幸。’我会让他们知道，我多么感激他们愿意向我倾诉，即使作为一名医护人员，我‘理应’了解他们的病史或生活习惯。但病史是个人隐私，有时难以启齿。在托格斯医院与退伍军人共事，每当他们坦诚谦逊地敞开心扉时，我总是感到荣幸，有时甚至感到惊讶。这加深了我们之间的关系，当他们需要询问有关预后或功能障碍等棘手问题时，他们会再次来找我。”
# ↩

HOW TO GIVE “BAD NEWS” IN A COMFORTING WAY

如何以安慰的方式传达“坏消息”

Sometimes, unfortunately, we find ourselves in the position of having to give bad news to our loved ones or others we are serving, and the delicate language of comforting needs to be put into practice. Jeff has much experience with this difficult role of being the messenger with bad news. He encourages us to be honest, humble, and gentle in our approach.
有时，我们不得不向亲人或我们所服务的人传达坏消息，这令人遗憾，这时就需要运用委婉的语言来安慰他们。杰夫在这方面经验丰富，他深知传递坏消息的艰难。他鼓励我们以诚实、谦逊和温和的态度来对待他们。
“We can beat ourselves up worrying about how to tell people bad news. We try to anticipate how they will respond and imagine all kinds of ways to say things right. When I’ve second-guessed what people were going to say, I’ve usually been wrong. I’ve learned over the years all this forethought tends to impair the communication. We need to get ourselves out of the way, our heads out of the way, and just speak from our hearts. It doesn’t take long for people to look through you when you are saying something with genuine care and concern. They can feel it in your voice and see it in your eyes. If we follow the lead of the person we are serving, and get our expectations and fears out of the way, the words will usually come out the right way.
我们常常会因为担心如何告诉别人坏消息而自责不已。我们试图预判他们的反应，并设想各种合适的表达方式。但当我揣测别人会说什么时，通常都是错的。这些年来我发现，这种过度思考反而会阻碍沟通。我们需要放下自我，放下思绪，用心去表达。当你用真诚的关心和体贴说话时，人们很快就能感受到。他们能从你的声音和眼神中感受到。如果我们顺应对方的意愿，放下自己的预期和恐惧，通常就能说出恰当的话。
“I often say, ‘There is no easy way to say this, but . . . I’m just going to say it . . . ,’ when I am giving bad news.
“我经常说，‘这件事很难说出口，但是……我还是要说……’，当我要宣布坏消息的时候。”
“Most people are more resilient than we think. I believe we can convey our belief in the strength of that person, and empower them without candy-coating the news. We can offer to walk alongside them, letting them know what’s involved in each step along the way. We can only offer our help as far as the next step goes, because we don’t see the final destination. In a sense, we are only able to see a little ahead at a time, and can’t see the whole picture. So, in giving bad news, talking about the near future, the next few steps, is more comforting than talking about the distant, more uncertain future.”
“大多数人比我们想象的更有韧性。我相信我们可以传递我们对他们力量的信念，并在不粉饰太平的情况下给予他们力量。我们可以陪伴他们，让他们了解每一步的进展。我们只能在下一步提供帮助，因为我们看不到最终的结局。从某种意义上说，我们一次只能看到一点点，而无法看到全貌。因此，在告知坏消息时，谈论近期的未来，接下来的几步，比谈论遥远而充满不确定性的未来更能让人感到安慰。”
Here are a few pointers to help communicate bad news:
以下是一些有助于传达坏消息的技巧：

1. Have your information right at hand. Sometimes we are the ones doing the hard job of explaining detailed or complex information to people in distress or to those we are serving as caregivers.
1. 将信息放在手边。有时，我们需要承担艰巨的任务，向处于困境中的人或我们作为照护者所服务的对象解释详细或复杂的信息。
“Be ready for referencing and showing the person your facts and information. You need the verification right in front of you, ready for when the person asks questions and wants to see the ‘proof’ of the information with their own eyes. When people are hearing bad news, they often want to see where this news is coming from. It’s not that they don’t trust you, it’s just that it helps things to ‘sink in’ when viewing the actual written materials. Having your information at hand conveys to the person you are organized (which helps them trust in you), as well as reassures them they are being included (‘in the loop’) of what is being assessed.”
“准备好向对方提供事实和信息。你需要将核实信息放在手边，以便在对方提问并希望亲眼查看信息‘证据’时能够及时回应。当人们听到坏消息时，他们通常想知道消息的来源。这并非因为他们不信任你，而是因为查看书面材料有助于他们更好地理解和接受信息。将信息放在手边，既能向对方表明你做事有条理（这有助于他们信任你），也能让他们安心，让他们知道自己被纳入了评估流程。”
2. Say, “Here’s what’s going on so far.” Lay out for the person what the latest reports are showing, and present the options for the next steps to take.
2. 说：“目前的情况是这样的。”向对方详细说明最新报告显示的内容，并提出下一步可以采取的措施。
“Let the person know the plan, for example, what is proposed for a course of treatment, or what the options are for any path to take, with their pros and cons. In a sense, we are thinking out loud with the person, planning with and empowering the person. This ‘knowledge is power’ approach is comforting in itself, as it alleviates the person’s fears of the unknown. Most people want to know ‘how bad’ or ‘how serious’ their situation is (say, if they are hearing about their lab test results after a biopsy), and we are there as interpreters to quantify the level of ‘badness’ in the results. We tell them ‘how bad it is,’ only taking one step at a time, one test result at a time. We need to be humble, and not jump to conclusions about the information. Offer phrases such as, ‘This is what we know now , as far as we can tell.’ ”
“让患者了解治疗方案，例如，拟定的治疗方案，或者各种治疗途径的优缺点。从某种意义上说，我们是在与患者一起思考、制定计划并赋予他们力量。这种‘知识就是力量’的方法本身就令人感到安慰，因为它能减轻患者对未知的恐惧。大多数人都想知道自己的病情‘有多糟糕’或‘有多严重’（例如，在活检后得知化验结果时），而我们的职责是解读结果，量化结果中的‘糟糕程度’。我们会告诉他们‘情况有多糟糕’，但每次只解释一个步骤，一次只解释一个化验结果。我们需要保持谦逊，不要对信息妄下结论。可以使用诸如‘就我们目前所知，情况就是这样’之类的措辞。”
3. Involve people you are serving in the decision-making.
3. 让你的服务对象参与决策。
“Show them the options for which course to take, but also offer them some time to think about it. Provide a follow-up plan for a check-in time, to take the next step.”
“向他们展示可供选择的课程，同时也给他们一些时间考虑。提供一个后续跟进计划，以便他们进行下一步的跟进。”
Jeff’s Dos and Don’ts for Comforters
杰夫关于被子的注意事项
# ↩

HONORING OUR HUMILITY

尊重我们的谦逊

Adrienne Dormody, M.Ed., LICSW
Adrienne Dormody，教育硕士，LICSW（持证临床社会工作者）
Patient Education Specialist
患者教育专家
Mayo Clinic, Rochester, Minnesota
梅奥诊所，明尼苏达州罗切斯特市
It helps to remember that no one human being can ever see the entire picture in relating to another person or situation.
需要记住的是，在与他人或事物交往时，没有人能够看到事情的全貌。
Core Comforting Qualities: Humility and Integrity
核心的安慰品质：谦逊和正直
I first met Adrienne in 1996 at a women’s spiritual retreat in Minnesota called A Gathering of Women, led by bestselling author Joan Borysenko ( Minding the Body, Mending the Mind ) and her colleagues. In a greeting ceremony at the start of the retreat, Joan had asked us to pick up a red rose (from dozens generously provided to us), then walk quietly toward a participant unknown to us, and hand it to them in silence. For some amazing reason, I felt guided to give my rose to Adrienne.
我第一次见到艾德琳是在1996年，当时我们在明尼苏达州参加了一个名为“女性聚会”的女性灵修静修营，由畅销书作家琼·博里森科（《身心疗愈》的作者）和她的同事们带领。在静修营开始时的欢迎仪式上，琼让我们从主办方慷慨提供的数十朵红玫瑰中挑选一朵，然后静静地走向一位素不相识的参与者，默默地将玫瑰递给她。不知为何，我感觉冥冥之中有种指引，要把玫瑰送给艾德琳。
We quickly opened up about our reasons for coming to the gathering, and found we both were seeking spiritual comfort in order to heal our bodies. Adrienne had recently completed a grueling regimen of treatments for endometrial cancer. She had known in her heart that sharing her story with other women at the retreat would bring her a sense of peace. In the end, this act of sharing inspired all of us women. In sharing our stories of facing radical life changes without maps, manuals, or mentors, we celebrated together our courage as well as our humility. We had taken our leaps of faith in thin air, courageously enough, but we admitted our humility in having to take many tedious, little steps before and after our leaps.
我们很快敞开心扉，谈起了各自来参加聚会的原因，发现我们都在寻求精神慰藉，以疗愈身心。艾德琳刚刚结束了一段漫长而艰辛的子宫内膜癌治疗疗程。她内心深处知道，在静修营里与其他女性分享自己的经历，会让她获得内心的平静。最终，这种分享的行为激励了我们所有女性。我们分享了各自在没有指南、没有手册、也没有导师的情况下，如何面对人生巨变的经历，我们共同庆祝彼此的勇气，也共同赞颂彼此的谦卑。我们勇敢地迈出了信仰的一步，但我们也承认，在迈出这一步之前和之后，我们不得不迈出许多艰难而微小的步伐，这本身就是一种谦卑。
Ever since our rose ceremony, Adrienne and I have been steady colleagues, helping each other to restore our dedication to our professions, preventing ourselves from suffering from the burnout of compassion fatigue. Adrienne has comforted me with her funny, feisty, yet compassionate responses to my life’s predicaments, and has taught me the value of humility.
自从玫瑰仪式之后，我和艾德琳就一直是稳定的同事，我们互相扶持，重拾对工作的热情，避免因同情疲劳而精疲力竭。艾德琳用她风趣、活泼又不失同情心的回应安慰我，让我不再为生活中的困境而烦恼，她也教会了我谦逊的价值。
Her gift of humility so generously shared with me has been reflected in all of her professional roles. She worked as a clinical social worker for the psychiatry department at the Mayo Clinic for more than eight years, providing group, marital, and family therapy. She arranged discharge plans for patients from around the world and from all walks of life. For another eight years, she served as a counselor for the Nicotine Dependence Center at the Mayo Clinic, and helped implement a counseling technique called Motivational Interviewing, with the goal of engaging patients more actively in their treatment. She taught this approach to many other professionals after being trained in it herself. Before her years at the Mayo Clinic, she was a teacher, a family educator, and a program coordinator for an in-home elder care service.
她谦逊的品格慷慨地与我分享，并体现在她所有的职业角色中。她曾在梅奥诊所精神科担任临床社工八年多，提供团体、婚姻和家庭治疗。她为来自世界各地、各行各业的患者制定出院计划。之后，她又在梅奥诊所尼古丁依赖中心担任咨询师八年，协助推广一种名为“动机式访谈”的咨询技巧，旨在让患者更积极地参与治疗。她本人接受过相关培训后，将这种方法传授给了许多其他专业人士。在加入梅奥诊所之前，她曾是一名教师、家庭教育工作者，以及居家养老服务项目的协调员。
She is now a patient education specialist at the Mayo Clinic. She plans, procures, and develops materials for educating patients about the prevention and treatment of illness and the promotion of health. Her challenge in this role is to serve as a reliable conduit between health care professionals and the educational needs of patients and families. It is essential that she be rigorous in the interpretation and dissemination of vital information going back and forth between many parties.
她现在是梅奥诊所的患者教育专员。她负责规划、采购和开发用于教育患者了解疾病预防、治疗和健康促进方面的材料。她面临的挑战是，如何成为医护人员与患者及其家属之间可靠的沟通桥梁，满足他们的教育需求。因此，她必须严谨地解读和传播各方之间往来的重要信息。
Considering the demands of being a primary liaison between the Mayo Clinic’s vast systems, it’s amazing how Adrienne brings forth her qualities of humility and integrity to establish and maintain reliable lines of communication. She can walk into an emotionally charged situation with a distressed patient, an anxious family, a frustrated nurse, and a harried physician, and diffuse the tension by being unassuming and attentive, asking simple questions and allowing all parties to clarify and specify their needs. In short, her humility helps her get herself out of the way so she can attune to others. Adrienne explains how she serves people at the Mayo Clinic:
“To be comforting, it helps to remember that no one human being can ever see the entire picture in relating to another person or situation. I find it humbling and comforting that I can only see part of the big picture, only part of the whole truth. In working directly with patients, I’ve tried to walk into a room without assumptions and expectations, to be totally present to them. This has been hard work, as it does not always come naturally to me. I’ve had to keep in mind that my view, the physician’s view, the nurse’s view, the patient’s view, and the family’s view are all only pieces in the bigger picture. I have gained great respect for what physicians and nurses do, especially with all the demands on them in these times. I believe they work extremely hard for their patients, though they see through their lenses, too, as we all do.
“In my role as patient educator, serving as a liaison between many health care professionals and patients, I need to be a comforting presence while listening to each person’s vital input in order to put the pieces together. If my ego, or my tension, or my biases interfere, I cannot fairly convey important health information, and much could be lost in miscommunication.”
考虑到她作为梅奥诊所庞大系统间主要联络人所面临的重任，艾德琳能够展现出谦逊和正直的品质，建立并维护可靠的沟通渠道，着实令人惊叹。即使面对情绪紧张的病人、焦虑的家属、沮丧的护士和疲惫的医生，她也能以谦逊和专注的态度化解紧张气氛。她会提出简单的问题，让各方有机会澄清和明确自己的需求。简而言之，她的谦逊让她能够放下自我，更好地理解他人。艾德琳解释了她在梅奥诊所如何为人们服务：“为了安慰他人，记住这一点很有帮助：没有人能够全面了解另一个人或一种情况。我发现自己只能看到全局的一部分，只能看到全部真相的一部分，这让我感到既谦卑又欣慰。在直接与患者接触时，我努力做到不带任何预设和期望地走进诊室，全身心地陪伴他们。这并非易事，因为对我来说，做到这一点并不总是自然而然的。我必须牢记，我的观点、医生的观点、护士的观点、患者的观点以及家属的观点，都只是更大图景中的一小部分。我对医生和护士的工作充满敬意，尤其是在如今这个时代，他们面临着如此多的压力。我相信他们为患者付出了巨大的努力，尽管他们也像我们所有人一样，带着自己的视角看待问题。作为一名患者教育者，作为众多医护人员和患者之间的联络人，我需要在倾听每一位患者心声的同时，给予他们安慰和支持。”个人的意见至关重要，它能帮助我们把所有信息拼凑起来。如果我的自尊心、紧张情绪或偏见干扰了沟通，我就无法公正地传达重要的健康信息，很多信息可能会因为沟通不畅而丢失。
Over many years, Adrienne and I have enjoyed our favorite, never-ending conversation about the importance of humility and integrity in our roles as comforters. We’ve discovered that true comforters can embrace the fallibility of themselves and others, as they understand how long-cherished beliefs can suddenly collapse in the chaos of a radical loss. Even our most sacred commitments and values can sometimes fall by the wayside in the turbulence of unforeseen changes. Because many comforters know very well how it feels when one’s world falls apart, they can sit humbly and openly with devastated people who don’t know what to believe anymore. Adrienne says:
“Absolute certainty is an illusion. Life can change instantly. We can think we have it all together, and then suddenly our world is turned upside down. A diagnosis of a life-threatening illness can do that to us. It happened to me fourteen years ago, when I was diagnosed with endometrial cancer three months after my wedding. I was starting a new life with a whole new family, full of joyous expectation. The resulting chronic issues challenged me to the core. My pain and consequent humility from that experience has brought me to a deeper sense of compassion and respect for comforting others and myself, and for educating patients and staff in my work. I still believe that no one has the last word on anything—at least, not for long!”
多年来，我和艾德琳一直乐此不疲地探讨着谦逊和正直在我们作为安慰者的角色中的重要性。我们发现，真正的安慰者能够坦然接受自己和他人的弱点，因为他们明白，在经历巨大打击的混乱中，那些我们珍视已久的信念也可能瞬间崩塌。即使是我们最神圣的承诺和价值观，有时也会在突如其来的变故中被抛诸脑后。正因为许多安慰者都深知世界崩塌时的感受，他们才能谦逊而坦诚地陪伴那些迷失方向、不知所措的人们。艾德琳说：“绝对的确定性是一种错觉。生活瞬息万变。我们可能以为一切尽在掌握，但突然间，我们的世界就天翻地覆了。确诊危及生命的疾病就可能让我们经历这样的巨变。十四年前，我结婚三个月后就被诊断出患有子宫内膜癌，这让我感同身受。当时，我正满怀喜悦地组建新的家庭，开启新生活。然而，随之而来的慢性疾病却让我身心俱疲。那段经历带来的痛苦和谦卑，让我对安慰他人和自己有了更深的同情和尊重，也让我更加重视在工作中教育患者和医护人员。我仍然相信，没有人能对任何事情拥有最终决定权——至少，不会长久如此！”
Recently, on New Year’s Day, Adrienne and I tenderly shared each other’s list of resolutions for 2010, as we tackled the same old goals we’ve been struggling with for decades. In acknowledging each other’s fallibility and lack of focus in reaching some of our resolutions, we felt much lighter when we declared we would honor how we handled the obstacles and detours that had taken us off course. As always, when I’ve panicked that I’ve lost my way and gotten off course with what I was “supposed” to be doing, Adrienne has reassured me that I’m a worthy person, whether off course or on course.
最近，在元旦那天，我和艾德琳温柔地分享了彼此的2010年新年计划，我们再次面对那些困扰了我们几十年的老目标。我们坦诚地承认彼此的不足，以及在实现某些目标时注意力不够集中，但当我们决定要尊重自己应对那些让我们偏离正轨的障碍和弯路的方式时，我们都感到轻松了许多。一如既往，每当我惊慌失措，觉得自己迷失了方向，偏离了“应该”做的事情时，艾德琳总是安慰我说，无论我是否走在正确的道路上，我都是一个有价值的人。

The Most Important Qualities of a Comforting Person
一个令人感到安慰的人最重要的品质
Adrienne says the following core attributes define a comforting person:
• humility
• warmth
• sincerity
• interest in others
• integrity
艾德琳认为，以下核心特质定义了一个令人感到安慰的人：谦逊、热情、真诚、关心他人、正直。
# ↩

ADRIENNE’S COMFORTING PRACTICES IN HER WORK

艾德琳在工作中采取的安慰措施

1. Smile and look people in the eyes.
1. 微笑并看着别人的眼睛。
Adrienne believes in the importance of smiling with our greetings. People feel instantly welcomed with our warmth and our friendly eye-to-eye recognition.
艾德琳认为，微笑问候非常重要。人们会立刻感受到我们热情友好的眼神交流，并感到宾至如归。
Smiling genuinely is a sure bet for the nonverbal language of comforting in the first five seconds of an encounter. We don’t need to give big, gregarious smiles and warm and fuzzy welcomes, but kind, modest smiles of acknowledgment make a world of difference for people in distress.
在初次见面的五秒钟内，真诚的微笑无疑是传递安慰的最有效非语言方式。我们无需展现热情洋溢的笑容和热情洋溢的欢迎，但一个友善而谦逊的微笑，就能给身处困境的人们带来莫大的安慰。

2. Establish an alliance by making it clear what our different roles are in serving the person, including our role as a provider.
2. 通过明确我们在服务该人时的不同角色，包括我们作为提供者的角色，来建立联盟。
Adrienne suggests we assist the person in getting acquainted with us in our role as comforter, and further, by explaining how our role fits in with other providers and social supports. The art of acquainting people with one another is one of the finer arts of comforting. In the Oxford Dictionary , the word acquaint means to “make someone aware or familiar with.”
艾德琳建议我们帮助对方熟悉我们作为安慰者的角色，并进一步解释我们的角色如何与其他服务提供者和社会支持体系相融合。让人们彼此熟悉是安慰艺术中精妙的一门。牛津词典对“acquaint”一词的解释是“使某人意识到或熟悉”。
People who step into busy, impersonal, or vast settings can get their bearings sooner by having providers acquaint them to the particular roles they are playing, and how to utilize their help. We feel more empowered when we know the appropriate go-to people for assistance with our needs. People in distress need easy, concrete orientations to acquaint them to new programs, activities, or routines.
人们进入繁忙、冷漠或广阔的环境时，如果服务提供者能帮助他们了解自己扮演的具体角色以及如何利用所提供的帮助，就能更快地找到方向。当我们知道在需要帮助时应该向谁求助时，我们会感到更有掌控感。处于困境中的人们需要简单明了的指导，才能熟悉新的项目、活动或流程。
As comforters, we might accompany those in distress with “walk-throughs” or tours to new places where they will be receiving services. Or, for more social and recreational activities, we can accompany them in meeting new faces and getting them started with new connections. In short, comforters can be great navigators and tour guides for paving the way for people in distress to get acquainted with new connections and networks.
作为安慰者，我们可以陪伴身处困境的人们，带他们“实地考察”或参观他们将要接受服务的新场所。或者，对于更多社交和娱乐活动，我们可以陪伴他们结识新朋友，帮助他们建立新的人际关系。简而言之，安慰者可以成为优秀的导航员和向导，为身处困境的人们铺平道路，帮助他们建立新的关系和人脉网络。

3. Ask people open-ended questions about their lives, and engage in talking about their interests and concerns.
3. 向人们提出关于他们生活的开放式问题，并参与讨论他们的兴趣和担忧。
Adrienne knows how to elicit conversation by finding topics of interest with the people she serves. She also has a pleasant, gentle curiosity about people’s lives.
艾德琳懂得如何通过寻找与服务对象共同感兴趣的话题来开启对话。她对人们的生活也抱有令人愉悦的、温和的好奇心。
Again, as part of acquainting ourselves, asking open-ended questions invites much more conversation than questions with yes or no answers. A good comforter can hone in on what interests the person might have, saying things such as, “Sounds like you haven’t missed an episode of The Dog Whisperer for years! What about the dogs in your life?” (Instead of asking, “Do you have dogs?”)
再次强调，在互相了解的过程中，提出开放式问题比只能回答“是”或“否”的问题更能引发对话。善于安慰他人的人会抓住对方的兴趣点，比如会说：“听起来你好几年都没错过《狗狗语者》的任何一集了！你家里养狗吗？”（而不是直接问“你养狗吗？”）

4. Acknowledge the importance of everyone’s roles.
4. 承认每个人角色的重要性。
Adrienne is able to respect and appreciate the many roles everyone plays in meeting the needs of those we comfort. Again, her humility serves her well in valuing how we each play a part in “seeing the big picture.” Comforters are important for reassuring the person in distress how everyone is vital in the roles they play, from the ones paying the bills, to the ones doing the surgery, to the ones dumping the trash. We all matter in the world of comforting.
艾德琳能够尊重并欣赏每个人在满足我们所安慰之人的需求中所扮演的各种角色。她的谦逊也让她能够更好地理解我们每个人在“把握全局”中所起的作用。安慰者之所以重要，是因为他们能让身处困境的人明白，每个人在各自的角色中都至关重要，从支付账单的人，到进行手术的人，再到倒垃圾的人。在安慰的世界里，我们每个人都举足轻重。

Adrienne’s Suggestions for Caregivers and Families
1. Show people you care, by telling them, writing them, giving them something, offering your help.
2. Acknowledge and clarify your role as a comforter, and acknowledge the roles others play in caring for them.
3. Listen and attend. Be fully present. Smile. Look them in the eyes. (Though this is hard to do these days with so many things demanding our attention.)
4. Touch their hand or arm, or give them a hug (with their permission).
5. Show interest in what they are interested in. Ask questions about their specific interests.
6. Invite them for a meal or a cup of tea.
7. For families, sit down for a meal with no interruptions, just to enjoy each other. Have a real conversation, and listen to one another’s stories (no cell phone talking, no TV on, no text-messaging).
8. Share with each other three things you are grateful for that day. (For children, this is a soothing activity right before bedtime.)
9. For children, play recordings of grandparents or loved ones telling a story. (I used to do this with my son when we lived far from his grandparents.)
艾德琳给照顾者和家人的建议：1. 通过言语、信件、礼物或主动提供帮助来表达你的关心。2. 明确并认可你作为安慰者的角色，同时也要认可其他人在照顾他们方面所扮演的角色。3. 倾听并全神贯注。全身心地投入。微笑。看着他们的眼睛。（尽管如今有太多事情需要我们关注，这很难做到。）4. 触摸他们的手或手臂，或者（在征得他们的同意后）给他们一个拥抱。5. 对他们感兴趣的事情表现出兴趣。询问他们具体的兴趣所在。6. 邀请他们一起吃饭或喝茶。7. 对于家人来说，坐下来不受打扰地吃顿饭，享受彼此陪伴的时光。进行真正的交谈，倾听彼此的故事（不要打电话、看电视或发短信）。8. 彼此分享当天三件值得感恩的事情。（对于孩子来说，这是一个睡前舒缓情绪的活动。）对于孩子，可以播放祖父母或亲人讲故事的录音。（以前我们住得离儿子祖父母很远的时候，我就经常这样做。）
COMFORTING THINGS FAMILIES CAN DO IN A HOSPITAL WITH SOMEONE WHO IS ILL
家人在医院陪伴病人时可以做的一些安慰事
• Show up, be there with the patient, be reliable about visiting when you say you are coming.
• 准时出现，陪伴在病人身边，信守承诺，按时探望病人。
• Act courteously and respectfully with all staff. (Which affects the patient’s care.)
• 对所有工作人员都应礼貌尊重。（这会影响患者的护理。）
• Make use of the chapel or a chaplain. Or walk on the grounds, courtyard, or quiet spaces.
• 您可以前往教堂或咨询牧师。也可以在场地、庭院或安静的地方散步。
• Share amusements and hobbies (if appropriate—check with provider first) such as crossword puzzles, knitting, books, photos, board games, toys, magazines, crafts, gifts, flowers.
• 分享娱乐和爱好（如果合适——请先与提供者确认），例如填字游戏、编织、书籍、照片、棋盘游戏、玩具、杂志、工艺品、礼物、鲜花。
• Eat a meal together (if appropriate).
• 一起用餐（如果合适）。
• Provide soothing touch (if appropriate—check with provider first). Rub their feet or hands, maybe add lotion.
• 给予轻柔的抚触（如果合适——请先咨询医护人员）。按摩他们的脚或手，可以涂抹润肤露。
• Provide music, entertainment.
• 提供音乐和娱乐。
Adrienne’s Dos and Don’ts for Comforters
艾德琳关于被子的注意事项
# ↩

KEEPING IT REAL

保持真实

Alicia Rasin
艾丽西亚·拉辛
Founder, Citizens Against Crime
公民反犯罪组织创始人
Victim’s Advocate, City of Richmond, Virginia
弗吉尼亚州里士满市受害者权益倡导者
Community Liaison, Richmond Police Department
里士满警察局社区联络员

Just show up, listen, keep it real, and be right there with them.
你只需要出现，倾听，保持真诚，并与他们同在。

Core Comforting Qualities: Genuineness and Empathy
核心舒适品质：真诚和同理心
For the past twenty years, Alicia Rasin has devoted her life to comforting grieving families devastated by homicide, gang violence, and other traumatic losses such as suicide, fire, and domestic abuse. She guides families through the steps of organizing funerals, memorial services, and candlelight vigils, and follows up with visits for grief counseling. She advocates for families, and provides them with contacts and vital referrals to legal aid, mental health, and other social services. She trains police officers at the Richmond Police Department in how to approach and serve families traumatized by murder and gang violence.
过去二十年来，艾丽西亚·拉辛一直致力于安慰因凶杀、帮派暴力以及其他创伤性事件（例如自杀、火灾和家庭暴力）而遭受重创的家庭。她指导这些家庭完成葬礼、追悼会和烛光守夜等各项事宜，并随后提供悲伤辅导。她为这些家庭争取权益，并为他们提供法律援助、心理健康和其他社会服务的联系方式和重要转介信息。她还为里士满警察局的警官提供培训，指导他们如何与遭受谋杀和帮派暴力创伤的家庭沟通并为他们提供服务。
Alicia loves her city enough to venture into neighborhoods immediately after a shooting, to reach households with her radiant compassion. She has even gone to homicide scenes before the police have been called. She is well known in Virginia for her courage and generosity of spirit, and has been named “Richmond’s Ambassador of Compassion” by former governor Tim Kaine, as well as the “The Mother Teresa of Richmond” by former police chief Rodney Monroe.
艾丽西亚深爱着她的城市，枪击案发生后，她会第一时间前往各个社区，用她那充满爱心的关怀慰问家家户户。她甚至在警方赶到之前就已抵达凶杀案现场。她在弗吉尼亚州以其勇气和慷慨精神而闻名，曾被前州长蒂姆·凯恩誉为“里士满的爱心大使”，也被前警察局长罗德尼·门罗称为“里士满的特蕾莎修女”。


W HEN I FIRST SPOKE WITH ALICIA on the telephone, she greeted me with a hearty hello and put me at ease right away. After I told her a little bit about this book, Alicia exclaimed, “People really don’t get enough comfort. It’s such a shame.”
我第一次和艾丽西亚通电话时，她热情地跟我打招呼，让我立刻感到放松自在。我简单地向她介绍了这本书之后，艾丽西亚感叹道：“人们真的太缺乏安慰了。这太可惜了。”
Alicia was remarkably open about her personal challenges with her health and well-being. She had survived stomach cancer years ago, and more recently had undergone heart surgery. She now volunteered as a victim’s advocate and police liaison with the City of Richmond, living on her disability checks, still working full-time, in constant demand. “I’ll probably need more heart surgery, too, my doctors tell me. I have a lot of heartache because I have a lot of grief, which is why my heart is having so many problems. It’s mostly from losing my dad a year and a half ago. I still miss him so much.”
艾丽西亚对自己的健康状况和生活状况毫不隐瞒。多年前她曾战胜胃癌，最近又做了心脏手术。如今，她靠残疾补助金生活，在里士满市担任受害者权益倡导者和警务联络员的志愿者，同时仍然全职工作，忙得不可开交。“医生告诉我，我可能还需要再做一次心脏手术。我心痛不已，因为我经历了很多悲伤，所以我的心脏才会出现这么多问题。这主要是因为我一年半前失去了父亲。我仍然非常想念他。”
Alicia had been her father’s primary caregiver for many years, and he had died in her arms in late 2006. She still lived in the house where she was raised, surrounded by his belongings.
多年来，艾丽西亚一直是她父亲的主要照顾者，2006 年底，她的父亲在她怀中去世。她仍然住在她长大的房子里，周围摆满了父亲的遗物。
I asked if her work with grieving families throughout the Richmond community was stressful for her, given her heart condition and her grief, and she emphatically stated, “Oh no, no—the work I do giving comfort to people really helps my heart a lot. It keeps me going. I’m doing the work God wants me to do. Comforting people is what my life is all about.”
我问她，考虑到她的心脏病和悲痛，在里士满社区为悲伤的家庭提供安慰的工作是否会让她感到压力，她斩钉截铁地说：“哦，不，不——我所做的安慰他人的工作真的让我感觉好多了。它给了我继续前行的动力。我正在做上帝想让我做的事。安慰他人就是我生命的意义所在。”
In the fall of 2008, I finally had a chance to meet Alicia in person at her home in one of the oldest neighborhoods in Richmond, Church Hill. Alicia had a huge Christmas tree lit up with blue lights, standing tall and touching her high ceilings in her sunny living room. Across her rose-colored walls and tabletops were many affectionately displayed pictures of her friends and family, plus the faces of the many families she had served over the years.
2008年秋天，我终于有机会在里士满最古老的街区之一——丘吉尔区——的艾丽西亚家中见到她本人。阳光明媚的客厅里，一棵巨大的圣诞树高耸入云，挂满了蓝色的彩灯，几乎触及了高高的天花板。玫瑰色的墙壁和桌面上，摆放着许多她与亲朋好友的温馨照片，以及多年来她服务过的众多家庭的合影。
We talked more about how hard it is for families and friends to find time to do comforting things with each other. Alicia related this problem to her own agenda of her busy weekend. “Today, I’ve got so much laundry to do, but I am trying to get out to see my friends who’ve waited to get together with me.”
我们进一步讨论了家人和朋友之间很难抽出时间一起做一些令人感到慰藉的事情。艾丽西亚把这个问题和她自己忙碌的周末安排联系起来。“今天我有很多衣服要洗，但我还是想抽出时间去见见我的朋友们，他们一直等着和我聚聚。”
I agreed that it’s sad that we have such a tough time putting time with our loved ones at the top of our lists.
我同意，我们很难把陪伴亲人的时间放在首位，这确实令人难过。
“That’s why, when we do finally get together, we need to be ourselves and give our hearts to each other. People need us to be all there with them, not just up in our heads. Our time together is so precious.”
“所以，当我们最终相聚时，我们需要做真实的自己，敞开心扉。人们需要我们全身心地陪伴他们，而不是只沉浸在自己的思绪中。我们在一起的时光如此珍贵。”
She spoke further about how we have been socialized to mask our feelings in our haste to make grieving people feel better. She laments, “If we don’t keep it real, we only make them feel worse. Because grieving people feel different from us, we can help them by showing we feel some of their sadness, or anger or fear, so they don’t feel so alone. They can feel us feeling with them, and that’s a lot of comfort right there.”
她进一步谈到，我们从小就被教导要掩饰自己的感受，急于安慰悲伤的人。她感叹道：“如果我们不坦诚相待，只会让他们更加难过。因为悲伤的人与我们感受不同，我们可以通过表达我们感同身受他们的悲伤、愤怒或恐惧来帮助他们，让他们不再感到孤单。他们能感受到我们与他们同在，这本身就是一种莫大的安慰。”
In our series of talks, Alicia has inspired me with her refreshingly honest and heartfelt observations about how we need to be ourselves when we offer comfort. Quickly feeling comfortable and open with her, I admitted that, even with my counseling training, there were times I lacked confidence in being authentic while consoling grieving parents. I’d never had kids of my own, and was worried that I might not be able to relate to mothers and fathers genuinely enough, from missing this experience. I felt a bit “different.”
在我们的系列谈话中，艾丽西亚以她坦诚真挚的见解深深地启发了我，她谈到我们在给予他人安慰时需要做真实的自己。我很快就和她感到自在，也敞开心扉地和她交流。我坦白说，即使接受过咨询方面的培训，有时在安慰悲痛欲绝的父母时，我仍然缺乏自信，无法做到真诚待人。我从未有过自己的孩子，担心自己可能无法真正理解为人父母者的感受，因为我错过了这种体验。我感觉自己有点“格格不入”。
“Alicia,” I asked, “how dare I try to know the pain of parents whose children have died?”
“艾丽西亚，”我问，“我怎么敢去了解失去孩子的父母的痛苦呢？”
She surprised me with her tender response, “I never had my own kids, either, Val. But I’ve been working with grieving parents for over twenty years, just by feeling their sorrow. I let their sorrow touch my own sorrow—my sorrow about my dad who died, or my friend who is sick, or my community in trouble—real sorrow. We are all human, and sorrow is in all of us. It’s okay if you don’t always know what to do when someone is in pain, as long as you can say with all your heart, ‘I am right there with you.’ People will believe you care if you just show up, even if you don’t have much to say. Just show up, listen, keep it real, and be right there with them.”
她温柔的回答让我感到意外：“瓦尔，我也没有自己的孩子。但我二十多年来一直在帮助那些失去孩子的父母，感受他们的悲伤。我让他们的悲伤触动我自己的悲伤——我为去世的父亲、生病的朋友、或是陷入困境的社区而悲伤——真切的悲伤。我们都是人，悲伤存在于我们每个人的心中。即使你不知道该如何安慰那些痛苦的人，也没关系，只要你能发自内心地说：‘我与你同在。’即使你没什么可说的，只要你出现，人们就会相信你在乎他们。只要出现，倾听，真诚待人，与他们同在。”
Alicia told me that she learned how to comfort by watching the different ways people comfort each other. Ever since she was a small child, she noticed what makes people feel better. “I’m still learning every day what comforts people, and I allow people to show me how to comfort them. I think we need to get better at observing more, listening more, tuning in to the little ways we can comfort others—people give us signs for what to do. Too many people don’t slow down enough to notice these subtle but important signs that tell us how to comfort each other.”
艾丽西亚告诉我，她是通过观察人们彼此安慰的不同方式来学习如何安慰别人的。从小她就注意到哪些事情能让人感觉好一些。“我每天都在学习如何安慰别人，也乐于接受别人的安慰方式。我认为我们需要更善于观察、倾听，留意那些可以安慰他人的细微之处——人们会给我们一些暗示，告诉我们该怎么做。太多人没有放慢脚步，注意到这些微妙却重要的信号，而这些信号恰恰告诉我们该如何安慰彼此。”
Alicia heartened me, reminding me of our human, universal sorrow and pain, giving us the integrity and “credentials” for being comforting with each other, no matter how different our personal experiences had been. I remembered women like Alicia, though “childless” themselves, who gave themselves to the children and families of the world, like Mother Teresa, or other women in spiritual and compassionate service. Alicia’s words reconnected me to this wider community of comforters. And I am forever grateful for the honest and generous time she spent with me.
艾丽西亚的话语让我深受鼓舞，她提醒我人类普遍存在的悲伤和痛苦，赋予我们彼此安慰的勇气和“资格”，无论我们个人的经历多么不同。我想起了像艾丽西亚一样的女性，她们虽然没有孩子，却像特蕾莎修女或其他在精神和慈悲中奉献的女性一样，将自己奉献给了世界上的儿童和家庭。艾丽西亚的话语让我重新与这个更广泛的安慰者群体建立了联系。我永远感激她与我共度的真诚而慷慨的时光。
ALICIA’S MOST IMPORTANT QUALITIES OF A COMFORTING PERSON
艾丽西亚作为令人感到安慰的人最重要的品质
• Accepts going into a situation without knowing how it will turn out
“We just don’t know what’s going to happen when we reach out. We need to let go and trust in something healing that happens beyond what we can control. It’s really taking a leap of faith to comfort someone in great pain . ”
• 接受在不知道结果如何的情况下进入某种境地。“我们伸出援手时，真的不知道会发生什么。我们需要放手，相信某种超越我们掌控的治愈力量。安慰一个身处痛苦中的人，真的需要莫大的勇气。”
• Feels what someone else feels, even without understanding that person’s experience
“Just by remembering we are human, we can tap in to our common emotions through our hearts.”
• 即使不了解他人的经历，也能感受到他人的感受。“只要记住我们是人类，我们就能通过内心感受到我们共同的情感。”
• Can see through a person’s pain to his soul
“A comforting person can see how someone is trying to cope with their pain. Comforting means seeing what they are doing to hold up, not just the distress they are in. We need to believe in that person and their own way of healing.”
• 能透过一个人的痛苦看到他的灵魂。“一个善于安慰的人能够看到别人是如何努力应对痛苦的。安慰意味着看到他们为了支撑自己所做的一切，而不仅仅是他们所处的困境。我们需要相信这个人，相信他们自身的疗愈方式。”
# ↩

ALICIA’S COMFORTING PRACTICES IN HER WORK

艾丽西亚在工作中采取的安慰性做法

Here is how Alicia comforts a family after a loved one has been murdered:
以下是艾丽西亚在亲人被谋杀后安慰家属的方式：

“We gather to say prayers and blessings out loud.”
“我们聚集在一起，大声祈祷和祝福。”
“First of all, right after I walk in the door, I ask everyone to gather around me and I say a few words of prayer with them. We have a kind of prayer huddle, all the family members, and sometimes friends or neighbors. I let other people say their own prayers if they want to.”
“首先，我一进门，就请大家围拢过来，和他们一起做个简短的祷告。我们就像一个祈祷小组，所有家庭成员都会参加，有时朋友或邻居也会加入。如果其他人愿意，我也会让他们自己祷告。”

“We hold hands in a circle, and share our memories and feelings.”
“我们手拉手围成一个圈，分享彼此的回忆和感受。”
“After our prayers, we stay in our huddle, and we all hold hands in a circle. I just listen to what people are saying and feeling about the loss.”
“祈祷结束后，我们围成一圈，手拉着手。我只是静静地听着大家诉说着失去亲人的感受。”

“We share hugs, if the children and families give us permission.”
“如果孩子和家人允许，我们会互相拥抱。”
“If they feel like it, the young ones will come up to me and hug and hold me. The kids seem to like that, and they smile, reaching out to hug me. It’s important that they have a choice to hug me or not. But most kids do want to give me a big hug. Some of those kids haven’t hugged anyone in a long time, especially if someone has died in their family.”
“如果孩子们愿意，他们会走过来拥抱我。孩子们似乎很喜欢这样，他们会笑着伸出手来抱我。让他们自己选择是否拥抱我很重要。但大多数孩子都想给我一个大大的拥抱。有些孩子已经很久没有拥抱过任何人了，特别是如果他们的家人去世了。”

“I check back on the family a few days or weeks later.”
“我会过几天或几周再去看看这个家庭的情况。”
“Later on, in a few days or weeks, I go back on another visit to check in on the family. It really helps to bring young volunteers from other grieving families with me. It gives the family hope when I come with other teens who have also lost someone, and who understand what the new family is going through. The kids can talk to the kids while I can talk to the adults, and it works very well.”
“过几天或几周后，我会再去探望这个家庭。带上其他失去亲人的家庭的年轻志愿者真的很有帮助。当我带着其他也失去亲人的青少年一起来时，他们能理解这个新家庭的处境，这能给他们带来希望。孩子们可以和孩子们交谈，而我可以和成年人交谈，这种方式效果非常好。”

“We take more time to share stories and memories.”
“我们会花更多时间分享故事和回忆。”
“When I visit families with the teen volunteers, it’s important to take a long time for sharing memories and going into details in our stories. A lot of times we talk about something funny and have a really good laugh. Sometimes the humor brings people together, because everybody wants to add more to a funny story, and it helps to get all kinds of feelings out.”
“当我带着青少年志愿者去拜访家庭时，我们会花很长时间分享回忆，详细讲述我们的故事。很多时候，我们会聊一些有趣的事情，然后开怀大笑。有时候，幽默能拉近人与人之间的距离，因为每个人都想为有趣的故事添油加醋，这有助于人们释放各种情绪。”
Alicia’s Dos and Don’ts for Comforters
艾丽西亚关于被子的注意事项
# ↩

THE POWER OF OUR PRESENCE

我们存在的力量

Reverend Patricia Ellen, M.Div.
Outreach Director, Center for Grieving Children,
Portland, Maine
Abbess of the Chaplaincy Institute of Maine
帕特里夏·艾伦牧师，神学硕士，缅因州波特兰市悲伤儿童中心外联主任，缅因州牧师学院院长。
When you give someone your total attention, you are creating a bubble of comfort, a little pocket of safety.
当你全神贯注地关注某人时，你就创造了一个舒适的泡泡，一个安全的港湾。
# ↩

CORE COMFORTING QUALITIES: PRESENCE AND CALMNESS

核心舒适特质：临在感与平静

As the outreach director at the Center for Grieving Children, Patricia oversees a program that reaches more than one thousand children and professionals a year, providing education and crisis support. When a school faces a death, crisis, or life-threatening illness, Patricia and the center’s staff and trained volunteers appear on site to support and comfort children, staff, and parents. Patricia fields questions and advises staff on concerns such as how children can be involved in wakes and funerals, how teachers can assist grieving children in their classes, how parents can be supported by school staff, or how to mobilize crisis intervention teams. She coauthored the book A Family’s Journey: A Handbook for Living with Illness and Finding Hope .
作为儿童哀伤关怀中心的对外联络主任，帕特里夏负责一个每年服务超过一千名儿童和专业人士的项目，提供教育和危机支持。当学校面临死亡、危机或危及生命的疾病时，帕特里夏会与中心的工作人员和受过培训的志愿者一起赶到现场，为儿童、教职工和家长提供支持和安慰。帕特里夏负责解答各种问题，并就诸如儿童如何参与守灵和葬礼、教师如何在课堂上帮助悲伤的儿童、学校工作人员如何为家长提供支持以及如何启动危机干预小组等问题为教职工提供建议。她与他人合著了《家庭之旅：与疾病共存并寻找希望的手册》一书。
Patricia is also the abbess of the Chaplaincy Institute of Maine, a role that dovetails beautifully with her outreach director position. In her work as abbess, she supervises and mentors chaplains in training to become interfaith ministers. In both of her positions, she serves as a guide to an individual’s personal and transformative journey through loss, the search for meaning, and spiritual growth. Patricia explains, “Our journeys through grief as well as through spiritual growth are processes fraught with turmoil, doubt, and ‘dark nights of the soul,’ but they can also bring us gifts of inspiration, compassion, and wisdom. Most chaplains have been through significant losses in their lives, and conversely, many people who have been through grief want to comfort others eventually, and are called to serve in some way.”
帕特里夏同时也是缅因州牧师学院的院长，这一角色与她的外联主任职务完美契合。作为院长，她负责指导和培养正在接受培训的牧师，使他们成为跨宗教牧师。在这两个职位上，她都致力于引导人们走过人生的转折之旅，帮助他们走出失去亲人的阴霾，寻求人生的意义，并实现精神的成长。帕特里夏解释说：“我们经历悲伤和精神成长的旅程充满了动荡、怀疑和‘灵魂的暗夜’，但它们也能带给我们灵感、同情和智慧的馈赠。大多数牧师都经历过人生中的重大损失，反过来，许多经历过悲伤的人最终也渴望安慰他人，并被召唤去以某种方式服务他人。”
She feels blessed to be working with organizations that value the importance of comforting the comforter, and practice what they preach with their own staff. “The staff at the Center for Grieving Children will drop everything to stop and be there for each other when we need it,” Patricia states confidently. “They support me in all that I do, as well as all that I don’t do to prevent burnout. Having true colleagues, reliable fellowship, and kindred values are vital for me in serving my community as a comforting professional.”
她觉得自己很幸运能与那些重视安慰施助者，并且言行一致的机构共事。“在儿童哀伤中心，每当我们需要彼此支持时，我们都会放下手头的一切，互相扶持，”帕特里夏自信地说。“他们支持我所做的一切，也支持我为了避免职业倦怠而选择不做的事情。拥有真诚的同事、可靠的伙伴和志同道合的价值观，对于我作为一名专业的安慰者服务社区至关重要。”


P ATRICIA AND I, both morning people, are together at seven a.m. for our breakfast meeting. Though we have a lot to cover and I am tempted to grab my notebook, she sits back in her chair with a relaxed smile, letting me know without words there is no need to rush. Her calmness is contagious, even in the fast-food restaurant on this Friday morning, where the townspeople of Gray, Maine, are increasingly streaming in behind our booth. I enjoy my coffee, and Patricia asks if our meeting spot was easy enough for me to find. Her directions were perfect, I answer, and wait to see if she has that “ready” look to get down to business with our interview.
我和帕特里夏都是早起的人，早上七点就约好一起吃早餐。虽然有很多事情要谈，我也很想拿出笔记本，但她却放松地靠在椅背上，脸上带着微笑，无需多言，就让我明白不必着急。她的沉稳很有感染力，即使是在周五的早晨，在缅因州格雷镇的快餐店里，她的平静也丝毫没有影响到我们。我们身后的卡座后面，人来人往，摩肩接踵。我一边喝着咖啡，一边听帕特里夏问我是否容易找到我们的会面地点。我回答说她的指示非常准确，然后等着看她是否准备好开始我们的采访。
She easily glided into a conversation with me about our common interests in spirituality and counseling work. She described how her teaching, presenting, administrative, and facilitation duties sent her to many appointments at venues scattered all over southern and central Maine. Patricia shared that she would be working to 9 p.m. that night, a frequent requirement for her, although I could not detect a bit of stress about her day’s itinerary. Working marathon hours just came with the territory of doing the work she loved. Like other highly comforting people I’d known, she could manage to be calm and friendly and appear unhurried on a very demanding day.
她轻松地和我聊起了我们共同感兴趣的灵修和咨询工作。她告诉我，她的教学、演讲、行政和协调工作让她奔波于缅因州南部和中部各地的众多场所。帕特里夏告诉我，她那天晚上要工作到九点，这对她来说是常态，但我丝毫没有察觉到她对当天行程安排有任何压力。长时间工作对她来说，是她热爱的工作的一部分。就像我认识的其他一些让人感到很温暖的人一样，即使在非常忙碌的一天，她也能保持冷静、友善，显得从容不迫。
In our conversations about comforting, even when discussing the sad news of the deaths of a few students at some schools recently, I felt Patricia’s serene acceptance of allowing people to grieve in their most natural ways. There were no right or wrong ways to grieve, and staff, parents, and kids were not to be judged for how they handled the unfolding crisis at their schools. Some teachers might have sought comfort in the teacher’s lounge and stared at the walls, while others researched grief on the Internet. Some social workers might have hugged parents; some principals might have made fifty phone calls in an afternoon. Some kids had written sympathy cards, while others played softball. For Patricia, everyone was doing what they needed to do to grieve, and she was there at the school to quietly stand in the background, to listen and help them find what grounded them, focused them, made things feel a bit more normal. Patricia served in a ministry of presence, gently offering her full attention and unconditional caring to people struggling with strong and often unfamiliar emotions.
在我们谈论如何安慰他人时，即使是在讨论最近几所学校发生学生死亡的悲痛消息时，我都能感受到帕特里夏平静的接纳，她允许人们以最自然的方式表达悲伤。悲伤没有对错之分，教职工、家长和孩子们都不应该因为如何应对学校里发生的这场危机而受到评判。有些老师可能在教师休息室里寻求慰藉，对着墙壁发呆；有些老师可能在网上搜索关于悲伤的信息。有些社工可能拥抱了家长；有些校长可能在一个下午打了五十个电话。有些孩子写了慰问卡，有些孩子则在打垒球。在帕特里夏看来，每个人都在做他们需要做的事情来表达悲伤，而她则在学校里默默地站在一旁，倾听他们的心声，帮助他们找到能够让他们安心、让他们集中注意力、让他们感觉一切又恢复正常的东西。帕特里夏从事陪伴事工，温柔地给予那些正在与强烈且往往陌生的情绪作斗争的人们全神贯注和无条件的关爱。
“When you give someone your total attention you are creating a bubble of comfort, a little pocket of safety. I call this sacred space. It’s possible to make a bubble of comfort in the midst of a crisis at a school after a student’s death, even in the hallways, just by walking and talking one-on-one with a child and being completely present.
“当你全心全意地关注某人时，你就创造了一个舒适的泡泡，一个安全的港湾。我称之为神圣空间。即使在学校危机之中，比如学生去世后，在走廊里，只要与孩子一对一地交谈，全心全意地陪伴在他们身边，就能创造一个舒适的泡泡。”
“We can serve as comforters by dropping the ‘to do’ lists in our minds, and by following the lead of the person in need. Does that person want to talk or walk or draw or just sit under a tree with you? Does that child or that teacher need to ask you questions, or want you to hear them think out loud, or sit down with them to make a difficult phone call?”
“我们可以放下脑海中的‘待办事项清单’，转而倾听需要帮助的人，以此来安慰他们。那个人是想和你聊天、散步、画画，还是只想和你一起坐在树下？那个孩子或老师是需要问你问题，还是想让你听他们倾诉，或者想让你陪他们一起打一个棘手的电话？”
Although Patricia is a phenomenally productive, busy, and accomplished person, sitting in her presence gave me a sense of serenity that lasted the whole day. She exudes a graceful trust in the natural flow of things, when we don’t force things to work—especially things like emotions. She reminds me we can’t drive our feelings at the same pace as our minds by our agendas, dreams, or even our best intentions. There is comfort in the presence of people like Patricia who always make time to listen to our feelings, and our stories.
尽管帕特里夏是一位效率极高、忙碌而又成就斐然的人，但和她在一起却能让我感到一整天的平静。她优雅地展现出一种对事物自然发展的信任，尤其是在我们不强求事情进展的时候——特别是像情绪这样的事情。她提醒我，我们不能用计划、梦想，甚至是美好的愿望来左右我们的情感，使其与我们的思维同步。像帕特里夏这样总是愿意抽出时间倾听我们感受和故事的人，会给我们带来慰藉。
I ask Patricia about her center’s unique role in providing comfort for entire organizations.
我问帕特里夏，她的中心在为整个组织提供舒适感方面发挥着怎样的独特作用。
“We can comfort an entire organization by comforting people one encounter at a time. Of course, it takes time, but there is a ripple effect, if you just keep showing up, steadily, quietly, in the background, making yourself present for the ones who privately seek you out. Families alone, as well as organizations alone, may not always be able to comfort themselves, when loved ones or coworkers are too busy coping to be readily available to each other. People from the greater community can be brought in to help hold them through the turbulence and loss. Our outreach program at the Center for Grieving Children comforts the caregivers at our schools, businesses, churches, and health care centers when they are too overwhelmed to be the comforters. Caregivers need the comfort first and foremost for themselves, and we can at least alleviate some of the fear and self-judgment they carry for not being comforting enough. By supporting staff this way, reassuring, guiding, and educating them, we strengthen their confidence as comforters.”
“我们可以通过一次次地安慰他人，来抚慰整个组织。当然，这需要时间，但如果你持续不断地、默默地、在幕后默默付出，让那些私下寻求你帮助的人感受到你的存在，就会产生涟漪效应。当亲人或同事忙于应对困境而无暇顾及彼此时，家庭和组织本身可能都难以获得安慰。这时，我们可以引入更广泛的社区力量，帮助他们度过动荡和失落的时期。我们儿童哀伤中心的援助项目旨在安慰学校、企业、教堂和医疗中心的照护者，帮助他们应对那些因不堪重负而无力提供安慰的困境。照护者首先需要的是自身的安慰，而我们至少可以减轻他们因无法给予足够的安慰而产生的恐惧和自我否定。通过这种方式支持员工，给予他们安慰、指导和教育，我们能够增强他们作为安慰者的信心。”
Patricia again returns to the idea of there being a power in our mere presence when we simply make time to be there. “I’ve learned a lot from the quiet, loving presence of my friends, especially after the death of my son. When people have offered their comfort without words, walking with me outdoors, or giving me a hug, or smiling and listening, I can feel their hearts speaking in sacred silence.”
帕特里夏再次强调，当我们抽出时间陪伴他人时，仅仅是存在本身就蕴含着力量。“我从朋友们安静而充满爱意的陪伴中学到了很多，尤其是在我儿子去世之后。当人们默默地给予我安慰，陪我散步，给我一个拥抱，或者微笑倾听时，我能感受到他们内心深处在神圣的静默中交流。”

PATRICIA’S QUALITIES OF A COMFORTING PERSON
帕特里夏令人感到安慰的特质
• Can be totally present
• 可以完全存在
• Trusts and respects the other person’s strength and wisdom
• 信任并尊重对方的力量和智慧
• Has an interest or curiosity in others
• 对他人感兴趣或好奇
• Is able to listen deeply without knowing the answers
• 即使不知道答案，也能认真倾听。
• Is open to knowing there is no single or right way to face loss
• 能够接受面对失去没有唯一或正确方法这一事实
# ↩

PATRICIA’S TIPS FOR COMFORTING CHILDREN

帕特里夏安抚孩子的秘诀

Many of the activities Patricia and her colleagues do in schools where a loss or crisis has occurred could be applicable in any situation where a child needs comforting. Following are the most important suggestions Patricia offers.
帕特里夏和她的同事们在学校里应对儿童离世或危机时开展的许多活动，也适用于任何需要安慰孩子的情况。以下是帕特里夏提出的最重要的建议。

Quietly engage children in doing simple, hands-on activities.
安静地引导孩子们进行简单的动手活动。
According to Patricia, for children and teens dealing with new and strong emotions, doing easy, concrete projects can be grounding and calming. When adults join in the activity, they can gently begin a conversation with a child in a relaxed, casual way.
帕特里夏认为，对于正在经历强烈情绪波动的儿童和青少年来说，做一些简单具体的活动可以帮助他们稳定情绪，平静下来。当成年人参与其中时，他们可以以一种轻松自然的方式与孩子展开对话。
“When I assist with a crisis at a school (often with other staff and trained volunteers), I usually arrange a room with a varied assortment of easy activities. I will just sit quietly doing my hands-on project, and allow the children to engage with their activity, and later, gently ask what they are making with their hands, establishing a conversation. If they are comfortable talking with me, I check in with how they are doing that day.
“当我在学校协助处理危机时（通常会和其他工作人员和受过培训的志愿者一起），我一般会准备一个房间，里面摆放各种各样简单的活动。我会安静地坐在那里做我的动手项目，让孩子们参与到他们的活动中来，之后我会温和地询问他们在做什么，以此开启对话。如果他们愿意和我交谈，我会问问他们当天的情况。”
“If they don’t want to talk about their loss or their concerns, I let them know that it’s fine if they need more time before they are ready to share. I provide opportunities to share thoughts and feelings around a loss or a problem, but that is all I do—offer the opportunities. Sharing is not a requirement for children or adults when they are grieving. I don’t push children to vocalize their feelings or worries, and I remind them we do have a choice and a right to keep our feelings to ourselves if that feels best. We as adults need to respect their privacy as well as each other’s privacy, and value their own timing for finding words for new and strange feelings of grief.”
“如果他们不想谈论失去亲人的痛苦或担忧，我会告诉他们，如果他们需要更多时间才能准备好分享，这完全没问题。我会提供机会让他们分享关于失去亲人或遇到的问题的想法和感受，但我所做的也仅限于此——提供机会。分享并非孩子或成人悲伤时的必要条件。我不会强迫孩子表达他们的感受或担忧，我会提醒他们，如果觉得最好，我们有选择权和权利将自己的感受藏在心里。作为成年人，我们需要尊重他们的隐私，也需要尊重彼此的隐私，并尊重他们自己寻找表达方式来描述这种新的、陌生的悲伤感受的节奏。”

THESE EASY-TO-DO ACTIVITIES HELP CHILDREN FIND CHANNELS FOR TENSION AND DIFFICULT EMOTIONS:
• Writing, drawing, painting, or decorating cards that express support for those affected by the tragedy (i.e., the parents who lost children)
• Coloring or rubber-stamping pages of a scrapbook for photos and writings
• Doing beading projects to make as gifts
• Painting posters or banners to convey our caring thoughts
• Making a collage or a collection of collages, cutting images out of magazines to describe how we care
• Decorating a basket or cardboard box for letters, cards, gifts, or keepsakes
这些简单易行的活动可以帮助孩子找到释放压力和负面情绪的途径：• 写字、画画、涂色或装饰卡片，表达对受悲剧影响的人（例如失去孩子的父母）的支持。• 为剪贴簿页面涂色或盖章，用于粘贴照片和文字。• 制作串珠作品作为礼物。• 绘制海报或横幅，表达我们的关怀。• 制作拼贴画或拼贴画集，从杂志上剪下图片来描述我们的关爱。• 装饰篮子或纸箱，用于存放信件、卡片、礼物或纪念品。
Provide one-on-one time or small group time.
提供一对一辅导时间或小组辅导时间。
Patricia says it helps to find quiet, private times with children to allow for them to offer their thoughts and feelings confidentially, such as when reading a story one-on-one, or taking a walk together outdoors. Children and teens often prefer to be away from other peers or siblings to feel private enough to share what is troubling them.
帕特里夏说，和孩子一起寻找安静的私人时间很有帮助，这样他们就能私下表达自己的想法和感受，比如一对一地讲故事，或者一起户外散步。孩子和青少年通常更喜欢远离同龄人或兄弟姐妹，这样才能感到足够私密，从而倾诉烦恼。
“It’s important to keep offering opportunities to share, as check-in times, and to create routines for these opportunities. This gentle acceptance and caring supports the griever in being patient and honest with themselves while handling confusing and unsettling emotions.”
“重要的是要持续提供分享的机会，比如定期沟通，并建立一些固定的沟通方式。这种温和的接纳和关怀能够帮助悲伤者在处理混乱和不安的情绪时，保持耐心和诚实地面对自己。”
Keep as normal as possible the same daily routines.
尽量保持日常作息不变。
Patricia says routines are comforting for all ages, especially for young children. Whether it’s feeding the goldfish every morning, going to a Sunday matinee, or putting on our slippers after dinner, routines help us step into the present moment and connect with the world around us. Above all, routines help our lives feel normal during times of loss and change.
帕特里夏说，规律的作息对所有年龄段的人都有益处，尤其对年幼的孩子而言。无论是每天早上喂金鱼、周日去看午后电影，还是晚饭后穿上拖鞋，规律的作息都能帮助我们活在当下，与周围的世界建立联系。最重要的是，规律的作息能让我们在经历失去和变故时，依然感到生活如常。

Tell the truth.
说实话。
Children need to know what is happening and have an adult to turn to with their questions.
孩子们需要知道发生了什么事，并且需要有成年人可以向他们提出问题。

Play with them—join in with what they are sharing.
和他们一起玩——加入到他们分享的内容中去。
Children often play out what is concerning them as a way toward understanding what they are facing. Younger children can communicate with dolls, toys, stories, stuffed animals, drawings, or playing games to share what they are feeling and learning about the situation at hand.
孩子们常常通过游戏来表达他们所担忧的事情，以此来理解他们所面临的困境。年幼的孩子可以通过玩偶、玩具、故事、毛绒玩具、绘画或游戏来交流，分享他们的感受，并了解当前的情况。

Patricia’s Advice for Parents Comforting a Child
帕特里夏给父母安慰孩子的建议
Following is a list of Patricia’s suggestions for parents or caregivers who want to help a child or children through a difficult time.
以下是帕特里夏为希望帮助孩子度过难关的父母或监护人提出的一些建议。
1. Snuggle under a special blanket together, when sitting together talking, reading, or watching TV .
1. 一起依偎在一条特别的毯子下，坐着聊天、读书或看电视。
2. Have regular family time.
2. 定期安排家庭时间。
3. Share meals together and tell stories.
3. 一起吃饭，讲故事。
4. Do bedtime stories and prayers together.
4. 一起讲睡前故事和祈祷。
5. Perform little acts of kindness and caring for each other—small things go a long way.
5. 做些小小的善事，互相关心——小事也能产生很大的影响。
6. Go outside to look at the stars and moon together, or just lie on the ground on a blanket and watch the sky (in the daytime watch the forms in the clouds).
6. 到户外一起观赏星星和月亮，或者躺在毯子上观赏天空（白天可以观察云朵的形状）。
7. Act out rituals of remembering, such as lighting candles or sharing memories around the dinner table.
7. 举行纪念仪式，例如点燃蜡烛或在餐桌旁分享回忆。
8. Create sacred space, such as a spot in a garden, a shelf for keepsakes, or a wall for special pictures.
8. 创建神圣空间，例如花园中的一个角落、存放纪念品的架子或用于悬挂特殊照片的墙壁。
