THE MAGIC IN A CONVERSATION

对话中的魔力

Reverend Hal Wallof
哈尔·沃洛夫牧师
Retired Presbyterian Minister
退休长老会牧师
Eastern Virginia
弗吉尼亚州东部
I have within myself a core belief that this world, with all of its possibilities for failure, sickness, and death, is the perfect place to grow our souls.
我内心深处坚信，这个世界虽然充满了失败、疾病和死亡的可能性，但却是滋养我们灵魂的完美场所。
Core Comforting Qualities: Generosity and Warmth
核心舒适品质：慷慨和温暖
Since retiring from his twenty-two-year post as minister of a Presbyterian church in eastern Virginia, Hal Wallof has been what he calls “freelance.” Busier than most “working” people I know, when he isn’t sitting down with soul-searching seminary students, feuding neighbors, troubled colleagues, or compassion-fatigued members of a church, he’s busy volunteering for Meals on Wheels or sitting on a committee for special education in the local schools. Hal also paints spiritually evocative pieces, often with angels as subjects, that have been featured in Richmond galleries and has extensive knowledge of the works of Carl Jung.
自弗吉尼亚州东部一所长老教会担任牧师二十二年后退休，哈尔·沃洛夫便开始了所谓的“自由职业”。他比我认识的大多数“上班族”都要忙碌。除了与那些寻求人生方向的神学院学生、争吵不休的邻居、焦头烂额的同事以及疲惫不堪的教会成员促膝长谈之外，他还忙于为“送餐上门”项目做义工，或参与当地学校的特殊教育委员会工作。哈尔还创作充满灵性的作品，常以天使为主题，这些作品曾在里士满的画廊展出。此外，他对卡尔·荣格的著作也颇有研究。
Over the course of the past fifteen years, Hal and I have met over coffee, hot chocolate, wine, nachos, or sushi, and he has graciously given me his time as a friend, an elder, a colleague, and a fellow “peaceful warrior.” Hal is so warm, spontaneous, and easy to be with that I’ve opened up and expressed things to him that only my cat has heard. And, for every problem I’ve ever presented to him, whether or not the problem was resolved, I’ve always left our conversations feeling better. There is just a certain glow that comes from being in his unconditional presence. Being around Hal, I am reminded that some of the best comforters are our friends. Indeed, says Hal: “I hesitate to call myself a mentor, spiritual director, or counselor—even though I have had training in these areas. I prefer to be known just as a friend. In the context of friendship, I try to awaken the inner seeds of comfort which I believe are within us all. Behind this approach is a belief that we are all created in the Divine Image, and as such, have all that we need within ourselves. This divine inner reality, which includes the seeds of comfort, is accessed when people relate to each other in a mutual exchange of touch, conversation, silence—perhaps over coffee, lunch, or a simple visit in a peaceful place.”
过去十五年间，我和哈尔经常见面，喝咖啡、热巧克力、葡萄酒、吃玉米片或寿司，他总是慷慨地抽出时间陪伴我，既是朋友，又是长辈，又是同事，也是“和平战士”的伙伴。哈尔热情、真诚、平易近人，我甚至会向他敞开心扉，倾诉那些只有我的猫才能听到的秘密。而且，无论我向他倾诉过什么问题，无论问题最终是否得到解决，每次谈话后我都会感觉好多了。他无条件的陪伴总能给人带来一种温暖的光芒。和哈尔在一起，我总会想起，最好的安慰者往往是朋友。哈尔说道：“我不太愿意称自己为导师、灵性导师或咨询师——尽管我接受过这方面的培训。我更愿意被称作朋友。在友谊的语境下，我努力唤醒每个人内心深处的慰藉种子。这种方法的背后，是我相信我们都是按照神的形象创造的，因此，我们自身就拥有所需的一切。这种神圣的内在现实，包括慰藉的种子，可以通过人与人之间的互动来触及——比如在咖啡馆里喝咖啡、吃午餐，或者在宁静的地方简单地拜访。”
Hal’s core qualities of warmth, kindness, and generosity as a pastor were his foundation for building trust and understanding with his congregants. Even as a young man, starting out his post, he inspired, motivated, and guided his congregation with his friendliness and genuine interest in people. But Hal’s story had a surprising twist that drew my attention. During his first year as a pastor, a couple of prominent, long-serving leaders in his congregation who disagreed with his initiatives were threatened by his rising popularity and warm rapport. Hal says:
“These guys had it out for me. They couldn’t wait for me to make a mistake and wanted me to fail. They intimidated me, but I had no idea how to stand up to them. I was not prepared to face these challenges as a pastor, as I had believed pastors were only supposed to act from their comforting qualities. As much as I wanted to emanate an affable and generous presence, I suddenly needed to convey more of a warrior presence, a ‘Don’t mess with me’ presence to protect myself. I had a hard time trying to reconcile my comforting presence with my warrior presence, and I was deeply conflicted for years.”
哈尔牧师的核心品质是热情、善良和慷慨，这些品质是他与会众建立信任和理解的基础。即使在他年轻刚上任之时，他就以友善和对人们的真诚关怀激励、鼓舞和引导着他的会众。但哈尔的故事却有一个出人意料的转折，引起了我的注意。在他担任牧师的第一年，教会里几位德高望重、资历深厚的领袖，由于不认同他的一些做法，开始对他日益增长的人气和亲切友好的关系感到威胁。哈尔说：“这些人跟我过不去。他们巴不得我犯错，想让我失败。他们恐吓我，但我却不知如何应对。作为一名牧师，我根本没做好面对这些挑战的准备，因为我一直认为牧师应该做的只是给人以安慰。尽管我多么想展现出和蔼可亲、慷慨大方的形象，但我突然间却需要展现出一种战士般的气场，一种‘别惹我’的气场来保护自己。我很难调和自己平和的形象和战士般的气场，这种矛盾困扰了我好几年。”
Wondering how other comforters have handled similar situations with difficult persons, I asked Hal how he finally resolved his dilemma.
我想知道其他安慰者是如何处理与难相处的人的类似情况的，于是我问哈尔他最终是如何解决这个难题的。
“My first solution was to hide or suppress my comforting qualities around these adversaries, so they wouldn’t take advantage of me. Guys can comfort their kids and be softhearted at home, but they have to hide this side of themselves at work and in public, more than women do, I believe. But hiding such a vital part of my true nature did not work very well in the long run. Finally I discovered the martial arts, particularly kung fu, and I learned how to ground and center my body and raise the energy (chi) through my body. I became certified in the energy work of Reiki I and II. My two years of intensive training changed my life, convincing me I could be both a comforting presence and a warrior presence at the same time—a kind of peaceful warrior. Now I can be keenly present, soft enough to be attentive and comforting, but also confident and dignified enough to be respected by others.”
“我最初的解决办法是隐藏或压抑自己温柔体贴的一面，以免被对手利用。男人在家可以安抚孩子，展现温柔的一面，但在工作和公共场合，他们却不得不隐藏这一面，我认为比女人更甚。但从长远来看，隐藏如此重要的天性并非良策。最终，我发现了武术，尤其是功夫，并学会了如何扎根大地，集中精神，提升体内的能量（气）。我获得了灵气一级和二级的认证。两年的强化训练改变了我的人生，让我确信自己可以同时拥有抚慰人心的力量和战士的气场——一种平和的战士。现在，我既能敏锐地感知周围的一切，温柔体贴到位，给予他人安慰，又能自信而庄重，赢得他人的尊重。”
Hal can now stand tall and stand his ground without tough words, just by his energized presence. In short, he can speak softly and carry a big presence. “The more I feel conflict heating up with someone, the more I come to my calm center.” He told me about a pivotal moment in which he saw the power of shifting energy away from conflict:
“A wise neighbor of mine was facilitating a meeting for a group of people who were getting tense and defensive over an unpopular topic. Dissension was heating up the room. He couldn’t manage to elicit a better group atmosphere. He sighed and stared hopelessly through the window. Suddenly, as if inspired by the sun streaming through the trees, he suggested the whole group step outside to eat lunch—have a picnic. Somehow this idea clicked, and everyone left the stuffy room to walk and sit down on the lawn to eat sandwiches. The whole mood changed in the group, and people started sharing stories and jokes. Later, they were able to return to their ‘sore subject’ and find a solution.
“I learned from this experience how to be more in the moment, and not so caught up in my intellect trying to solve problems. We are often challenged beyond our know-how and our expertise. Being aware of our surroundings and each other, and tuning in to the little opportunities for comforting that arise, we can be guided by the many nonverbal cues that give us signs for what to do.”
如今，哈尔无需言语就能昂首挺胸，坚定立场，仅凭他充满活力的气场就能做到这一点。简而言之，他说话轻声细语，却气场强大。“我越是感到与他人冲突升级，就越能保持冷静。”他跟我讲了一个关键时刻，他从中体会到了将精力从冲突中转移出去的力量：“我一位睿智的邻居正在主持一个会议，与会者们因为一个不受欢迎的话题而变得紧张而充满防备。争论的气氛让会议室变得异常紧张。他竭尽全力也无法改善大家的氛围。他叹了口气，无奈地望着窗外。突然，仿佛受到阳光透过树叶洒下的启发，他提议大家到外面吃午饭——来一次野餐。不知怎的，这个主意奏效了，大家都离开了闷热的会议室，走到草坪上坐下吃三明治。整个会议的气氛都变了，人们开始分享故事和笑话。之后，他们才得以重新讨论那个‘棘手的问题’，并找到了解决方案。“我从这次经历中学会了如何更好地活在当下，而不是过于沉迷于用我的智力去解决问题。我们常常会遇到超出我们知识和专业能力范围的挑战。”留意周围环境和彼此，并留意那些可以给予安慰的小机会，我们就能从许多非语言线索中获得指引，知道该怎么做。
After undergoing bypass heart surgery years ago and finding his way to a more balanced lifestyle, Hal tells me that he is basically a happy man. He loves the simple joys of life: “Life doesn’t get much better than that first cup of coffee you bring to your wife, or she brings to you, and that morning walk in the woods.”
多年前接受了心脏搭桥手术后，哈尔找到了更加平衡的生活方式。他告诉我，他基本上是个快乐的人。他热爱生活中的简单乐趣：“没有什么比你给妻子端来的第一杯咖啡，或者她给你端来的第一杯咖啡，以及清晨在树林里散步更美好的了。”
Recently I pinned Hal down on exactly why he thinks he’s so content with his life; he laughed and replied, “I’m old enough now that I don’t have to prove myself to anyone anymore. I’m retired—that helps, but mostly, these days, I can sit down with people without having anything to prove.”
最近我追问哈尔，他为什么对自己的生活如此满意；他笑着回答说：“我现在年纪大了，不需要再向任何人证明自己了。我已经退休了——这当然有帮助，但最重要的是，现在我可以和别人坐下来谈天说地，而不用再证明什么了。”
The more I thought about this, the more it sank in that when we are being truly comforting, we aren’t trying to prove anything at all, either to ourselves or others. Comforting has nothing to do with proof. Our comfort comes naturally when our care for someone else is more important than proving anything. And that’s a beautiful relief.
我越想越觉得，真正给予安慰的时候，我们根本不需要向自己或他人证明什么。安慰与证明无关。当我们对他人的关怀胜过任何证明时，安慰便会自然而然地流露出来。这真是一种美好的解脱。
HAL’S MOST IMPORTANT QUALITIES OF A COMFORTING PERSON
哈尔作为令人感到安慰的人最重要的品质
• Can embrace, or at least accept with some compassion, the shadow-side of ourselves
• 能够接纳，或者至少以某种同情心来接受我们自身的阴暗面。
• Can see a human being in front of them, no matter how different from them they may be
• 能够看到眼前的人，无论对方与自己有多么不同
• Can spontaneously give of themselves, and expect nothing in return
• 能自发地付出，不求回报
• Has been through any kind of pain or loss and learned compassion from it
• 曾经历过各种痛苦或失去，并从中学会了同情。
Hal’s Comforting Practices with Others
哈尔安慰他人的方法
HERE ARE HAL’S THREE BEST WAYS TO GET A COMFORTING CONVERSATION STARTED:
以下是哈尔提出的开启轻松愉快对话的三种最佳方法：
• Find the right place and atmosphere.
• The key is, the space needs to feel comforting to the person you are supporting. The right spot makes a big difference in providing a good connection, especially to help start a conversation. Certainly pick a quiet spot, as free from interruptions and distractions as possible. If you are indoors, sitting at a small table or booth with a warm drink and a snack can be comforting. Find a corner, a private nook, a tree, a bench.
• 找到合适的地点和氛围。• 关键在于，这个空间需要让被支持的人感到舒适。合适的地点对于建立良好的联系至关重要，尤其是在开启对话方面。务必选择一个安静的地方，尽可能避免干扰。如果是在室内，坐在小桌子或卡座里，喝杯热饮，吃点小吃，会让人感到舒适。找一个角落、一个私密的角落、一棵树或一条长椅。
• Get started with easy warm-up topics, undemanding, “no brainer” comments (the weather, the sports game on TV last night, good food, the traffic today, how the kids or the dogs are doing, something attractive, like a necklace that the other person has on).
• This may only seem like “small talk,” but most people need a minute or two to transition into the meeting space and settle into it a bit, before “getting down to business.” If the person you are working with is very silent, just following the lead of the person is best, and allowing a moment of quiet.
• 可以先从轻松的热身话题开始，比如一些不费脑筋、无需思考的闲聊（天气、昨晚电视上播的体育比赛、美食、今天的交通状况、孩子或狗狗的近况，或者对方佩戴的项链之类的吸引眼球的东西）。• 这看似只是“闲聊”，但大多数人需要一两分钟的时间来适应会议环境，放松下来，才能真正进入正题。如果对方比较沉默寡言，最好顺其自然，给对方留出一段安静的时光。
• Instead of directly asking, “How are you?” let them know you have been thinking about them and wondering how they are doing. Then you might say, “How has this week been going for you so far?” Or, “How has it been going for you today so far?” Or, “How did the test go last week?”
• It helps to start with a limited time frame or simple frame of reference when asking someone how they are doing. When people are distressed or grieving, having a context that they can grasp easily is usually more comforting.
• 不要直接问“你好吗？”，而是让他们知道你一直在想念他们，想知道他们过得怎么样。你可以说：“这周过得怎么样？”或者，“今天过得怎么样？”或者，“上周的考试考得如何？” • 询问别人近况时，最好从有限的时间范围或简单的参照物入手。当人们感到痛苦或悲伤时，一个他们能够轻松理解的背景通常会让他们感到更安心。
• Avoid probing questions and “why” questions.
• People don’t like to be pinned down, especially when in distress. The freer they feel, the more likely they are to offer information. In the art of comforting, asking a question means inviting conversation and not fact-checking.
• 避免追问和“为什么”之类的问题。• 人们不喜欢被束缚，尤其是在感到痛苦的时候。他们越感到自由，就越愿意提供信息。在安慰他人的艺术中，提问是为了开启对话，而不是为了核实事实。
SUGGESTED COMFORTING ACTIVITIES FOR CAREGIVERS AND FAMILIES
为照护者和家人提供的舒缓活动建议
• Have picnics, or just walk in a park and sit under a tree for a sandwich.
• 可以野餐，或者在公园里散步，在树下坐下吃三明治。
• Tell stories at the dinner table, even if they are not about yourself (movies, TV shows, news items).
• 在餐桌上讲故事，即使这些故事与你自己无关（电影、电视节目、新闻事件）。
• Read poetry and passages from books with each other.
• 一起朗读诗歌和书籍段落。
• Share comics and jokes with each other, and put cutouts of comics on the refrigerator.
• 互相分享漫画和笑话，并将漫画剪报贴在冰箱上。
• Play with your pets together.
• 和你的宠物一起玩耍。
• Make food or drinks especially for each other—comfort food (though this might not always be healthy . . . sometimes a little goes a long way to feeling better).
• 为对方特意准备食物或饮料——安慰食物（虽然这可能并不总是健康的……但有时一点点就能让人感觉好很多）。

哈尔关于如何进行安慰性对话的建议和禁忌

CHAPTER 3
第三章
When People Resist Our Comfort
当人们抗拒我们的舒适感时
# ↩

When Loved Ones Resist Our Comfort

当所爱之人拒绝我们的安慰时

C OMFORT COMES TO US if we can soften a little, open a little, receive a little, but that’s not easy when pain is gripping us. Even when someone offers their time, patience, interest, love, or listening skills, we might hold back. Some grieving people resist completely, perhaps feeling that their vulnerability is just too risky to reveal. Think back to a time when you were going through a hardship of some kind and others approached you to offer comfort. Were you too scared, confused, angry, proud, or overwhelmed to allow yourself the gift of comforting? When we understand our own barriers to receiving comfort, we are better prepared to be patient and accepting when we face the barriers of others.
如果我们能稍微放松一些，敞开一些，接受一些，安慰就会降临到我们身上。但当痛苦攫住我们时，做到这一点并不容易。即使有人愿意付出时间、耐心、关心、爱或倾听，我们也可能有所保留。有些悲伤的人会完全抗拒，或许觉得袒露自己的脆弱太过冒险。回想一下，当你经历某种困境时，如果有人前来安慰你，你是否因为害怕、困惑、愤怒、骄傲或不知所措而无法接受这份安慰的礼物？当我们了解自己接受安慰的障碍时，就能更好地面对他人的障碍，从而更加耐心和包容。
My own personal experience has opened my eyes to how un comfortable we can be about receiving comfort, especially when we are starving for it. Sometimes, the more we need it, the more we hide our need, to the point that when someone offers it freely with no justifications, no agendas, and no keeping tabs, we get scared and suspicious. And it can be just as hard for the comforter to persist past this resistance as it is for the one in pain to open up and receive their comfort. Anxiety, self-doubt, and anger can fester when our gestures of comfort are ignored, questioned, or rejected. What are we doing wrong? We doubt ourselves and worry about what is wrong with us.
我自身的经历让我意识到，我们有时会多么不习惯接受安慰，尤其是在我们极度渴望安慰的时候。有时，我们越需要安慰，就越会隐藏自己的需求，以至于当有人毫无保留、不带任何目的、也不加任何考量地给予安慰时，我们反而会感到害怕和怀疑。而对于安慰者来说，克服这种抵触情绪可能和痛苦的人敞开心扉接受安慰一样困难。当我们表达的安慰被忽视、质疑或拒绝时，焦虑、自我怀疑和愤怒就会滋生蔓延。我们到底做错了什么？我们开始怀疑自己，担忧自己究竟哪里出了问题。
When our attempts at comforting someone we love are rejected, it can be incredibly painful. Nonetheless, it is quite common for persons in distress to view their closest and dearest ones as the very last people they want to comfort them. Too much is at stake. Sometimes it feels safer and easier for them to spend time with less intimate people like new friends, health care providers, coworkers, hairdressers, classmates, church members, or neighbors. They prefer to reach out to someone with whom they don’t feel guilty about burdening, or seek others in support groups with common dilemmas, or relax with easygoing, undemanding old buddies. In the meantime, the loved one trying to offer comfort might begin to feel jealous or rejected that others less close have been chosen to give the tenderness and affection they long to give. What am I doing wrong? they ask themselves.
当我们试图安慰所爱之人却遭到拒绝时，那种痛苦难以言喻。然而，身处困境的人往往会把最亲近的人视为最不愿接受安慰的对象，这其实很常见。因为他们肩负着太多的责任。有时，对他们来说，与关系不那么亲密的人相处会更安全、更容易，比如新朋友、医护人员、同事、理发师、同学、教会成员或邻居。他们更愿意向那些不会让他们感到愧疚的人倾诉，或者加入互助小组寻找有类似困境的人，又或者和随和、不爱提要求的老朋友放松一下。与此同时，试图给予安慰的亲人可能会开始感到嫉妒或被拒绝，因为那些关系不那么亲近的人却得到了他们渴望给予的温柔和关爱。“我到底做错了什么？”他们会这样问自己。
In the caregiver support groups I’ve facilitated, I’ve heard many stories of loved ones being pushed away. One woman in a group, jealous that her husband with leukemia had only confided in his physician, exclaimed with a well-known line, “What am I, chopped liver?” Feeling left out and unappreciated is especially hard for spouses, siblings, and adult children in caregiver roles, because they believe they are supposed to be the primary comforters. But, in the spirit of comforting, we need to be willing to give up our previous roles.
在我主持的照护者互助小组中，我听到了许多亲人被疏远的故事。一位女士在小组里，因为患有白血病的丈夫只向医生倾诉，而感到嫉妒，于是脱口而出一句众所周知的话：“我算什么？一块肉吗？” 对于那些承担照护责任的配偶、兄弟姐妹和成年子女来说，感到被冷落和不被重视尤其难受，因为他们认为自己理应是主要的安慰者。但是，本着安慰他人的精神，我们需要愿意放弃以往的角色。
Grief, in all its forms, surprises and tries us, calls us to think on our feet, listen with our hearts, and go with our guts. We can accept our loved one’s resistance to us when we respectfully support their unique ways of coping, their ways of “holding up.” And once we have, we might find some satisfaction in knowing that we have fostered the courage, hope, and dignity they have needed for their long, difficult journey.
悲伤，无论以何种形式出现，都会让我们措手不及，考验我们，迫使我们随机应变，用心聆听，并跟随内心的指引。当我们尊重并支持他们独特的应对方式，支持他们“支撑”的方式时，我们就能接受他们对我们的抗拒。一旦我们做到了这一点，我们或许会从中获得一些慰藉，因为我们知道，我们已经培养了他们在漫长而艰难的旅程中所需要的勇气、希望和尊严。
# ↩

Facilitating the Comfort of Others

为他人带来舒适感

When we, as loved ones, are deliberately kept out of a comforting role by the person in distress, we can still facilitate care and comfort by letting go of our need to provide more immediate comfort and helping in other, more resourceful ways. We can still be a vital, supportive presence without expecting our loved one to be receptive to our gestures of comfort and, in doing so, lessen the pressure on them. When we “back off” a bit, we are really upholding their freedom, integrity, and privacy.
当我们作为亲人，被身处困境的人刻意排除在安慰的角色之外时，我们仍然可以通过放下急于提供即时安慰的念头，转而以其他更有效的方式提供帮助，从而继续给予他们关怀和慰藉。我们依然可以成为他们重要的支持者，而无需期待他们接受我们的安慰，这样做也能减轻他们的压力。当我们稍稍“退后一步”时，实际上是在维护他们的自由、尊严和隐私。
Support , according to the Oxford Dictionary , means to “bear the weight of.” In our supporting roles, as facilitators, we can help to bear the weight of our loved one’s distress, by serving to sustain a comforting environment and contributing to related activities and resources.
根据牛津词典，“支持”一词意味着“承担……的重量”。作为支持者和帮助者，我们可以通过营造舒适的环境、参与相关活动和利用相关资源，帮助我们所爱的人减轻痛苦的负担。
Being facilitators of comfort involves serving in a supportive role, sometimes in the background. We can be supportive in a wide variety of ways, such as organizing enjoyable activities, coordinating services, assisting in chores, and enhancing comforting environments.
营造舒适环境意味着扮演支持性的角色，有时是在幕后默默付出。我们可以通过多种方式提供支持，例如组织有趣的活动、协调各项服务、协助处理家务以及营造舒适的环境。
My friend Morna, for example, served as a facilitator of comfort in the first few days of our visit when I was grieving after my divorce. Before I was ready to open up and talk soulfully with her, she followed my lead and supported me in activities I initiated, in pastimes and interests that felt “safe” for me. At times, she gently offered opportunities for talking more intimately, but was willing to accept my refusals and didn’t take my resistance personally.
例如，我的朋友莫娜在我离婚后悲痛欲绝的最初几天里，给予了我莫娜莫大的安慰。在我还没准备好敞开心扉和她促膝长谈之前，她顺从我的意愿，支持我参与我主动发起的活动，以及那些让我感到“安全”的爱好和兴趣。有时，她会温和地提出一些可以更深入交流的机会，但她也愿意接受我的拒绝，并且不会把我的抵触情绪放在心上。
Serving as a facilitator of comfort also means accommodating someone else to be a comforter in a favorite activity with the person in distress. A particular companion, volunteer, or family member might be preferred for walking the dog, a game of cards, gardening, going to the movies, giving a foot massage.
提供安慰也意味着安排其他人陪伴处于困境中的人参与他们喜欢的活动，从而起到安慰作用。例如，可以请特定的朋友、志愿者或家人陪同遛狗、玩牌、园艺、看电影或进行足底按摩。
If we cannot serve as comforters ourselves, we can graciously facilitate comfort in keeping with our loved one’s interests. In the ever-changing and delicate art of comforting, we can take turns with each other. It helps not to be attached to our roles, our egos, our sense of importance, and step openly and unassumingly into the present moment.
如果我们自己无法给予安慰，我们可以体贴地、以对方的意愿来营造舒适感。在安慰这门瞬息万变、微妙而又充满挑战的艺术中，我们可以轮流给予。重要的是放下对角色、自我和重要性的执着，坦诚而谦逊地融入当下。
Many caregivers and loved ones find themselves playing both of these vital roles, alternating frequently, but always dedicated to the mission of comforting.
许多照顾者和亲人发现自己扮演着这两个至关重要的角色，经常交替出现，但始终致力于安慰他人。
# ↩

When Colleagues Resist Our Comfort

当同事们不愿让我们感到舒适时

Offering comfort in the workplace is highly important, but it can be a delicate process for many of us. We might feel especially awkward when reaching out to people who are not as close to us, as we are not as familiar with their ways of coping with grief or stress. Also, in professional settings where our livelihoods and reputations are carefully upheld, we tend to be more guarded and scrupulous about how we approach our colleagues or others in our community.
在职场中给予安慰至关重要，但对许多人来说，这可能是一个微妙的过程。当我们向不太亲近的人表达慰问时，可能会感到格外尴尬，因为我们不太了解他们应对悲伤或压力的方式。此外，在职业环境中，我们的生计和声誉都至关重要，因此我们往往会更加谨慎小心地对待同事或社区中的其他人。
Recently, a few of my coworkers and clients have lost loved ones, all within a few months. I have attended funerals, written sympathy cards, sent flowers, handed out chocolates, dropped off baskets of little gifts, given hugs, and shared heartfelt remembrances at memorial services. Yet after doing these seemingly appropriate tasks, and going “by the book” with the etiquette of condolence, I admit that I have absolutely no clue how well some of these offerings have been actually received. The art of comforting is even more of a mystery when we are serving people we don’t know well, and I still struggle spiritually to allow and accept the mysterious ways our comfort comes around and goes around.
最近，我的几位同事和客户在短短几个月内相继失去了亲人。我参加了葬礼，写了慰问卡，送了鲜花，分发了巧克力，送去了装满小礼物的篮子，拥抱了他们，并在追悼会上分享了真挚的回忆。然而，在做了这些看似恰当的事情，并“按部就班”地遵循了吊唁的礼仪之后，我不得不承认，我完全不知道这些举动是否真的被接受。当我们服务于不太熟悉的人时，安慰的艺术就更加神秘莫测了，我仍在努力从精神层面去接受和理解这种安慰传递的神秘方式。
Likewise, many of my friends and colleagues, as well as dozens of participants in support groups have lamented how hard it is to ever “know for sure” if what they did to comfort their peers really helped or not. And sometimes, unfortunately, we stumble upon situations where a coworker flat-out refuses our comfort. One support group participant shared how embarrassed she felt after giving a hug to a coworker who had just returned to work after a month-long bereavement leave.
同样，我的许多朋友和同事，以及数十位互助小组的成员都感叹，他们很难“确定”自己安慰同事的行为是否真的有效。有时，不幸的是，我们会遇到同事断然拒绝我们安慰的情况。一位互助小组的成员分享了她拥抱一位刚刚结束一个月丧假返回工作岗位的同事后，感到多么尴尬。
“Sandra had seemed to be a ‘huggy’ type to me, as I had watched her share hugs with many coworkers over the years. I was there the day she got the phone call about the death of her sister from a car accident, and saw her hurry out of the building. When she came back to our office after being gone for a month, I welcomed her back and reached out to give her a big hug. She was absolutely frozen, and barely moved her arms when I held her. I was so embarrassed that I actually blushed, and quickly excused myself. I could hardly look her in the eyes, and she avoided looking at me. I felt so shocked at her response to my hug that I had to run out to my car in the parking lot to have a good little cry. I was especially surprised at myself for feeling so ridiculous and awkward. It took me a while to compose myself before I returned to my desk to work near Sandra. I respectfully allowed her some privacy, yet I felt so powerless.”
“在我看来，桑德拉一直是个喜欢拥抱的人，这些年来，我经常看到她和同事们拥抱。那天，她接到电话，得知妹妹因车祸去世，我就在现场，看到她匆匆跑出大楼。一个月后，她回到办公室，我热情地迎接她，并伸手想给她一个大大的拥抱。她却僵住了，我抱她的时候，她几乎一动不动。我尴尬得脸都红了，赶紧找了个借口离开。我几乎不敢直视她的眼睛，她也刻意避开我的目光。她对我的拥抱的反应让我震惊不已，我跑到停车场，躲到车里痛哭了一场。我尤其惊讶于自己当时的反应如此荒唐尴尬。我缓了好一会儿才平静下来，回到办公桌前，在桑德拉旁边工作。我尊重地给她留了一些私人空间，但我却感到无能为力。”
Similar scenarios have haunted many of us, when we might have missed the cues of the person we tried to console, or blurted out a gaffe in front of our coworkers. And when, indeed, someone did resist our offer of comfort, we blamed ourselves for not doing the right thing. But it’s heartening to remind ourselves that these very messy, difficult encounters of trying to comfort others can sometimes present an opportunity for a breakthrough, resulting in more closeness and trust. In the art of comforting, we need to allow for surprises and hidden blessings.
类似的场景或许困扰着我们许多人：我们可能错过了想要安慰的人的暗示，或者在同事面前脱口而出一些不恰当的话。而当对方真的拒绝了我们的安慰时，我们往往会自责自己做得不够好。但令人欣慰的是，我们要记住，这些看似混乱、艰难的安慰他人的经历，有时反而会带来突破的契机，增进彼此的亲密和信任。在安慰他人的艺术中，我们需要允许惊喜和意想不到的美好出现。
Back to the story about Sandra: Fortunately, weeks later, Sandra bravely sent her embarrassed coworker a lovely card thanking her for giving her a hug at a “terrible time” for her. From what I’ve heard since, these two coworkers still share a cubicle three years later and feel closer to each other out of this experience.
回到桑德拉的故事：幸运的是，几周后，桑德拉勇敢地给那位尴尬的同事寄了一张温馨的卡片，感谢她在自己“最难熬的时候”给了她一个拥抱。据我后来了解，三年过去了，这两位同事仍然共用一个办公隔间，而且因为这段经历，她们的关系更加亲密了。
Based on what I’ve learned from employment assistance professionals (EAPs), human resources professionals, counseling colleagues, support group participants, and my own personal encounters, I can suggest a few thoughts to keep in mind when we face someone who resists our comfort at work.
根据我从就业援助专业人员 (EAP)、人力资源专业人员、咨询同事、支持小组参与者以及我自己的个人经历中学到的知识，我可以提出一些建议，当我们在工作中遇到阻碍我们感到舒适的人时，请记住这些建议。

Accept and allow the person in distress to respond in their own unique way, even if they don’t appear to acknowledge your offer of comfort.
即使对方似乎没有回应你的安慰，也要接受并允许处于困境中的人以他们独特的方式做出反应。
It’s common for employees returning to work after a loss to brace themselves, and be on guard against revealing any lack of professionalism or lack of focus, especially when they need to concentrate on their work duties and get back up to speed. (And let’s face it: In this economy, they might be afraid of losing their job if they appear less than proficient after being on leave for a while.) Also, they may be numb and drained from undergoing surges of strong emotions in private, and are not able to express themselves openly. It might be difficult for them to return displays of affection, show appreciation, or engage in conversation. And keep in mind that the coworker might not appear to be functioning in their previous, “normal” ways, as grieving people often struggle with memory, attention, and a lack of energy, motivation, and confidence.
员工在经历丧亲之痛后重返工作岗位时，通常会做好心理准备，时刻警惕自己是否表现出任何不专业或注意力不集中，尤其是在需要集中精力履行工作职责并尽快恢复工作状态的时候。（而且说实话，在如今的经济形势下，他们可能会担心休假一段时间后，如果表现得不够熟练，就会丢掉工作。）此外，他们可能因为独自承受强烈的情绪波动而感到麻木和疲惫，无法坦诚地表达自己的感受。他们可能难以回应他人的关爱、表达感激之情或进行正常的交谈。请记住，这位同事可能看起来不像以前那样“正常”，因为悲伤的人往往会出现记忆力下降、注意力不集中、精力不足、缺乏动力和自信心等问题。
It helps to pause and remember the coworkers or classmates who have accepted and supported you over the years, when you were going through your own rough patches in your life. What did these comforters at work or at school do to help you? Reflecting on this is one way we can consider how we can support and compassionately accept the grieving or distressed people returning to our workplaces after a great loss.
停下来，想想那些在你人生低谷时接纳和支持你的同事或同学，或许会有所帮助。这些在工作或学校里给予你安慰的人，究竟做了些什么？反思这些，或许能让我们思考，如何支持和体谅那些在经历重大损失后重返工作岗位的悲痛或痛苦的人们。

Even if your first offer of comfort is refused or ignored, don’t assume this is a final, permanent statement or verdict about your relationship with that coworker.
即使你第一次提出的安慰被拒绝或忽视，也不要认为这是对你与那位同事关系的最终、永久性的表态或结论。
It’s important to keep the lines of communication open, by being patient, unassuming, and flexible, and occasionally offering small, reassuring gestures that you are thinking about that person. You might send a “Thinking of you” card a few months later. But, once again, give this freely with no expectations.
保持沟通渠道畅通很重要，这需要耐心、谦逊和灵活，偶尔做出一些小小的、令人安心的举动，让对方知道你在想念他们。几个月后，你可以寄一张“想念你”的卡片。但再次强调，这样做是出于自愿，不要抱有任何期待。

Avoid personalizing the experience of having your comfort refused or ignored.
避免将你的舒适感被拒绝或忽视的体验个人化。
Step back and observe the needs of that person at this time, and try to learn from your experience, being as nonjudgmental with yourself as possible.
退后一步，观察这个人此刻的需求，并尝试从你的经验中学习，尽可能地对自己不加评判。

Increase your knowledge of the experience of grief, or about the issues the coworker is facing.
增进你对悲伤经历的了解，或者了解你的同事正在面临的问题。
The more you learn about the grief process, trauma, or serious illnesses, the more you can examine your difficult experience with that coworker from a wider perspective, and develop compassion and understanding.
你对悲伤过程、创伤或重病了解得越多，就越能从更广阔的视角审视你与那位同事的艰难经历，并培养同情心和理解力。

Join in activities with other coworkers who are doing things to comfort the person in distress.
与其他同事一起参与安慰受难者的活动。
You can add to what others are doing to reach out to the coworker, such as writing with others in a sympathy card, placing your homemade banana bread in a gift basket, or putting a picture into a thoughtful scrapbook the team is making. Sometimes opportunities to offer comfort as a group arise spontaneously and casually, when coworkers get together for lunch or coffee.
你可以加入其他人的行列，共同表达对同事的关怀，例如一起写慰问卡、把自制的香蕉面包放在礼物篮里，或者把照片贴到团队正在制作的精美剪贴簿上。有时候，当同事们聚在一起吃午餐或喝咖啡时，就会自然而然地出现集体安慰的机会。

Find friends and confidants outside of work to share your feelings of disappointment, anxiety, or powerlessness if the situation with a coworker in distress continues to upset you.
如果同事的困境持续让你感到沮丧、焦虑或无力，可以找工作以外的朋友和知己倾诉你的感受。
Some workplaces also provide EAPs , organized by human resources staff.
有些工作场所还提供员工援助计划 (EAP)，由人力资源部门人员组织。

Learn more about what your workplace can do to support employees in distress or grief, or inform yourself about what other workplaces have done that works well.
了解您的工作场所可以采取哪些措施来支持处于困境或悲伤中的员工，或者了解其他工作场所采取了哪些行之有效的措施。
Following are some common, comforting practices and policies that many workplaces support:
• Giving coworkers and supervisors time off to attend funerals and memorial services
• Sending sympathy cards and flowers as a group or as individuals
• Providing food, food baskets, care boxes, or care baskets
• Offering thoughtful gifts or collecting cash
• Helping the employee by providing flexible hours or reduced workloads
• Assisting with transportation and other arrangements
• Making phone calls on behalf of the employee (with their permission)
• Providing time off and family and bereavement leave
• Providing opportunities for supportive listening, acknowledging the loss, and offering condolence from coworkers and supervisors
• Providing EAPs to counsel employees who are affected by the loss (usually organized by human resources managers)
以下是一些常见的、令人感到慰藉的做法和政策，许多工作场所都支持这些做法和政策：• 允许同事和主管请假参加葬礼和追悼会；• 以集体或个人名义送上慰问卡和鲜花；• 提供食物、食品篮、关怀盒或关怀篮；• 赠送贴心礼物或收取现金；• 通过提供灵活的工作时间或减少工作量来帮助员工；• 协助安排交通和其他事宜；• （经员工同意）代表员工拨打电话；• 提供休假、家庭假和丧假；• 提供机会让同事和主管倾听、理解并慰问员工的损失；• 提供员工援助计划 (EAP)，为受损失影响的员工提供咨询服务（通常由人力资源经理组织）。
As much as we’d love for all of our efforts at comforting to be instantly appreciated, it is often not possible for people going through extreme pain to anticipate our feelings as sensitively as we might hope. Therefore, it is best that the gift of comfort be given freely, with no expectation of receiving anything in return.
我们当然希望自己所有的安慰之举都能立刻得到回应，但身处剧痛之中的人往往无法像我们希望的那样敏锐地察觉我们的感受。因此，最好的做法是无私地给予安慰，不求任何回报。
# ↩

PART TWO
第二部分
The Words of Comforting
安慰的话语
# ↩

CHAPTER 4
第四章
Speaking Words of Comfort
说些安慰的话语
F OR MANY OF US, the most difficult way to offer comfort is face-to-face—just sitting quietly and talking with someone in distress. In these intimate moments, we can get so hung up on trying to use the “right” words that we lose track of what it is we really want to say. But why is it so hard to administer this most vital form of comfort?
对我们许多人来说，最难的安慰方式莫过于面对面——只是静静地坐着，与身处困境的人交谈。在这些私密的时刻，我们往往会过于执着于寻找“正确”的措辞，以至于忘记了自己真正想表达什么。但为什么给予这种至关重要的安慰如此艰难呢？
# ↩

The Challenge to Comforting Language: A Hard World to Be Soft In

对安慰性语言的挑战：在一个艰难的世界里保持温柔

In this fast-paced world, it can be difficult to slow down and just “be there” for someone who needs us. We are so accustomed to all the “breaking news” about this “situation” or the other that stream constantly on cable television and on the Internet that our ability to comfort the people right there next to us can become compromised. Has all this instant communication decreased our patience and thoughtfulness for listening to grieving people who just can’t seem to “get to the point” fast enough? Unfortunately, patience, one of the important qualities involved in comforting, is being tested across the globe. Yet it is patience that we need now more than ever.
在这个快节奏的世界里，放慢脚步，静静地陪伴需要我们的人，有时真的很难。我们早已习惯了电视和网络上铺天盖地的“突发新闻”，以至于我们安慰身边人的能力都受到了影响。这种即时通讯是否降低了我们的耐心和同理心，让我们难以倾听那些急于表达自己想法的悲伤者？不幸的是，耐心——安慰他人的重要品质之一——正在全球范围内经受着考验。然而，我们比以往任何时候都更需要耐心。
It’s not easy to find good role models for comforting conversation in our media. You just don’t see a lot of comforters on television or hear them on the radio. Comforters are too compassionate to spar with the in-your-face people who appear on reality shows, and too unassuming to be on contests like American Idol or The Apprentice . And they are certainly not cut out to go one-on-one with those experts on “news” shows who point their fingers at us demanding that we “get over” our problems—who claim they “share our pain” but with a twinkle in their eye that hints at their disdain for our credit card debt, our joblessness, or our insomnia. No, if we want to learn how to inspire truly healing conversations, better that we train ourselves to tune out all this noise and listen to our hearts. This said, I believe that we can slow down a little when necessary to offer comforting words to those around us, and still make money, meet our bottom lines, stay with our itineraries, and keep on our schedules. The world won’t come to a grinding halt just because we care enough to speak a more empathic language—even to ourselves.
在当今媒体中，找到善于抚慰人心的对话榜样并不容易。电视上很少见到这样的人，广播里也听不到他们的声音。善于抚慰人心的人太过富有同情心，无法与真人秀节目中那些咄咄逼人的人针锋相对；他们也太过谦逊，不会参加《美国偶像》或《学徒》之类的选秀节目。他们当然也不适合与那些“新闻”节目中的专家一对一交流，这些专家指责我们，要求我们“克服”自己的问题——他们声称“感同身受”，但眼神中却闪烁着对我们的信用卡债务、失业或失眠的鄙夷。不，如果我们想学习如何激发真正具有疗愈作用的对话，最好是训练自己屏蔽所有这些噪音，倾听内心的声音。话虽如此，我相信，在必要时，我们可以放慢脚步，对身边的人说些安慰的话，同时仍然可以赚钱，完成目标，按计划行事，按时完成工作。即使我们足够关心他人，愿意用更富同理心的语言——哪怕是对自己说——世界也不会因此而停滞不前。
# ↩

What to Say and What Not to Say

该说什么，不该说什么

As mentioned, many of us find that when we are face-to-face with someone who needs our love and support, we forget what it is exactly we want to express. It can be helpful to sit down in advance of your meeting to explore the key, meta message or messages you wish to communicate. Here are a few examples:
• I’m there for you. I’m available. I care.
• I’m listening. I’m following you. I’m with you.
• I’m interested in what you’re telling me, and I’m willing to learn more from you about what you are going through.
• I’m feeling some of what you’re feeling (sorrow, frustration), even if I personally have not been through what you’ve been through.
• I’m open, receptive, and I’m not going to judge you. I’m a “safe” person you can trust.
• I’d like to offer my assistance and my support with something specific.
• I would like to stay connected with you, beyond our meeting today.
正如前面提到的，我们很多人都发现，当我们面对需要我们关爱和支持的人时，往往会忘记自己究竟想表达什么。因此，在见面之前坐下来，仔细思考你想传达的关键信息或核心信息，会很有帮助。以下是一些例子：• 我会支持你。我随时都在。我很关心你。• 我在倾听。我关注你。我与你同在。• 我对你所说的话很感兴趣，也愿意更多地了解你的经历。• 我能感受到你的一些感受（悲伤、沮丧），即使我个人没有经历过你所经历的一切。• 我持开放、包容的态度，不会评判你。我是一个你可以信任的“安全”之人。• 我想在某个具体的事情上提供帮助和支持。• 我希望在今天的见面之后，也能与你保持联系。
These statements, or similar ones, express our desire to truly “be there” for the one in pain and, as such, are quite different from the words many of us default to when we’re nervous or unsure of ourselves. When we feel uncertain about what to say, we tend to “default” to platitudes—the comments and sayings we’ve heard over the years from others—rather than speak in our own words and from our hearts.
这些话语，或者类似的话语，表达了我们真心实意想要陪伴在痛苦中的人身边，因此，它们与我们许多人在紧张或不自信时脱口而出的话语截然不同。当我们不知该说什么时，我们往往会“默认”说出一些陈词滥调——那些我们多年来从别人那里听到的话语和格言——而不是用自己的语言，发自内心地表达。
Beware of platitudes! Our words can distance us from others, especially if they express that we think we know “what is best” for them. Devastated people in the first weeks and months of a loss or trauma can feel unheard, invalidated, or “preached at” by well-intended teachings and words of wisdom. Just listening and responding genuinely to what the person is saying is much, much more helpful.
谨防陈词滥调！我们的话语可能会疏远他人，尤其当我们自以为知道“什么对他们最好”时。在经历失去亲人或创伤的最初几周甚至几个月里，那些饱受打击的人可能会觉得被忽视、被否定，或者被那些出于好意的教诲和人生格言“说教”。其实，真诚地倾听并回应对方的话语，远比这些更有帮助。
Think back and remember the comments others may have said to you when they were reaching out to offer you reassurance or comfort. Did they or do they now strike you as insensitive or dismissive? Take note of these words and try to avoid them.
回想一下，当别人试图安慰或鼓励你时，他们可能说过哪些话。这些话当时让你觉得冷漠或轻蔑吗？记下这些话，并尽量避免使用。
Over the past sixteen years as a support group facilitator many of the bereaved, traumatized, or gravely ill people I served have shared with me some of the statements others have made to them in their attempts to offer comfort as well as their “backfiring” effects. It’s amazing when you think about it just how common these platitudes are. Following is a list of these common platitudes and suggestions for more helpful things to say to someone in need of your love and support.
过去十六年来，作为一名互助小组的组织者，我服务过的许多失去亲人、遭受创伤或身患重病的人都曾向我倾诉过别人试图安慰他们时说的一些话，以及这些话适得其反的效果。仔细想想，这些老生常谈的话语竟然如此常见，真是令人惊讶。以下列举了一些常见的老生常谈，并提出了一些建议，希望能帮助你更好地安慰那些需要关爱和支持的人。
“Be Strong” Platitudes
“坚强起来”之类的陈词滥调
“Be Positive” Platitudes
“保持积极”的陈词滥调
“Be Faithful” Platitudes
“忠诚”的陈词滥调
New Age Platitudes
新时代陈词滥调
“Get Over It” Platitudes
“别再纠结了”的陈词滥调
Other Helpful and Less Helpful Statements
其他有帮助和不太有帮助的陈述
“I Understand” Comments
“我明白了”评论
Comparison Comments
对比评论
“Some Have It Harder”
“有些人处境更艰难”
“We All Go Through It” Comments
“我们都经历过”评论
“You Can Always Get a New One” Comments
“你总能买到新的”评论
“Call Me When You Need Me” Comments
“需要我的时候给我打电话”评论
“You Already Said That” Comments
“你已经说过这话了”评论
“You Need to” Comments (Or “ought to” or “should”)
“你需要”评论（或“应该”或“应当”）
Asking “Why” Questions
提出“为什么”的问题
# ↩

Beginning the Conversation

开启对话

Often when we visit someone who is going through a terrible time it can be difficult to encourage them to share with us what they are thinking and how they are feeling. Sometimes just sitting with them quietly is what is needed. Other times, you may sense that they want to talk. Here are a few suggestions for beginning a healing conversation with someone who might be ready to engage with you:
• Verbal invitations to comforting:
“I’m wondering . . .”
“It sounds like . . .”
“How have the . . . (lab tests, job interviews, dates with Jen) been going lately?”
“What’s been happening with the . . . ?”
“I can only imagine how hard it is . . .” (Instead of saying, “I understand.”)
“What’s been helping you get by these days?”
“Do you feel like talking about it today?”
当我们探望那些正经历人生低谷的人时，常常很难鼓励他们敞开心扉，分享自己的想法和感受。有时，静静地陪伴他们就足够了。而有时，你或许会感觉到他们渴望倾诉。以下是一些建议，帮助你与那些可能愿意与你交流的人开启一段疗愈性的对话：• 用言语表达安慰：“我在想……” “听起来……” “最近……（化验结果、工作面试、和Jen的约会）怎么样？” “……那边发生了什么事？” “我能想象到这有多难熬……”（而不是说“我明白。”） “最近是什么让你感觉好一些？” “你今天想聊聊吗？”
Once you have initiated the conversation, it is important to let it run its course naturally—don’t force it. Take a look at the following list of common errors we comforters tend to make that halt the conversation when this is precisely what we don’t want to do.
一旦你开启了对话，重要的是让它自然发展——不要强求。看看下面列出的这些我们这些安慰者常犯的错误，这些错误往往会扼杀对话，而这恰恰是我们最不想看到的。
• Verbal barriers to comforting:
Giving advice
Interrupting long silences
Changing the subject
Asking probing, “why” questions
Asking too many questions
Asking only yes or no questions
Preaching, lecturing, pep talks
Overinterpreting
Talking too much about yourself and your own “similar” experiences
Talking too fast
Talking too loud or too high-pitched
Telling the person that they are repeating themselves
Telling the person they don’t need to explain something to you that you already know a lot about
Sounding clinical, technical, authoritative, smarter, or just plain bored
• 安慰他人的语言障碍：提供建议、打断长时间的沉默、转移话题、追问“为什么”、问太多问题、只问是非题、说教、训诫、鼓励、过度解读、过多谈论自己和自己“类似”的经历、语速过快、声音过大或音调过高、指出对方重复、告诉对方你很了解的事情不需要解释、语气生硬、技术化、权威化、自以为是，或者只是单纯地感到无聊
Hopefully, having looked over the contrasts between these less helpful and more helpful phrases and common barriers to conversation, we can clarify our own messages as comforters. Yet we need to keep in mind that our communication is essentially 80 percent nonverbal—our tone of voice and the expression in our eyes can say a lot more than any words we speak. Just the way we look at someone, beholding them with our gaze, speaks volumes about how much we care. Following are some ideas for sending nonverbal signals that will indicate to the person in distress that you truly care.
希望通过对比这些不太有效和更有效的表达方式以及常见的沟通障碍，我们能够更清晰地表达安慰之意。然而，我们需要记住，沟通中80%的内容是非语言的——我们的语气和眼神远比我们说的任何话都更有说服力。我们注视他人的方式，用目光倾听，就能充分表达我们的关心。以下是一些传递非语言信号的方法，可以帮助那些身处困境的人感受到你的真切关怀。
• Nonverbal invitations to comforting:
Eye contact at the same eye level
An occasional gentle smile
Softly nodding the head at times
Gently showing interest and caring
Shoulders down
Arms unfolded but comfortable and relaxed
Listening for long stretches of the person’s story without interrupting
Being seated comfortably, tuned in, but not reclining
Sometimes leaning forward slightly
• 非语言安慰方式：与对方保持视线水平的眼神交流；偶尔露出温柔的微笑；轻轻点头；温和地表达兴趣和关怀；肩膀下垂；双臂自然垂放，保持舒适放松；长时间倾听对方讲述，不打断；坐姿舒适，专注聆听，但不要后仰；有时身体略微前倾。
If genuine, it’s sometimes helpful to empathically reflect back to the person a gesture they made, such as shaking our head in disbelief with their disbelief, or a shrug of our shoulders as they shrug, or sighing with them when feeling the depth of their grief. (But if this is not coming honestly from us, these mirrored gestures will look awkward.)
如果真心实意，有时可以感同身受地回应对方的举动，比如和他们一样摇头表示难以置信，或者和他们一样耸肩，或者和他们一起叹息，体会他们的悲痛之深。（但如果我们并非发自内心，这些模仿的举动就会显得很尴尬。）
• Nonverbal barriers to comforting:
Taking notes (sometimes in a professional setting this may be necessary but still try as much as possible to maintain eye contact)
Watching the clock or looking at your watch
Doodling
Not turning off your cell phone
Answering your cell phone or texting
Looking distracted—looking down, looking up, looking around . . .
Looking for something while the person is talking
Rigid posture, shoulders up, and too tense
Eyes not at the same level as the person in distress
Arms folded
Hands on hips
Sunglasses on (move to a shaded place)
Fidgeting or rocking
Playing with your hair
• 非语言安慰障碍：做笔记（有时在专业场合这可能是必要的，但仍应尽可能保持眼神交流）；看钟或看手表；涂鸦；不关手机；接听手机或发短信；心不在焉——低头、抬头、环顾四周……在对方说话时寻找东西；姿势僵硬，耸肩，过于紧张；眼睛与处于困境中的人不在同一水平线上；双臂交叉；双手叉腰；戴着太阳镜（移到阴凉处）；坐立不安或摇晃身体；玩弄头发
The language of comforting is a language like any other—it can be learned but, once mastered, can become as effortless as breathing. And if our words and gestures are warm, empathic, and respectful, they will help to create a safe space for the comforter and the one being comforted to inhabit.
安慰的语言和其他语言一样——可以学习，一旦掌握，就能像呼吸一样自然流畅。如果我们言语和举止温暖、充满同理心且尊重他人，就能为安慰者和被安慰者创造一个安全舒适的空间。
